text: University of Minnesota advises clear plastic for real solarization. They're way up north. Hard to understand how black plastic could do much of any real solarization, as in soil heating. Keeping the sunlight away from the soil doesn't heat soil. Their web page makes it clear that black plastic is more useful for occultation, which is just to block light from weeds.  So if this is about weeds, take your pick - black versus clear. Two ways to kill them. If it's about killing fungi and borers, clear is the only hope. But I suspect it's a poor way to do it. Borer coccons can be six inches deep, and solarization heating won't ever reach them. I guess if you don't turn over the soil after solarization, it might be an effective preventative for fungal infection, by killing fungal spores on the surface. https://extension.umn.edu/planting-and-growing-guides/solarization-occultation

My experience is squash vine borers are going to find your squash.  The adults are flying moths.  If you killed any that wintered over in your beds, another moth will fly in and lay an egg.  They lay one egg, unlike squash bugs, so they are hard to see.  Some people wrap their stems (just the part closest to the ground) to prevent the borers.  Others just check.  You can use a skewer in the hole.  There's almost aways only one grub and the stem can heal. I have nothing against solarizing, it might work for you.  However, I would suggest you figure out what the disease is, refrain from growing cucurbit for a year or 3 and then get varieties resistant to the disease.  Watch out for plants just labeled "disease resistant."  It might be resistant to all sorts of diseases you've never been plagued with and not resistant to the one that you suffer from. Cucumber, Squash, Melon & Other Cucurbit Diseases | Home & Garden Information Center

text: Something you need to be aware of, if you cover the base and trunks of the trees, this will lead to them slowly dying. You should never put soil above the 'heel' of the tree, it's not good for them as it will cause rot. If you can cut up a large pot that fits around the tree leaving an air gap between the trunk and the pot this will help.

You need to show the entrance. Do you have a foyer? Does front door open right into the living room? Please provide measurements. See below for how to post. Layout precedes decor and color choices. You have a very small space. Keep the beige/ivory wall color so all the spaces flow together and make it seem bigger. As others have said, a sectional is going to swallow the room. You don't mention which direction the short side of the sectional is, so that will dictate which wall on which to place the long side. You don't mention if this is where you'll watch TV. You don't mention of front door opens into living room. If possible, fit the long side under the window and short side on the right, that would allow more space to enter the room. But we don't know how big your sectional is. Otherwise, you have to put long side on long wall, which means you run right into it coming into the room. Notice in this living room that curtains blend into wall color. Very little is on the floor. Good use is made of the walls to draw the eye upward.  Decor: Keep wall color the same as it goes with the floor and connects to other spaces, which makes them an extension of the living room, therefore seeing larger. Get white ceiling to floor light curtains, either white or same as wall color and wood colored rattan shades. Get your green in sofa pillows, art, rug. Accents should be wood or rattan--natural organic looking.      Here is how to post a Design Dilemma to get the best results. You need to show the whole space—all four sides of an entire space—even if it’s about one specific Dilemma. A layout fix is often a Design Dilemma fix even if it doesn't seem like that. Commenters need to see doorways, windows, closets, finishes throughtout the space to make informed suggestions. State right at the beginning what the room will be used for and who will use it. State the non-negotiables at the beginning, what has to be kept. Give some idea of the budget. And provide approximate measurements https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6417709/unofficial-design-dilemma-boot-camp Keep in mind that you're inviting some design pros and people with a design eye into your home via photos. If they walked into your actual space, they would take in all of it: all four sides, doorways, floors, windows, ceiling, built-in fixtures, lighting, trim--the "givens"--then the features that can be changed--furnishings, paint, art, rugs, decor items, etc. It's all one first impression. Same thing with photos. That's why it's important to provide well lit photos of the entire space, taken from all sides of a room regardless of the size of your problem.

Your existing built-in trough light is probably fluorescents. Which are larger fixtures, and you would have a dropped ceiling to allow them above the cover. The condo might have flat plate construction with all electrical and fixtures being ceiling mounted. What all this means is you should have room to fit a standard integral LED retrofit fixture (such as what wdccruise links) - you don't need wafers. Which gives you more and better choices. 6" recessed works and are still chosen by people for 8' ceilings, but because of the distance between them you don't have the refinement you might want to place exactly where you'd like with cabinets (both functionally and aesthetically). It's like using a sledgehammer on a thumbtack, IMO they are chosen for a value-oriented project.

Let's look for "cross-over" between hot and cold water.  Turn off either supply valve to washing machine then test sinks.  If that doesn't cure the problem do the same to SINGLE HANDLE  faucets.   Some but not all single handle showers have screws on valve that are exposed when cover plate is removed.  In the absence of means for turning shower supply off to single handle shower, try moving handle to various positions in hopes of hitting a sweet spot that stops cross-over.   It's necessary to install repair kit in shower valve if it is crossing-over.   Replacing fill valve on washing machine is the solution if it's found to be crossing over.

I grow a selection of annuals in the caryophyllaceae family - silene, vaccaria, viscaria and gypsophila. I am not always clear about the botnical differences in these airy, seed grown flowers, but always try to add a couple of varieties every year as bouquet fillers and fast-growing additions in the perennial beds. There is a blue viscaria - 'Blue Angel' which I will be growing this year, along with a deep pink gypsophila 'Kermesina'.  All do well when direct sown and are easily added to any existing gaps. I generally try to grow some annual phlox too, porkchop. There is a blue selection called 'Moody Blue' and another variety called 'Sugar Stars' which are more amenable to sowing in modules for a later transplanting. Have also grown the wittily named 'Phlox of Sheep'. I agree - these lovely, oldfashioned varieties of annuals are really only available as seeds - I always thought no-one would pay for short-lived annual plants, back when I had fond ambitions to raise and sell such plants...but the enormous success of vegetable plug plants and bedding plants has convinced me that there would be a niche in the market for a UK version of Annies Annuals - selling exactly those familiar, but overlooked plants such as flax, nasturtiums, centaurea, orlaya, godetia, lavatera, nemophila, phlox, linaria etc.etc.

I think the scale of box store gardeners vs curious gardeners is so overwhelming that it's hard for an annual phlox to compete.  Until you can get a phlox which fills a six inch pot, is lumpy and covered in bloom at sale, and blooms all summer, they're always going to be "specialty" plants. Easy is so tempting for gardeners who are on the lazy side like myself, and to plan ahead, sow seeds, care for them, plant them out -compared to finding a few starts in May and filling a flower-saturated pot or bed in one afternoon- it's so tempting... except for the cost of course. Would others agree that it's harder to find unusual seeds or is that just me fooling myself?  Back in the day when a seed catalog would show up I'd spend hours scouring the pages and editing lists, but today clicking on webpage links just seems more tedious.  Also I spend way too much time scrolling rather than sitting down with a nice seed list and of course that's all my own fault. Sorry for wandering off topic.  I did end up at a plant sale the year before last where one of the vendors had made a try at filling Campanula's niche idea for unusual annuals.  I picked up some night blooming phlox, cool linaria, a couple nasturtium including a cutting grown form which I promptly killed, and a few other things.  This spring I hope to at least get a few nicotina sylvestris going since they refuse to self-seed, and my fingers are crossed the Nigella I finally grew last year will reappear as well as Orlya.

"Would others agree that it's harder to find unusual seeds or is that just me fooling myself? Back in the day when a seed catalog would show up I'd spend hours scouring the pages and editing lists, but today clicking on webpage links just seems more tedious." Oh, definitely agree with that.  It is so relaxing to sit with a good catalog and thumb through the pages -- or in my case, soak in a hot bath LOL!  It is tedius clicking through webpages to find if they have what I want. I think it is harder to find more unusual seeds nowadays, so many thing have fallen out of favor.  Phlox drummondi being one of them.  I can find seeds of a couple colors, but unfortunately none that I want, whereas in times past there was lots of colors to choose from.  Select Seeds carries heirloom varieties, if you're interested in looking there, and they do publish a catalog every year. Suzy mentioned lavatera -- I used to grow that and enjoyed it.  It didn't bloom all summer for me, though, and up here if an annual peters out after a good flush of bloom or two, they're not worth growing because our "annual season" is so short.  I realize it's much different in the UK, lucky you if you can enjoy lavatera for an extended time.  :0)

So much for less scrolling today... the bath would have been nicer, but I did end up at a desk with the Select Seeds site open.  Apparently I need more pelargoniums, antique ones when possible. Lavatera is awesome, the annual one is the one I'm thinking of and it also peters out for me.  I think our hotter summers are part of the problem, it wants to get those seeds set before the rest of summer turns the garden into a desert or a tropical rain forest depending on the whims of our weather.

If you had water come out of the crack, that means you filled the pot up enough that the saucer overflowed. Same thing can happen with a pot and an unattached saucer. It's just a lot harder to see how much is too much with that kind of pot. There isn't any way to snap it open more. You can snap the saucer off the pot, but you could break either or both in the process.

The bottom will snap off if enough force is applied. You can see where protrusions molded onto the saucer were pushed up through the pot's bottom. Try supporting the pot by resting the rim on 2 parallel boards so the pot hangs from the rim below the boards, then using a 1/4 or 5/16 drift punch if available,   or alternately, a wooden dowel rod or metal bolt similar to the punch, using it to gently tap on the protrusions sticking up through the pot bottom. You can set the pot on blocks above the saucer which will increase the amount of water the saucer can hold once the pot is no longer displacing most of the saucer's volume capacity, or add a larger saucer.  It's best to flush the soil as you water to prevent dissolved solids (salts) from accumulating in the soil/ soil solution. Raising the pot above the saucer bottom ensures salts flushed from the soil have no pathway by which to make way back into the soil. Water retention is driven primarily by the size of the particles your soil is made from, so any improvement (decrease) in water retention will be governed by the fact that you can eliminate the pot sitting in water that collects in the saucer. There ARE other tricks you can use to actually decrease the volume of water the planting (pot + soil) is capable of holding if you have interest. These tricks would significantly more beneficial than your original plan. You could also simply melt a few holes in the bottom of the attached saucer with a heated 5/16-3/8" bolt or nail head  and utilize a new saucer larger in diameter than the attached saucer by an inch or two. Happy New Year. Al

I came back to your post to see what ideas might’ve popped up. No luck yet I see.  I don’t think pouring paint will avoid the bumps unless you’re able to completely tape them off.  My thought was to use a stencil brush to ’pounce’ the color(s) on the bumps. The size of the round & stiff stencil brush head should be a bit smaller than the bumps to be able to keep the paint on the bumps. The color can be pale or dark since it’s controlled by how long the brush is pounced (tapped) onto the bump.  Color gets deeper with each pounce.  For paint I’d use stencil / craft paint - small bottles you can find in a craft store with the stencil brushes & in every color you can think of. All you need to decide is colors / design. To give the piece some depth I’d fade the colors from dark to lighter either going from center outward or edges inward.  You could test colors on a big piece of butcher paper or poster board while learning to pounce with a stencil brush  & trying to decide on colors & design.  The brush is washable & the paint is not $$ so practicing on a mockup before putting paint on the piece is highly recommended.  Use a paper plate for your paint palette.

I would paint the entire piece a solid color, including the bumps.  Then take a slightly lighter color, in the same color family, and dab the corner of folded paper towel in it.  Then pat as much paint as possible off of the paper towel and swipe it over the bumps.  It will give the bumps dimension.

text: Bed is highly friable and well amended with compost to a depth of at least 14 inches. I load on compost and turn the soil over at least to a shovel depth. Many of my carrots are only 4 inches long. My soil has been tested almost yearly. I have PLENTY of all nutrients. Appropriate thinning might be an issue. I tend to skimp a bit on spacing, but I would think that putting them too close together would affect both width and length, and not just length. Mine are plenty wide.

I'd consider Roberts advice, and I'm not trying to be rude but you always insist you have plenty of nutrients, and I'm wondering if you ever fertilize at all over the season relying solely on a soil test.  Carrots are short rooted plants just like onions so their roots don't go deep or spread far.   Denitrification happens very fast in the top soil with microbes in direct competition with plants for nitrogen.  Top soil nitrogen is lost in a few weeks or even a few days being used by plants and microbes, denitrified or leached as nitrates deeper beyond the root zone. Fertilize with a little 1-0-3 or 1-2-3 ratio fertilizers 3 or 4 weeks after they come up and a again   mid season with more than the first fertilization.  Carrots don't need a lot of nitrogen but there still needs to be a careful balance between foliage tops to root bottoms.   Let your plants show you what they need  and not a a soil test that will change daily for nitrogen.  Carrots will respond very fast to nitrogen and easily seen in the foliage in just a few days, and good tops are required to supply the storage roots with sugars, because they are biannual and the reason roots get big to begin with. years ago I thought I had enough nutrients after one and done broadcasts of fertilizers prior to planting but usually had short carrots and never fertilized after planting.  One year I threw some Potassium nitrate (13-0-45) on my pathetic looking carrots and they went wild with better looking tops in a couple days, and a dim light went on.  Later on when I checked for size they had turned into horse carrots, and some could choke a horse at a foot long, with some bolting meaning I may have applied to much nitrogen, and the light got brighter.  Tweaking the amounts and fertilizing two times now gives me nice sized carrots,  but now I add just phosphorous before planting and the nitrogen and potassium during the season.  But instead of expensive potassium nitrate I use  potassium chloride and Urea.

author_name: daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)

I would treat the fungus gnats right away. If left alone, you will end up with potentially hundreds of gnats indoors and they will spread to any other house plants and clogging up fans and air purifiers in your home, in my experience. What always works for me is treating plants with Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (BTI). Buy any "mosquito bits" or "mosquito dunks" products with BTI and treat once a week for 3-4 weeks. By the last treatment they completely disappear. Good luck.

When I started my veggie garden 3 years ago, I was appalled the find the soil the worst clay I've ever seen.  I garden in permanent beds, not raised, with wood mulched paths in between.  The first fall I piled leaves, picked up from friends' yards, on the beds, add some non peat based compost, and covered all with hay that didn't have weed seed.  The following season, when I peeled back the hay, I chopped in the leaves with a Korean hand hoe and sowed seed..  Plants I just popped into the ground surrounded by the hay and leaves underneath.  Of course I was also using organic fertilizers--Coast of Maine and Espoma products.  Also, when a crop was finished, say lettuce, I chopped it up in place and added more hay.  For bulkier crops, like cabbage, I added the green side leaves to the beds under the hay.  I had no access to manure. Now, at the end of the third year, the soil is hugely improved.  My worst problem now are the moles, all eating the earthworms after they exploded with all the goodies now available to them.

"Ginger plant" means the combination of ginger, sugar and other ingredients that you add to water and allow to naturally ferment to produce ginger beer, a ginger flavoured version of home made root beer.   Once it has combined with wild yeast from the air, it becomes a living thing that needs to be regularly fed with more sugar.  Usually one drops a few white raisins into the mix at the start as there are generally some yeast cells clinging to the outside of them. It's not a plant with leaves and roots etc. When the process is complete, you have a mildly fizzy, ginger flavoured soft drink. If you bottle it before the yeast is exhausted, it continues to ferment in the bottle and pressure builds up, often resulting in a messy explosion.  When I used to make ginger beer, we kept the bottles in a closet in a sturdy plastic crate with a number of old telephone books piled on top.  We had a friend who kept his in a kitchen cupboard and a rogue bottle blew the door off.

I’ve been on GW/Houzz for over a decade, and I’ve learned so much. Don’t put new counters over old cabinets. If that means you wait to upgrade your space until you can afford to do the cabinets, wait. In the meanwhile, plan, collect inspiration images, look at finishes that give you the mid-century feel you really want. You may not follow this advice, and I wish you the best regardless, but google new counters old cabinets before you make any decisions. I think you’ll see that new counters make old cabinets look older and more tired, and they tie you into doors when you really need drawers, and force you into a layout that may be sub-optimal (e.g., your stove and sink are too close together, and your island is likely a barrier island).

I have no idea what your budget is or how much you want to invest in this kitchen, how long you will be staying in this home or the answers to any of the questions that are required to make a good financial decision. A full gut renovation of a kitchen is an expensive choice.   It will cost you twice what you will get back when you sell, the other 50% negative ROI is what I call the joy factor - it will bring you joy over the years that you are using the kitchen, and that is worth something too.   Only you know where the break even point is between saving toward your next home and spending on your current home. Another thing that only you can determine is your quality tolerance.    I know a lot of people without lots of money who paint their own cabinets and re-do it every 5-6 years when it starts to chip . . .   It is what they can afford to do.    I know others who have had their cabinets professionally painted and the paint lasts about 8-10 years before needing to be done again. Factory finishes last longer, but even those can eventually start getting banged up.   A good wood can last decades. Your cabinets are neither awful or great - they are normal cabinets. The finish does not go well with the flooring that was selected or the countertops that were selected. (Would you wear a shirt the color of your countertops with shorts the color of your cabinets?) That is a bit problematic. I do see a path to salvation without burning a huge hole in your pocket. The current countertops look like they are formica and the older formica with the squared edge rather than the bullnose edge.   This is one of the easiest, inexpensive updates you can do to a kitchen.   You can buy the Formica sheets for about $100 per 4'x8' sheet.   You simply glue and cut the new color onto the current countertop.  (Sink has to be lifted, more than likely your backsplash was done after the formica and will need to be redone.) Replacing the backsplash is another, not impossible, not too expensive, DIY project. Green is mother nature's solution for bringing all colors together - I would paint the walls of the kitchen something like Evergreen Fog, Paint the island something darker - Dried Thyme/ Rosemary.   Use this countertop and pick a white backsplash that is the same whites as one of the whites in the countertop.         For <1000 you have a completely different look and feel and have minimized the impact of the clashing floor/cabinet issue.

Wow dadoes, even in 2008 that was really inexpensive. What do you think the motivation was for this machine? It seems better than the typical HE wash plate TL HE machine. It reminded me of a dryer-is it the F&P?-that is loaded at the top.  Do you use yours often?

The Neptune TL was presumably Maytag's answer to Whirlpool's Calypso.  The service manual is dated 2003, which predates the Oasis/Cabrio/Bravos. The Calypso (which I have one) is much better IMO.  The TL has trouble tumbling some types of loads, lightweight fabrics.  I once watched a load of 22 typical button-down shirts not roll even once through the entire wash period.  I restarted it and manually helped the load roll. The TL has two fill levels.  Low level is for wash and interim rinses and is lower than you may expect.  High level (which is to approx the hubs of the tumblers) is the final rinse on all cycles and for the Bulky cycle (the wash and final rinse, I don't immediately recall if also the interim rinses).  More water is added to all fills if needed to reattain the target level after tumbling begins regards to saturating the load, not appreciably different in that respect to frontloaders which tumble during fills. TL washplate machines, at least the WP brands, have seemingly become anemic.  The early models, F&P AquaSmart and Oasis/Cabrio/Bravos based on F&P's design, produce more action. My TL's serial indicates production in December 2005 so it had been warehoused for almost 2.5 years (and discontinued) when I bought it in May 2008. I used the TL as my primary washer for ~6 months, until the clutch/pulley malfunctioned.  Took it down for pending warranty service (instead of DIYing it since it was within the warranty period), then moved it to occasional use as one of several spare machines. I have four F&P topload dryers.  Two refurbed for use (self and mother), two spares that haven't yet been touched.

The tile, the grout and the caulk are not the place where waterproofing happens. Grout will always have gaps and caulk will dry out. The waterproofing layer is behind the tile. It is either a waterproof membrane or painted on sealant. There are several different methods, but none of them rely on the surface caulk or grout. You cannot fix a leaky shower with caulk. There is nothing that can be applied to the outside that can make this waterproof. It all has to be ripped out and put together right with major attention to waterproofing before any tile goes on.

I prefer drift of mist at this point but I’m a little worried about contrasting trim color. Nothing to worry about. They belong to the same hue family - they live in the same place in color space - and they also have similar chroma. This means they share two different attributes. Quartz is not heat resistant.  Quartz slabs are factory made.  They contain crushed quartz particles, 33.5% plastic resins by volume, and dyes. Doesn’t matter whether the unit has a gas or induction cooking surface. To mitigate the issue, have the builder install a fireproof wall behind the stove.  That is, steel studs…not wood, with cement board in front of the steel studs. My contractor did this in our kitchen, even though we have a rangetop with separate wall ovens…and have ceramic subway tiles behind the rangetop. To be especially safe, use a sheet of stainless steel behind the oven…as others have suggested. Be forewarned.  Quartz counters can be damaged by simply placing the lid from a hot pot, directly onto the counter. I'm in Northern Michigan and can plant outside about the end of May, but I'll get my first frost in September or October if I'm very lucky.  Chard is pretty sturdy, but won't withstand too many hard freezes, although I've picked it out of the snow a couple of times.  So, I have a growing season of about 90-110 days, normally. So, plant the end of May, it'll be ready to cut in late July, maybe.  It doesn't seem to come back well after I cut it, so I plant part of my row, wait a couple of weeks, plant some more.  Some of the first planting will bolt in the August heat.   I try to plant a mix of greens so I have different varieties available.  I usually plant kale, collards and swiss chard which mature at various times according to the timing of the planting.  I can get spinach, swiss chard and mizuna later into the fall if I put them into the raised bed hoop houses and close the "lid", but I usually have lettuces in there.  I have two raised beds, 4x8, one currently has a hooped top, so am somewhat limited in space.  My favorite greens though, are the tops of the beets, those never go to waste. My "real" garden is about one acre outside. Our project this year is to make the hooped tops stronger, usually a couple of inches of snow and they just collapse onto whatever is growing inside as they are plastic tubes and rolled plastic covers.  They do make great hot houses, though, and my cabbages and other crucifers like spring in there far better than they do inside under the lights.   Annie

To answer your question: yes, it would look odd.. You didn't really post your Design Dilemma to get the best advice. The pros on Houzz don't just look at one element. They need to see the big picture. Here is how to post a Design Dilemma to get the best results. You need to show the whole space—all four sides of an entire space—even if it’s about one specific Dilemma. A layout fix is often a Design Dilemma fix even if it doesn't seem like that. Commenters need to see doorways, windows, closets, finishes throughtout the space to make informed suggestions. State right at the beginning what the room will be used for and who will use it. State the non-negotiables at the beginning, what has to be kept. Give some idea of the budget. And provide approximate measurements https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6417709/unofficial-design-dilemma-boot-camp Keep in mind that you're inviting some design pros and people with a design eye into your home via photos. If they walked into your actual space, they would take in all of it: all four sides, doorways, floors, windows, ceiling, built-in fixtures, lighting, trim--the "givens"--then the features that can be changed--furnishings, paint, art, rugs, decor items, etc. It's all one first impression. Same thing with photos. That's why it's important to provide well lit photos of the entire space, taken from all sides of a room regardless of the size of your problem.

Sampling is so important, especially when you're going to paint a large area and maybe pay someone to do it since you have high ceilings.  DH bought a standard sized piece of drywall, cut it into four pieces and we sampled colors on it to get a good idea of what colors would look like.  Paint chips are too small, although they're a good starting point.  Samplize samples, which are about the size of a piece a paper, are a good intermediate step. Some rooms are more difficult than others to find the right color for.  Sometimes I hit it on the first try, others I have had to try ten different colors for, and the average is 3-5.  A color can look surprisingly different on a large sample than on a small one.  Leave the boards out for at least a week so you can look at the colors under different lighting conditions.

The regulator freezes even when the tank is filled with 80% capacity. liquid propane may be entering into the regulator causing it to freeze up. Maybe try filling only to 50% for time to see what happens to prove it or disprove it. another issue maybe that the regulator is too small for the appliances attached to it all drawing at the same time? You identified that the water heater was replaced at some point? If the issues go away as the tank is drawn down, I would be leaning toward filling tank to full. Maybe the fill indicator is faulty the tank has shifted some how. Fill to 50%, take notes. Fill to 60% take more notes. If the issues still occur at 50% tank level and lower, you'll need to investigate from the perspective of moisture or some other foreign matter getting into regulator clogging it or the regulator itself is too small for the draw of the appliances attached to it. Thick black smoke indicates incomplete combustion, typically due to lack of combustion air. This air would be CO heavy and dangerous if not fixed properly. Vinegar in the rinse helps too, but I don't recommend it since there is a lot of mixed information about using it in newer washers. I don't often find I need to do vinegar on material, I would imagine new sheets should have less sizing on them than a stiff cotton, lol.

When we were first married, dinner was pretty light as we had both had good lunch at work. When I became a SAHM, I could go to the grocery store, buy $200 of groceries, and have no idea what to make for dinner. We lived on baked chicken or fish, rice or a pasta, and peas or broccoli. When 4:00 rolled around, I’d get anxious just thinking about dinner. I was afraid of my Joy of Cooking, it was so thick! Finally I subscribed to a dinner menu-planning service. Every week they sent a list of 6 menus, with the recipe for the entree, suggestions for sides, and shopping list. The shopping list was a full page! It was really an ingredients list, because most of the items were just staples you have on hand like grain products, seasonings, oil and vinegar, etc. The subscription followed the seasons, so it was heartier in winter, and more grilling or lighter fare, taking advantage of fresh produce, in warmer months. Changed our lives. We were eating much greater variety of produce, the kids enjoyed it rating each meal with ”smilies”, and DH took good leftovers to lunch each day. If I was late coming home, the recip was there and someone could start it. The whole system saved time, and money, and was healthful and fun, and I learned how to cook! When DH  went independent and moved his office home, he wanted to cook as his creative outlet. He likes to cook. After a couple of months we figure out that he wasn’t using the menus, he would take an ingredient or two and then wing it, so a lot was going to waste, so I said if you’re going to cook, you should shop. Well, now it is a kind of predictable rotation of food, vegetables are an afterthought so broccoli, peas, or salad/lettuce. And around mid-afternoon he asks, what should we have for dinner? I ask, well, what were you planning? (no plan) and sometimes the answer is ”shazaam”, which means someone goes to the store for something from the deli or hot bar. I really miss my menu days.

It appears that your posts were added before there was a requirement for a metal base (post base/post anchor) to be placed between the wood and the dirt/ground.  What you want is to avoid direct contact between the wood post and the soil. I can't tell if there is an issue with the way your drain spout has been buried.  I have zero expertise in this area - except for having my drain spouts buried as yours has been.  However, I do know that mine are buried so that they are down hill from the foundation of the house. I assume that the grading of your yard was done to keep water away from your foundation.  Having the gutter buried between the post and the house seems like it would cause the water to run away from the foundation = towards the wood post.  Add the lack of a metal barrier between the ground and the wood = rot. There are ways to address the rot without replacing the entire wood post - depending upon how bad it actually is.  You may be able to cut away the damaged bottom of the post + treat the remaining wood to make sure that no rotted wood has been left + add a metal base + a new piece of solid wood (or use Bondo to replace the rotted wood that you've removed). However, depending on the extent of the rot, it might be best to completely replace the post for structural integrity.

Dan, when you harvested your tiny little puny bulbs did they consist of separate cloves or just one little mass like an onion?  It's a sign the clove was not chilled long enough... or just not ready.  California Early is in the soft neck artichokes group and some of these varieties, because of the soft necks, will fall over prematurely before completely mature, or a combination of hot weather and soft necks.  My artichokes often fall over early. Did you determine maturity because they fell over or the number of dried up leaves?  Softnecks that fall can still be a week plus away from maturity and when most of the bulbing happens.  I'm just presenting possibilities to consider. If Calf. early  just doesn't grow good in your area try something else.  Garlic isn't just  hardneck and softneck, these are sub species, but a combination of 11 different groups;   Artichoke, Asiatic, Creole, Middle Eastern, Porcelain, Purple Stripe,  Glazed Purple Stripe, Marbled Purple Stripe, Rocambole, Silverskin and Turban. The Artichoke is what you planted and in the same group as the Inchelium Red that I plant, the difference is yours evolved around Gilroy CA and mine in the coleville forests in Wa.  I'd suggest Researching each group to find garlic originating in climates similar to yours and see what works. I suggest first looking at the Creole group which originated around the Mediterranean area that are hardnecks you can grow.  I planted Red Sulmona Garlic (known as Aglio rosso) of the Creole group and Bogatyr garlic of the Marbled Purple Stripe group known as the oldest garlic from Russia for the first time last fall.  I'll see how well they will grow and if I even want to continue planting them. 10 out of 11 groups are photoperiod plants but daylight required to trigger bulbing is only 12 to 13 hours.  It's not like long and short day onions and garlic will grow anywhere, the only difference is climate temperature.  Cooler garlic varieties can be grown in warmer climates and only requires more care and attention in warmer areas.  Some garlic needs longer chilling periods before planting, all garlic growers in California chill the bulbs up to 2 months before planting. I know you had a debate about mulching but it does give major benefits for garlic.  Garlic doesn't like dry feet what's so ever, and need consistent uninterrupted moisture for good growth.  The mulch reduce evaporation from the soil and when wet will naturally cool the ground through the process of evaporative  cooling, it's the smart thing to do. First, CBU + Schluter waterproofing surface membrane = waterproofed walls. Second, he has sent you photos of authentic zellige tile  = handmade and more irregular = part of it's beauty.  What you have is faux zellige tile that is not handmade = much more consistent in size (although, the edges are not straight). I had Bedrosian Cloe White tile (a very popular faux zellige tile) installed in a tub/shower surround - in a vertical stacked pattern also - and the lines do NOT look like yours do.  While the edges are not perfectly straight (in order to give the impression that it is handmade tile) the horizontal and vertical grout lines are straight when looking at the surround. Cloe White (and other colors of Cloe tile - white has been the most popular by far) tile installations are posted all over this site.  Many people used it for their kitchen backsplashes + others have used in a shower or shower/tub combo surround.  While all of the installations have not been in a vertical stacked pattern, many have been + some have been installed in a horizontal stacked pattern.  I don't remember seeing any of those stacked installations having the issues that your surround does. I do know that this can be a difficult tile for some installers to install correctly - I have a friend who posts his work over on the tile subreddit - so, I've read comments by installers about not being fond of this type of tile.  HOWEVER, if the installer has experience, while he/she may not enjoy installing this type of tile, the installations look good.  I've also seen photos posted over on that sub by diy homeowners - several where the project was the first tile installation ever done - and the installations have looked better than yours (and most have been in a vertical stacked pattern). Also, your installer should have mixed up the tiles in order to avoid having a section where so many light tiles have been installed next to each other.  My eyes went immediately to the third and fourth rows from the bottom on the back wall because of how many lighter tiles are grouped together (especially in contrast to the first and second rows from the bottom where the tiles all appear to be a darker shade). Cloe White tile is a V4 variation (the highest variation) - my tile installer spent time mixing the tiles up in order to avoid exactly what has occurred on your wall(s).  Your tile appears to be a V3 - maybe a V4 (but I think Cloe White has more variation than your tile appears to have).

It's possible the misalignment could look better once it's grouted, if you use a grout close to the tile color, but that's never going to fix the color variation. Any experienced tiler knows to mix the boxes of tile up so different dye lots are distributed throughout the job. Or if there is vast variation between boxes, you can exchange some to get a better match. I hope you haven't paid for this yet!

I've looked at various german brands when i've been to kitchen trade shows and there are certain features about them that i like, for example their ergonomic design based on the height of the individual user, this is why you have 780 cabinets with various height plinths as these cater to the height of the individual user, they consider the optimal height for your worktop is 15cm below the height of your elbow bent at 90 degrees, so for someone whose 180cm tall, you may need a 95cm worktop height but if you're 160cm tall then you have a 90cm worktop height. They also tend to work on a 125mm to 130mm drawer size matrix and the big manufacturers will buy/make their doors in these combinations [ie schuller who have 3 different cabinet heights] and various plinth heights. Here in the uk we limit ourselves to 720/730 heights and 150/160 plinths mainly. We also limit our cabinet depths to suit 600 deep worktops which not all german kitchen do, again this is a waste of space as if you have a quartz worktop the depth of this is much more flexable as its templated to suit the required depth, Another feature is the size of the void at the back of the cabinet, a uk kitchen will have a 40 to 50mm void for pipework whether you need it or not, again another waste of space, this also resticts the depth of the drawers to only 450 deep, whereas with a 20-30mm void you could have deeper 500mm drawers which is popular with higher end german kitchens. Looking at the construction of the cabinets, the german kitchens do say that they are made of a 'higher' density particle board [chipboard] and 19mm thick, in the uk though we use a lot of chipboard [to various density] with the most popular being from egger, this can come in a much wider range of colours/woodgrains than i've seen offered by any german manufacturer, i also think the construction of the backboard is important, having a thin hardboard back panel, slotted in a groove and stapled doesn't offer any structural strength, it doesn't guarentee the cabinet is square, you can't fix a back box to it for a socket and overtime i've seen these start to bow and fall out [tall larders], a sold 18mm backboard will keep the cabinet rigid and square, prevent the unit from twisting and racking so when you come to fit the doors these will be all level and in line. I get all my cabinets made to order and made from 18mm egger board including the backs, with the limiting factor being the doors i can get, for me to make cabinets at 780 tall instead of 720 would incurr a small surcharge per unit, to make them extra deep wouldn't be a problem, made with a 20mm void not a problem, 500mm deep legrabox comes as standard from my carcase supplier, true handleless isn't a problem, i also tend to only have the handle rail at the top only, i don't really like the mid rails on the drawers and instead offer 'tip on' push to open lower drawers but thats up to the client. Any wireworks can be prefitted at the factory for you and can be supplied by any of the quality manufacturers [kessebohmer or vauth sagel]. For doors, if you opt for something like fenix, this is supplied as a laminate sheet which is then bonded to a substrata, this can be anything like mdf [so it would need to be edged] or something like birch ply and the edge is polished up and lacquered/stained, looks really smart. These are all pretty easy to do, not overly complicated to design and depending on the size of the kitchen a lot less than 40k, for me to do this i've come out with fenix doors a bit more than a top price wren kitchen. if you have something like a Serica [supermatt 18mm mdf edged door] or acrylic faced door then it would be cheaper. My first day at university - which is the day that I moved from the farm where I grew up to the Rice University campus on Main Street in Houston, with Hermann Park and the Texas Medical Center across the street, and the art district just a few blocks north - easily walkable. I was very depressed (almost suicidal) as a teenager - at least until I went to high school in the next town, which had a sizable population (35,000 at the time), but I was still living at home.  To get away from my parents (especially my father) was a huge change in my life, and it allowed me the freedom to be who I really was.  I loved Houston and all of the opportunities it had, and I loved the university, with its beautiful secluded campus, just minutes from downtown.  I did not have a car, but there were lots of city buses on Main Street, which made it easy to get around.  Roommates had cars, and so they could also take me places as well. The night before we drove to Houston, I had a dream of being on campus, even though I had never visited the campus and had never seen photos of where I was going to live.  In one part of the dream, I entered a stairwell which went up half a flight and then down half a flight into an open quadrangle.  In my dream, I thought to myself that it was very strange to go up half a flight and down half a flight to get from one courtyard to a grassy quadrangle in the middle of the residential college, and when I experienced in person exactly what I had dreamed the night before, I became somewhat dazed, like I was in a trance - very much like a déjà vu experience, but it was extremely vivid, as I had dreamed the experience exactly the night before it happened.  Some people did notice the dazed look I had, but I did not explain it to anyone at the time. I've had other experiences like this, but not recently, although they used to happen fairly frequently when I was in my 20s and 30s.

You called? Any roof blower (of appropriate flow rate performance, duct size interface, etc.) can be used with any hood/duct combination, but not necessarily with any hood's particular controls.  The task you or your electrician must perform is to investigate the existing control and see whether: a) the connection to the blower motor is two conductors plus ground operating at mains voltage.  In that case the motor is probably an induction motor, and mains voltage Broan motors/blower assemblies can be used directly if the current requirements are similar.  The hood control will likely be a smooth operating rotary potentiometer, but a stepped switch cannot be ruled out. b) the connection to the blower motor has more than two conductors with ground, in which case the control is likely a rotary switch with multiple positions, or multiple push buttons.  These would drive a multiply-wound motor.  Replacement with the Broan induction motors named above would require either adapting a phase-type motor control to the hood, or mounting it separately in the hood or in a wall, counter, or other suitable location. Note motor controls, often available from electrical distributors and big-box hardware stores, differ from light controls by going from OFF state to maximum motor power, then reducing power (actually phase fraction) as the control is rotated clockwise.  Light controls go from OFF state to minimum power fraction, and increase power as rotated clockwise. NuTone's motor controls have (had) a fancier wall plate than generic controls which may expect a nominal light switch wall plate to be supplied separately.  I expect that Broan/NuTone still sell controls for their blowers but haven't looked. The Broan/NuTone roof blower assembly used with my Wolf hood, is an induction type, and my hood (actually manufactured by Independent ca. 2009) uses a hood specific knob/resistor/diac/triac circuit typical of early motor phase controls.  More modern controls may have integrated circuits. All that said, you need to confirm that it is your blower that failed and not the control.  Check wiring between control and blower to see if voltage is present when it should be.  If not, you have a control problem which may be fixable, particularly in case (a), by repair or replacement.  Case (b) controls could be anything inside, so I won't comment on their repairability, which would require an electronics tech as a minimum.

You are not understanding stone support requirements.  Anything over 9" requires support every 24" at a minimum.  That support must come within 6" of the edge.  And a large cantilever like that does not have enough base to counteract the seesaw lever of someone leaning on that, even with support. An angle type support is only as good as that wall that the angle attaches to, and that wall is only as good as the attachment of the wall construction to itself and the subfloor.  Often, lag bolts are required, in order to counteract the huge amount of leverage created by a large overhang like that. You can do a large center post, with steel spokes radiating outward from it.  You can do multiple  legs, or you can do a welded steel substructure, dogged into the subfloor framing. Or you can do a table, with stretcher bars and legs in more of a rectangle shape. "What kind of damage are you talking about? Eaten leaves? Eaten branches? Bark stripped branches? Bitten branches? I'm personally not familiar with rabbit damage." I'm in a similar situation as @prairiemoon2 z6b MA: in winters like this one where we get relatively deep snow cover over an extended period, rabbits tend to change their diet to mostly woody material and they'll go after the lower limbs of any shrubs or trees they can reach, which is higher than normal when aided by snow or ice accumulation. Rabbit damage looks like "clean" pruning cuts, since their incisors are very sharp, as opposed as to the ragged/torn damage left by deer. On larger limbs (especially on apple trees), they'll strip the bark completely and can totally girdle (and likely kill) the trunks of younger plants I fence as many of the rabbit "favorites" as I can: Fothergilla, Hamamelis, Hydrangea quercifolia, Japanese maples, anything in the apple family. I also definitely protect any shrubs/trees that were newly planted in the fall, but I don't have the time or energy to fence everything, and if the snow persists for a while, they'll go after anything. The last few winters, with warmer temps and more minimal snow cover here in upsate NY have been a bit of a "reprieve", but this winter has been significantly more "wintry", and the rabbit feast has resumed. Just over the past few weeks, they've started chewing on my unfenced Clethra, Diervilla, Itea, and any lower limbs on nearly any unfenced young trees. The only option now is to be "generous" and frequent with Liquid Fence sprays for things they've already started on. I typically don't try to "repair" any of the damage they do, and just keep an eye on how the plant regrows in summer. If I'm not happy with how it looks, I'll make "adjustments" in the following dormant season.

We have a studio apartment down the hall from our main apartment and wanted to make it a comfortable and safe place for my aging parents to spend lengthy amounts of time in and live in if ever needed.  I learned a ton a long the way from my father (an engineer who did lots of public building design including ADA), an OT we hired who specializes in aging in place home design, and from reading a ton online. * ADA requirements are not actually what you want to use in a home.  (Dad + OT agreed.) ADA standards are made for the general public and are created to accommodate the average person.  Your home should be made to accommodate your loved one.  Have your mother-in-law reach out and see where *her* arm goes to grab for stability, balance, and coming to standing.  Base things on *her* height.  I had my mom and dad test a lot of arm reaches and positions to see what would be comfortable for *them* to grab. * Only 7% of older adults become wheelchair bound.  Is there something in particular that indicates that your mother-in-law is going to be destined for a wheelchair?  If not, the much more important things to focus on are: 1. Balance and stability - as those are issues that so many adults have - a long countertop is useful for this, not having to step to different locations to reach for cosmetics, toiletries, being able to set things on a counter if an action needs to gets broken down into many parts.  Yes, a short sink is helpful if she is in a wheelchair but if she is the other 93% of the population, having a taller sink is better so she doesn't have to bend down so far to use it. 2. How to move around the space with two people in it - if she ever needs assistance with grooming or on the toilet - I'd never put pony walls on two sides of a toilet as you then cannot stand by her side if she needs help.  Have a grab bar on one side.  If she ends up needing one on the second side, install one that can hinge up and down from the wall as needed. 3. Reducing fall risks - Make sure floor surfaces have a high anti-slip rating - don't just rely on the adage that grout on mosaic tile will do enough to reduce slipping; Don't use grab bars that double as towel rods - cause of lots of accidents, use grab bars for balance and hooks for towels; Make a very good lighting design so there are no shadows, the room is well lit, it is easy and logical where to turn on the lights (remember no electric and plumbing in a pocket door wall); add plenty of outlets so you don't have to move around the room a lot to plug something in; have a place to sit down and dry off. 4. Make open floor space for a walker to live while she is on the toilet or in the shower.  (Twice as many people use walkers as use wheelchairs and way more than that use canes.) Wonderful that you are doing this.  I cared for my father-in-law for many years and loved him as I do my own father.  I get it!  He had dementia and needs so much help but was never in a wheelchair.  Went from walking to bed bound.  Same was with my two uncles with parkinsons, walking to bedbound.  My grandmother used a wheel chair for two weeks.  We made do without wheelchair accessible accomodations.

Hallett & Co is correct (as usual!) - you need to confirm what the place of origin is for the marble tiles that you are looking at purchasing.  Country of origin = where the marble was mined - not where it was manufactured. For example, only marble mined from Italy is actually Carrara or Calacatta marble - although many places will call the marble they sell "carrara" or "calacatta." A few years ago, one of my sisters bought some marble tiles from F&D.  They had several different types.  She purchased Bianco Carrara and Thassos.  The Bianco Carrara country of origin was Italy and the Thassos was from Greece.  It showed the country of origin under the specifications on the website. However, she told me that when she went to purchase some hexagon mosaic tile sheets for her fireplace last year, F & D no longer listed the country of origin on its website.  She had to call the store to find out which mosaic sheets were made with marble from Italy. The mosaic marble sheets made with Italian marble were manufactured in China - and didn't have consistent spacing between hexagons - so, her installer had to remove some of the hexagons and hand set them + use some spacers to make the grout lines a consistent size. You also want to look through any boxes you buy to see if any of the pieces are broken/cracked/etc.  F&D sold the marble tiles by the piece - so, she could return those types of pieces. People have posted issues on here related to marble mined in China - it appears to have more iron inside which can rust with continued exposure to water.

Floor and Decor is seconds quality.  Mostly packaged as firsts.  Especially the stone. Lots of iron, copper, and other inclusions in the stone that will rust or turn other colors with exposure to water and oxygen.  More fissures, holes, and things that wouldn't pass QC from a better manufacturer. If you ever looked at travertine tiles and seen the difference between the big canyons and holes, vs the soda pop bubbles, you could easily understand some of the differences between good and bad quality.

Random thoughts on step-in vs. wheel-in: - If you're in a wheelchair now, or if you have a debilitating condition that might suggest future need, consider the wheel-in options.  If you don't fit that profile, your chances of being permanently in a wheelchair (due to normal aging) is about 4%.  That's pretty low -- and if you were in that 4%, you'd probably need to move anyway. - Someone will say, "Better to have it ..."  Yeah, I see that line of reasoning, but roll-in showers are more expensive to build, require more space, and (because they're harder to install and fewer people have experience with them) they more often spill water out onto the bathroom floor.  Don't spend more and risk trouble for a low-possibility event, especially when other options exist. - Consider that step-ins aren't all the same.  My bedroom shower curb (from the 1970s) is something like 6" high, and I stub my toe on it fairly often -- hate that thing.  A minimum curb is only 2" -- we went with that when we replaced our hall shower, and it's a whole different ballgame -- a wheelchair can roll over 2", especially with help entering /exiting the shower.  Consider, too, that shower curbs can be very narrow or rather wide -- and that can make a difference in stepping over. - Consider a slide-in bench.  These are wide benches that allow you to sit down, then "slide over" into the tub /no curb concerns. - Or consider the most simple of all options:  A simple hospital shower chair; most wheelchair users can walk a few steps (especially if you're talking about normal aging and not trauma or neurological issues) and get into the chair. - Do not build in a bench -- if you want seating now, go with a teak stool.  A built-in bench could remove the possibility of using these simple add-ons later. - No to a full wet room.  That's overkill. Other thoughts about making a shower elder-friendly: - Definitely place your grab bars now.  Adding them later will almost certainly penetrate your waterproofing barrier and cause mold behind your tiles. - Ideally you'd have a vertical bar just outside the shower /another just inside the shower to assist with entry /exit.  And you'd have a horizontal bar across the back side of the shower.  And you'd have a vertical bar next to the shower head so you can hold onto it while reaching for the shower head. - Note that grab bars "cut into" your shower's size -- so go a bit larger than you think you actually need. - Instead of the expected glass door, go with a shower curtain.  It's easier to keep clean now, and -- if you need it in the future -- it'll allow you wider access to the shower. - Go with a floor-to-ceiling curtain (perhaps custom-made), and it'll look better than a glass door too. - Definitely go with a hand-held shower head.  (No need for a standard shower head in addition.)  Consider one on a sliding rail, which will allow you to easily use it from a standing or sitting position.  Be sure, too, that the shower head can reach the farthest corner of the shower enclosure for easy cleaning. - Position your on /off switches so you can reach in and turn the water on without entering the shower /without committing your body to the initial cold spray. - Place your shower niche (or other storage) low enough that it'll be useful from a sitting position. - Position your towel bars so that you can easily reach them from the shower. - Consider a Tornado Body Dryer and eliminate the need for towels. - Consider that if you need a walker or wheelchair, you may need to get rid of throw rugs, which are trip hazards.  As my grandmother neared 100, her #1 problem wasn't getting through doorways or entering the shower -- it was those nasty thresholds and changes in flooring and throw rugs, which would make her fall /throw her to the floor.  If you think loss of your bath mat will really bother you, consider building in heated flooring. - Everyone on this board seems to consider tile a necessity.  Consider linoleum instead.  It's softer underfoot and will be kinder to your ankles and knees as you age, and -- if you do fall -- it's softer /less likely to lead to a broken bone.  It's also warmer underfoot.

The theory behind bare root roses is that they are planted in late *winter*, so they go to sleep, then wake up in their new home. This can be problematic in places that don't get winter, since they aren't establishing when it is cool and damp. The usual way around this is to hill soil or mulch around the canes, and keep the hill damp until the rose sprouts. Then a relatively gentle spray from a hose washes the hill away without damaging the new sprouts. There used to be a line here that if bareroots weren't snowed on at least once, they were planted too late.

From a fellow Californian, my guess is that you planted your bare root in full sun and it got fried a bit. Similar to what Mad said, when you plant bare roots, you should always either cover them well with soil or mulch, or provide some sort of temporary shade if you're planting them in full sun. It's one of the reasons I always pot my new bare roots in 5 gallon pots after soaking in water for a few days. I leave them in shade and then very gradually move them to full sun. The other reason I do this is to make sure they're the right variety before putting them in their permanent home. I've never received a mislabeled rose from Regan, but I've received three mislabeled bare roots in the past ten years from my local (high quality) nursery! Interestingly, all were from Weeks. Anyway, next time you get bare roots, protect them more from the full sun after planting :-D

Hi, with sliding doors you can actually remove the sliding and fixed panels and do these separate, one side at a time; and do the tracks separate too. With aluminium sliding doors like as your image, the aluminium panels are separated by a mohair pile strip that prevents rubbing and also acts as a draft stopper. In most doors this strip can be slid out and replaced or can be masked up before painting. Handles, latches and fly-wire screens can also removed, masked, painted and re-fitted. If you only want to change the internal colour of an aluminium door or window in selected rooms, you can also choose to just paint the internal visible faces leaving the external faces that then still match all your other windows and doors around your home. Hope this helps, Malcolm.

Judging by the size of the cobble edging and the surrounding plants, that area is far too small to accommodate any of the previous suggestions with the exception of the helianthemum. And that is really the only species suggested that offers much of a ground covering habit as well. IMO, that's a good choice for this area. There are a few reasons the efflorescence can get so bad on a 10 year old brick walls, and build quality  is one.  I rarely see efflorescence on 100 year old brick walls this bad so suspect the walls on that house used poor quality mortar, old mortar or wrong mixing ratios.  If the mortar can be scraped off with a fingernail is was old or cheap.  Mortar will go bad just sitting in the bags and seen it go bad in less than a year. The bricks could be low quality soft bricks with high salt content (All bricks have hardness ratings).  A butter knife can easily rub off brick material on cheap soft bricks.  I suspect cheap materials because the efflorescence is running so high up the walls and not normal at all. Because the knowledge level and quality of home inspectors are so low I'd pay a expert in the field to take a look.  You don't want to buy a house with bad mortar unless you're willing to pay 10's of thousands to have a mason grind out 3/4-1 inch of mortar and apply new mortar. Another problem is the algae growing on the wall, the brick is very damp to do this.  I noticed the soil level is above the bottom bricks.  Bricks are porous and will wick up moisture from the ground, and the bottom brick row shouldn't be below ground level.  In fact the bottom row should have weep holes to allow moisture to weep out from behind the bricks, I don't see any, or they are buried below the ground, or they didn't put weep holes in.  Google weep holes in brick walls to see what I'm talking about. Brick walls aren't in contact with the wall behind them, they are actually about an inch away from the wall and held off with tabs nailed to the wall and then attached between rows of brick.  On the wall behind the bricks is a layer of waterproofing material like tar paper or equivalent.  The cavity between the bricks and wall is deliberately made along with the weep holes to channel moisture down the back of the bricks and out.  I don't know what's going on for sure so do not hesitate bringing in a professional mason to evaluate the problem.

I don't disagree (much) with the more laissez-faire answers you've been given, in general, but this is a tart shell.  It needs to be thin and strong, and the bigger it gets, the more strong it has to be.  Unlike most pies, tarts are removed from the tin.  That's why the bottom comes out.  I don't know for sure, but I thought the egg was for glue.  Certainly, the GF pie crust recipes with egg use it that way.  So I do agree that estimating the different measure to exactly scale the recipe should work fine, and a little variance likely won't have any effect, but too much moisture, especially non-eggwhite moisture, could undermine the strength of your tart shell, and too little could be too brittle.  Tart shells are structurally different from most baking.  You're not looking for pockets of air or steam.  You don't want bubbles or flakes.  Chloebud mentioned shortbread crusts with no eggs—that's a stong stucture that also is generally made much thicker, especislly in the corners, than the French style with egg.  I'd think that a bit too little egg would be better than too much. Here are some furniture tricks that always work no matter the space: FURNITURE TYPE Get furniture that is lower to the ground. Has legs that you can see with open space. Has shorter arms and narrower arms - looks less bulky. Has a tight back - not as many lose cushions. Check out this short video of Amanda Seyfried's apartment.  https://www.youtube.com/shorts/lDZ76KAbOnk SOFA Her living room is small and has a sofa with a very short chaise. CHAIRS I have had a lot of dinner parties in smaller spaces and it is nice to have appetizers, drinks, and desserts while sitting in the living room area instead of at a tight table.  I'd get two arm chairs and place them closer to the fireplace, on an angle facing the sofa. It will be nice seating for drinks and dessert. TABLE Remove the counter height table and stools.  Get a drop leave table.  Have it pushed up against that wall and set up for seating for two regularly.  Then when guests come, pull it out from the wall and put up the second leave.

You could get a drop-leaf table that fits where your existing table fits now, but can be pulled out to seat more in that space, with some folding chairs. Have you ever had a pool?  Do you want to take care of it?  Or pay someone to take care of it?  Realistically, how often will it get used, especially in your climate?  How often do your adult children spend an afternoon at your house now?  What will happen as their lives get busier and busier? A pool could be great or it could be an expensive, labor-intensive headache. Is the bayside house in a flood zone?  Have you checked into flood insurance?  Do you walk for exercise or pleasure?  Realistically, how often will you visit the beach?  As a life-long walker who appreciates beautiful scenery, I'd take the beach location over a pool any day of the week but that's my priority.  Try to be realistic about how you really live rather than imagining a lifestyle that isn't realistic for your personality or circumstances. Get the house that works best for you now and in the future.  Good luck house hunting!

I suspect appliance garages became popular as folks got more small appliances, like food processors and bigger mixers, that they didn't have room for in cabinets. As kitchens have become more efficient (all drawers instead of a base cabinet with a half shelf, for example), there is less need to keep appliances on the counter. One of the goals of my first kitchen remodel was to design in enough storage space that I could get all the things OFF the counters: toaster, knife blocks, canisters of dry goods, phone chargers. I succeeded! Knives and canisters went in drawers; the toaster and other small appliances went in the super susan, chargers went to a cabinet built with outlets on the inside. I would get Arborvitae plugs and plant them carefully, using a trowel, not a shovel to dig.  If you were going to do planters, I would just have them big enough to cope with plugs.  Arbovitaes have shallow root systems, which spread horizontally.  They will get cramped in any planter.  Between the planters and 6 foot Arbs, you'd be spending a lot of money and if they were still thriving in 5 years, I'd be surprised. They would probably make for a good hedge that won't disturb the utility lines, but you'd need to start small and dig like you're an archaeologist, not a gardener. Otherwise, pick a different plant.  I will observe that big bluestem grass, which comes in a bunch of pretty cultvars is 6-8 feet tall, easy to find in plug or seed form.  Again, with plugs, you have to dig carefully, but a big bluestem plug from The Pollen Nation is 4.5 inches deep and a couple inches wide. An Arborvitae plug (not available from The Pollen Nation, I got mine from O'Donal's) will be much bigger, but still of a size where slow, carefully digging with a trowel is tedious, but possible.

I've been sewing for more than 40 years. Most of the fancy stitches and features of any machine will go unused.and I use the straight stitch, the zigzag, a stretch stitch, my buttonhole maker, and that's about it. The real test for a sewing machine is the quality of its straight stitch: Will the machine consistently stitch a straight, even line of stitche that looks nice on both the top and the bottom? The most common problems with so many machines are: the tension goes off, the bobbin tangles easily, the bobbins don't wind consistently well, etc. It can be frustrating, particularly for new sewists, who don't know how to troubleshoot. My best advice is to go to a sewing machine shop in your town or nearby, and ask them to see used machines. A $300 used machine from them will be a consistently better machine than the bells and whistles machines you can buy new. text: Jena, You commented that your roses' blooms are turning sideways as shown in your photos.  In your first photo, I see a not yet open bud turned sideways with what looks like a scar on the neck of the bud on the side where the bud is facing.  That could be rose midge fly damage done when the bud was younger, as young as when the bud was smaller than a pea. Are you aware of the rose midge fly and the considerable damage its maggots do to rose tip growth?  Destroying flower production at new growth points at the worst, and damaging flowers from blooms either opening improperly, or grossly deformed flowers, are signs of rose midge fly. Damage is mostly done at the very earliest stage of a flowering tip, or a little later on until the stage where the young bud is the size of a garden pea.  After reaching a pea size, rose buds, if not caught by RMF maggots, usually are not eaten being too tough, and go on to grow and bloom normally. Rose Midge Fly is a serious pest in the North East USA, having a particular stronghold in many localities.  Unfortunately, there are no dependable organic control methods I know of, so conventional insectIcides are sprayed on a strict schedule to control the damage done by RMF. I hope my observation is incorrect, but I thought you should be alerted to the possibility of a problem. Moses.

From one senior to another wrestliing with housing decisions . . . It sounds like it's time for you to make a change.  What you do next depends on several factors -- your age, your health, your finances and whether you have family nearby to help you as you age.  We won't live forever and chances are we will need some help as we get older -- what's the plan for that?  Have you spoken to a financial advisor about your future? What does your family think? There is no law that requires you to purchase another house when you sell your current home.  You can invest the proceeds of the sale and use it to cover rent in a nice home for a long time.  Or you can invest in a senior living community where you can live the rest of your life. Or you can buy a small condo with less upkeep and you can travel as much as you like without worry. If your current community is in decline, do you really want to purchase another property there?  Have you looked at nearby towns that would be a better place for you to grow old?  Have you considered moving closer to family members? You don't have to replicate what you've always done, think outside the box. Bottom line, being stuck in a place where you no longer want to live is a terrible way to go.  You make a good case for why you should move.  Now take some time to figure out WHERE you should move and for how long.  Will this be for five to ten years?  Or are you looking for a place to live for the rest of your life?   Be realistic about aging and what your future needs might be. This is more than just a real estate decision. Talk to your family and your accountant.  Start exploring different housing alternatives, even if you're pretty sure they're not for you. This is a big step, I know, but you can do this.  Take your time, be smart, and you'll find the right home for the next phase of your life.  Luck!

We have a reach-in pantry at one end of our galley kitchen.  Shelves are 12” deep, which is perfect.  More efficient use of space, than needing to accommodate my body. Nothing gets lost, and the shelves hold a ton.  The shelves hold small appliances, like a rice cooker, air fryer, popcorn maker.

My mother designed two reach-in pantries for her kitchen. One was just  deep enough for 12” shelves and maybe 6’ or maybe it was 8’ wide. All shelves, held all the food for the family. (well, pb was next to the bread drawer and refrigerator, cereal was in the cabinet by the brakfast table, near the bowls and spoons, rice was near the stove.) The other held 4 or 5 24” deep shelves, was about 3’ wide. It held things like picnic and bbq gear, large rolls of foil, that kind of thing. I think it all depends on how you use a pantry. If you also keep the broom and swiffer in there for tending to the floor after meals, maybe you want a walk-in with a side wall for hanging it, or hang it on the back of the door. If you will keep napkins and placemats thre, maybe you want drawers. But yes, I would take pullouts over drawers for many lower storage situations involving cookware and bakeware, if those are going in the pantry. In any kitchen storage (well, ANY storage) planning, it is essential ESSENTIAL to make an inventory of what you have, how you use it, what will go where, measure the items and how much space they need, note if they have accessories that should be stored with them, if they will be used where they are stored, etc. THEN you can start planning the space and work it out.

@dan1888, here the sink run of lights do not have upper cabinets. So they can be placed anywhere within the 24" footprint of the base cabinets to perform their function of task lighting. In this particular kitchen the lighting looks to be placed fairly appropriately, it is just a wide galley with the displaced island which makes a cohesive lighting plan a bit more difficult to make simple. And, there is no such "recommendation" that recessed fixtures be placed 6" inside the counter edge. In fact, that is a poor location and should stop being always recommend by you, as they will be only 2"-4" from the face of an upper cabinet, which causes a hot(ter) spot on the cabinet, and cannot also light up the inside of the base cabinets. Placing them at the counter edge, because you do not lean your belly against the counter edge while you stand there, allows the light to also get inside the base cabinets as it simultaneously lights up the counter and inside the upper cabinets, while not causing a shadow on the counter from your body and reduces the hot spot on the upper face. Also, no homeowner will get a photometric done to see that there is 450 lumens on the counter.

The simple way for the op to check is to stand at the counter and observe the shadow position of the hands and body when thinly slicing an onion or cutting fish or meat. A standard 4" trim opening centered 6" in from the edge of a 25.5" counter is functionally correct for task lighting. 3  and 2" are also available. The cone of light depends on the beam angle of the bulb. A 15-degree narrow or more common wide spot/narrow flood is a standard choice. Not a 40-degree flood. The different depths of the source also impact what is illuminated.  They aren't going to illuminate the interior of uppers. Ambient light is for that at a lower needed lumen level than task lighting. A lumen graph is common for fixtures and bulbs. It's available info for those who look because it's significant for a lighting plan. You may also see footcandles. 10.76 lumens per footcandle. 450 lumens are about 42 footcandles. 70-80 footcandles or 750-860 lumens at the counter is preferred. That means the height of your ceiling will impact your light beam optic choice. And that's why a concentrated beam like a wide spot/narrow flood is necessary to get enough light from a 1500 lumen small opening in the right position over your work zone. The op has wider openings and can try 1600 lumen flood bulbs to bounce light around and lessen shadowing. It'll be usable and save from replacing everything.

Testing against your current wall color is hurting your ability to see what works with the colors that are going to remain when you are done with everything else.   The current wall color is going away. The key is being able to find the neutral color that works beautifully with your flooring and your cabinets and reduce the confusion that gets introduced when we start trying to account for all the impacts of internal lighting, shadows . . . . The easy way to do this without any special tools is to take a plank of your flooring, a door from your cabinets and a pile of paint samples and look at the combinations in natural daylight. (Ideal - 2:00 in the afternoon on a clear day).     You don't need to get the sample jars for the first round of this process - the paper samples from the paint store will get you really close to the perfect color.   They are free, so you can look at dozens and dozens of them and eliminate anything that looks too pink, green, purple, yellow . . . It is amazing how the undertones become apparent when seeing the colors together with natural daylight. Once you have narrowed the choices down to those where the paper samples look good you can move on to actual samples and narrow to that one "best" color. I often find that Shoji White works when Natural Choice and Oyster White are going too green or murky.  The fact that you are seeing one of those colors as green and the other pink when they are so similar tells me that the lighting and shadows and the current wall color are confusing your perception.   They do typically go green, not pink.
