Unless the last truss will be ripped out later, you have your soffit. It's all the way to ceiling, so it's like a full wall. I think it works well. One problem will be how to light the ref block, pantry cabs, and nook table from the vault. OP's often ask specific questions, and the commentariat brings up other stuff. Sometimes OPs get offended by that, I hope you don't. There a couple things I see that bring up a few questions: - The drawings are not correct, both the architect's and yours. Sometimes that doesn't matter, but it seems here you have some clearance conflicts where it does. You have some as-built dimensions now thinking about circulation clearances, but you need a full as-built of the space as it stands now. It should be drawn correctly and with the kitchen plan inserted. That would be helpful in seeing how say, the stair wall aligns with the nook window and if it interferes with the table seating, what dimension the hearth extension can be (will circulation have to cross over it), or where the existing hallway/beam aligns with all this (your last drawing shows a pocket door to the bathroom and impossible dimensions for a hallway). Field adjustments to design are a normal occurrence, and some parts of your design impinges on what exists in reality which is different than what was shown on paper. - There might be a concern with how your contractor made these alterations. Your former truss system had the "ceiling" bottom chord which kept your walls from pushing out. When you choose the alternate structural framing method of a ridge beam, that takes the place of the "ceiling" tying your walls together to keep them upright. However, the trusses were demo'd without the ridge beam installed, and no shoring was put under the old trusses/newLVLs as they went along removing each truss. I see you have snow currently on the roof, and no matter how little, there is a load + dynamic load on the roof. What can happen, and immediately, is because there is no ridge beam, the ridge of the rafters will sag, and simultaneously the top of walls will push out. This can be just 1/2", but that can wreck a lot of plans. The contractor must verify the plumbness of the rafter heel walls and run a laser to check for sag at the ridge. - The other structural concern is in regards to the gable end wall. Before when you had trusses, the entire truss system including the gable ends worked as a diaphragm to brace against lateral loads. So the gable wall was split at the top plate (at about 8') which matched the truss ceiling. This all worked as it should. However, now that the trusses are removed (the remaining "soffit" truss has no structural value for lateral loads), your gable wall still has that top plate (at about 8') break in the wall, which acts as a hinge point. Winds and roof loads will cause the wall to "fold" at that top plate. Again, it may be only 1/2" but over time with high winds can wreck a house. The contractor will eventually have to install the post in the wall for the ridge beam, but you also need full height studs (balloon framing) going from floor to top of gable wall uninterrupted to eliminate the hinge. These studs might only need to be say every 48"o.c., it would be based on your Montana wind loads.

Researched this a lot for my parents and hired an OT / design specialist.  Here is what I learned. No pony wall or separate toilet area.  Grab bar on one wall and other side of toilet have enough space for a caregiver or helper if ever needed.  Should it come to needing a grab bar on that second wall, you can install one on the wall behind the toilet that folds down. Forget ADA compliant.  That is designed for public usage to accomodate the average person.  In a home you want to accomodate a specific person - your parents.  Mount things at a height that makes sense for their height, where their arm extends to when they reach out. Put blocking in the walls for lots of grab bars.  You don't have to install them now.  Just know where they are so they can be installed in the future. Don't get a grab bar that doubles as a towel rod.  Lots of falls happen from people grabbing those and the towel on the surface makes it not gripable.  Use strategically placed grab bars and towel hooks instead.  Never make a surface that can be grasped and leaned on that isn't totally safe to take weight. Have the door open out.  If they fall in the bathroom and the door opens in, they might be in front of the door and it makes it very hard to get into the bathroom to assist them. Height of sink, again, based on their height. Nice to have a lot of counterspace so they don't have to look down, lean down, twist around to get things from lower cabinets.  (Think head rush, off balance, leading to falls when you bend down and stand up.) Unless they have a specific disease where you know they will be in a wheelchair, it isn't not necessary to make this wheelchair accessible.  Only 4-7% of elders end up in a wheelchair. Place shower controls at arm reach height, again not bending.  Place a vertical grab bar near controls so they can hold the bar while adjusting the controls. Have lots of horizontal bars in the shower to hold on to while washing their body.  Don't make the shower too big.  It gets cold.  And they have to walk farther to on a wet surface to reach the bench and controls. Really nice to have a place to sit and dry off and a surface or hooks to put clothes on that they will wear for the day. Don't believe that mosaic tiles provide enough non-slip traction because of groutlines.  Get anti-slip rated tiles.

For the cold feed [assuming you don't have the anti flood device] just add extra long hoses and connect to the isolator under the sink [when joining use the brass fittings not the cheap plastic ones]. "I want to replace the boob light with a fan and light combo..." You cannot simply replace a ceiling light with a fan. "I want to replace the boob light with a fan and light combo powered by a  single pole lutron maestro switch..." If there are only two wires (plus ground) from the switch to the ceiling light, you won't be able to do that. You'll need a fan with a remote control to adjust the fan and light. I've redone 2 of my own NYC coop kitchens now.  You are going to have a hard time getting quality work done for $15-20k max.   I have neighbors who did renovations for around that, and they loved their kitchens, but the quality sucked.  I mean 6 months later and things are falling off of the wall kind of sucked and the use of space was horrific. How long have you lived in this apartment and how badly do you need a kitchen renovation?  One thought is to make a few temporary improvements while you save a few years to be able to afford more quality renovation.  I'm still talking about getting an Ikea kitchen in a few years, but a well done job. For now, for $1,000 you could put down a nicer looking linoleum floor.  Paint the walls and ceiling. Get a new light fixture and faucet.  Add a few free standing storage pieces to the empty wall.  And make it aesthetically more appealing.  This will hold you over for a few years. If you do end up renovating, here is what I have learned to keep the costs down in a coop renovation: - Read your house rules.  Know what kinds of contractors you can and cannot use, what kinds of fees you might have to pay to do work in the building, to reserve the use of elevators, to have the plumbing shut off for work if needed - that kind of thing.  Depending on your rules it can add to your total budget. - Don't move the location of any plumbing, gas, or electric.  At all.  Like not even a few inches. - Know what your walls are made out of, where there are concrete columns and concrete beams. - Don't add extra j-boxes or recessed lights to the ceiling if your ceiling is plaster. - Life is easier if you have worked with contractors who know where to park in your neighborhood and who have worked in your building.  (Some may charge you if they get lots of tickets or if they have to pay to grease the palms of the maintenance workers in your building.) - Understand where demo debris gets taken to and what costs are involved. Most folks on Houzz do not live in the city.  Most costs they give you as estimates do not account for the insane cost of labor here, doing work in an old apartment building where removing walls is costly and often involves permission, working in an apartment where walls are uneven, walls are plaster, things are not easily hung, and contractors will sometimes give you beef about using Ikea cabinets.  (They don't want to sit and fiddle with putting together Ikea cabinets.  They'd rather sell you their own cabinets because everybody's gotta guy who can get you cabinet for less.  What brand are they and what are they made of?  Who the hell knows!)

It was virtually all painted from when the house was build and a lot of it was beautiful pieces of wood (Although the species didn't always match because it was meant to be painted) On the other hand where I grew up most of the houses were turn of the 20th century with a second wave of houses built between about 1946 and 1980. The older ones had some nice woodwork, but just big, not necessarily fancy and the post wars mostly had really cheap millwork and the vast majority of it was varnished or shellacked. The house my parents rented had orange fir plywood cabinets and panel doors  with the knots filled in with patches of wood. So did a number of our neighbors houses. And pine woodwork (orange) and oak floors (yellowish orange). All pretty ugly really, and a lot of it not painted still. In the late 60s and 70s the woodwork was all yellow. Again not nice wood. I follow certain areas of real estate and I have been for years and I see some places come on the market a number of times over the years. And I've seen the houses I remember from growing up over the years come on the market. And usually what I see happening is that if what was not essentially retained (sometimes preserved, sometimes refreshed)--if it was removed, particularly if the house is "updated" into whatever is current, regardless of how this sits in the house, the end result is banal, generic, looks like it could be in a new build finished last week. Because that seems to be what the majority of people want. It becomes banal because usually there is no real color or texture reintroduced, and it's no longer layers of it in the room. And you can take a room with some character and furnish and decorate it relatively minimally and it will still be okay. But I room that is a rectangular white box is usually going to be a rectangular white box unless it is filled with nice things, and usually houses are not filled with nice things any more because they aren't within the finances of most people, or aren't within the current desires of most people, because furniture and decor have become disposable things. You can look at an empty room in a house with some characterful details in real estate listings and "get" what that room looks like. Is your counter really going to be 24"D?  Generally, they're 25.5"D.  Non-inset base cabinet boxes, without doors or drawer fronts, are 24"D.  Doors & drawer fronts add another 1" or so to the depth.  Pulls and knobs add another 0.5" or so. Counters overhang boxes by around 1.5" to cover the cabinet boxes, doors/drawer fronts, and, usually, hardware.  The overhang prevents drips/spills from dripping into cabinets and/or drawers and down the cabinet doors/drawer fronts -- drips will damage both. Inset cabinets can get away with 1" overhang b/c the doors/drawer fronts are inset into the cabinet box, but I would not go any shallower. So, what will/is the true depth of your counters? If this is an existing Kitchen that has a countertop that is not being changed and you measured them to be 24" from the wall to the counter edge, then that's what you have (for your sake, I hope it's not!) Hello, Yes that's Travertine and it can be installed and hold up in colder climates. A sand-based installation helps to minimize the probability of cracking in freezing temperatures.

Do you know the manufacturer and specific name of the white tiles? I had some Bedrosian Cloe White 2.5 x 8 tiles installed on the walls around my tub/shower combo.  They are glazed ceramic tiles - not porcelain.  I noticed a few tiles on the bottom row of the wall looked discolored (partially - some more than others). I am having a doggie shower built in my laundry room - but currently use this tub to wash my small dogs.  This discoloration happened after I used my handheld shower head to rinse out the tub + walls after cleaning them.  Apparently, too much water hit the wall tiles/grout lines in a certain area - and the tiles retained water.  It took awhile for the discoloration to go away (= the tiles to dry out). Are you certain that your tiles are porcelain - not ceramic?  Porcelain tiles absorb much less water than ceramic tiles.  If they are porcelain, what type of porcelain tiles are they?  Glazed or unglazed?   Are they through body porcelain tiles (= the same color on the face and through the body of the tile? Do you know if your tiles had 95% mortar coverage or if your installer used spot bonding method?  Spot bonding allows water to run and sit behind tile (it should be 95% coverage).  Do you know what mortar was used to install the tiles to the wall?  Was it a premixed bucket or did the installer mix it up when using it?  Premixed = mastic - while a bucket may allow it to be used on a shower wall, best practice is not to use on shower walls.  Also, manufacturers prohibit it from being used on shower walls if a surface waterproof membrane was used. The reason I'm asking all of the above is to figure out if water absorption is responsible for the color change.

And provide approximate measurements https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6417709/unofficial-design-dilemma-boot-camp Keep in mind that you're inviting some design pros and people with a design eye into your home via photos. If they walked into your actual space, they would take in all of it: all four sides, doorways, floors, windows, ceiling, built-in fixtures, lighting, trim--the "givens"--then the features that can be changed--furnishings, paint, art, rugs, decor items, etc. It's all one first impression. Matthew, can you please narrow down where you are in AZ?  If you live in the deserty part of AZ then the grass you want will be either bermuda or St Augustine.  If you live in the elevated part of AZ, then you'd be looking at fescue (in the shade) and Kentucky bluegrass in full sun. Dogs and grass get along just fine if you keep the grass fertilized.  Well, if you have two Labrador puppies, they will tear up some grass, but if you have the grasses I mentioned, they should come back just fine.  As for pee spots, that is entirely a fertilizer issue.  If you develop pee spot, the problem can be remedied quickly by dropping a heaping handful of table sugar on the spot.  Within 3 weeks the stunted yellow spot will turn into a tall, dense, and dark green spot.  Follow that up with an organic fertilizer over the entire yard.  If you normally use chemical fertilizers, I strongly recommend adding one app of organic each year to keep your soil healthy.  I have switched entirely to organic fertilizer since 2002.  It does make a difference.

Rusts are host specific. So rose rust is not the same thing as hollyhock rust, or evergreen rusts. Be careful about when you spray. High temperature limits are easy to find. Low temperature limits can be impossible to find, but exist. Don't spray if the forecast is for a  low below 40F. The results of a freeze on freshly sprayed plants is very similar to the black spots in your photographs. This is bad. Trust me. If you are spraying for rust, use a fungicide for rust. Many aren't. If it is one plants, look into what is different about that one. Is it in more shade? Is it in a wetter or drier place in the garden? That may help solve the problem.

Hi Lili, For a room with a ceiling height of 7'4", I’d suggest going with the slim flush mount light option rather than two wafer lights. The flush mount light will provide a more uniform light spread without creating the glare that wafer lights often produce, especially in smaller spaces. Plus, the flush mount will be more space-efficient for a lower ceiling. If you're aiming to keep things simple and avoid clutter, you can still achieve a good level of illumination with one well-chosen fixture. In terms of lumens, 800-1000 lumens should work well for both the office and bedroom, but consider dimmable options so you can adjust the light based on the time of day or mood you’re trying to create. Remember, lighting is a key element in setting the tone of a room. A slim flush mount light offers clean, contemporary design without drawing too much attention to itself, while providing adequate illumination for both work and relaxation. Each quartzite may react in different ways, so you will need to test samples. We are lucky to have had a geologist on the forums who wrote a series of helpful posts. Testing is important, as we've seen in the many posts here about quartzite staining (as well as some solutions.) The stains might come from water or other sources. Here are a few of those posts.

Some quartzites are hard like quartzite should be, but can be porous like marble. These quartzites need to be sealed.   Many of the "white/gray" quartzites are porous.  Buyer beware.  Don't believe the sales pitch from anyone and do your own testing at the slab yard.  Even better if the slab yard will chip off a corner for you to test at home. I have used Taj Mahal quartzite in 2 kitchens, a fireplace surround and an outdoor kitchen.  Taj Mahal is a quartzite that seems to be consistently very durable.  In reading these forums for many years, I only remember one person having a staining issue with Taj Mahal, out of the thousands of installation of Taj Mahal that have been posted on this forum.

The chart food posted above shows the natural phenomenon that I think makes the anger about changing the clocks seem unfounded. The shortest day of the year is the Winter Solstice, December 21. From then until the Summer Solstice (June 21), sunrise time gets earlier and sunset time gets later. After the Summer Solstice, the opposite happens, earlier evening darkness and later sunrises. No matter whether time zones are shifted or not. For those who get upset about the time change, does the nearly 1 hour later sunrise as the calendar passes from July to August anger you? Or losing an hour of evening daylight from July into late August as sunset gets earlier?

Squash is very refreshing. I drink it! I found this recipe that made me laugh. Orange Squash 10 oranges, juice and zest of (which should give you 1 litre of orange juice) 4 lemons, juice and zest of (which should give you 300ml of lemon juice) 500ml water 300g sugar 40g citric acid Zest the oranges and lemons. Add the lemon and orange zest and simmer for another 10 minutes. Thereafter cool. When cool – sieve the zest out if you want a clear squash, however, cloudy is very much in vogue. Since you’re after warm beige tones that complement your house, Indian sandstone is a great natural choice. It weathers beautifully, developing a more rustic, characterful look over time. However, it is more porous, which means it can stain and attract algae in damp areas, so sealing and occasional pressure washing are needed to keep it looking fresh. Porcelain, on the other hand, is non-porous, meaning it resists stains and algae better. It won’t change much over time, which can be a pro or con depending on whether you like a more ‘lived-in’ look. If you don’t mind a bit of maintenance and like the idea of natural aging, sandstone could be the way to go. If you prefer a lower-maintenance, more uniform look that stays as it was installed, porcelain might be better.

This is not good.  It's not just the butterflies -- all insects are on the decline.  The problem is multifaceted, but something as simple as incorporating native (to your area) species of flowering annuals/perennials in your flower beds and native shrubs and trees can go a long way. I'm not a native purist -- I do think there is a place for both natives and non-natives in an attractive landscape.  Incorporating proportionately more natives into my property at this house was intentional, and I have noticed a greater diversity of insects who visit -- not just butterflies, but all pollinators.  Along with that, more birds.  Remember, birds feed their young insects - few insects = few birds.   It takes time, but that old saying holds true -- plant it and they will come. What's not attractive about oaks, maples, birches, or tuliptrees?  Those are all native to the midwest and beautiful trees.  For midwestern shrubs - fothergilla, winterberry hollies, some virburnum, and various types of conifers, to name a few.  Tons of different outstanding native perennials, wherever you happen to be located. ETA:  And STOP nuking the cr*p out of your plants and lawn.  When I see a perfectly manicured lawn, to me that is not beautiful it is sad -- devoid of diversity and not supporting the ecosystem in any way; in fact, destroying it by all the chemical application.  Not every spot on a plant need spraying with something (even organics can be very harmful), and no one driving down the street cares if you lawn has a patch of violets in it, it's all green so it's fine. (FWIW - I think lawns with dandelions and violets in bloom together is beautiful.  I do acknowledge dandelions are demonized, though -- at least keep the wild violets, people.  Or let the dandelions bloom and then make dandelion wine, drinking which will get your mind off your less than pristine lawn. LOL!)

Great thinking as it is most likely wood instead of wrapped MDF. A primer like Zinsser 123 will sort that out in no time. First a light sanding with a fine grade sandpaper. Can you post up a picture or two?  If the primary driver isn't total glass (i.e. frame size) area, and the retrofit was working before, there is nothing to say that it won't continue to work. Are the current, possibly retrofit, windows capped as well?  When we tear out a retrofit and capped window, we inspect all the wood that is under the capping (sill, old frame, trim, etc.).  Most times, assuming the previous window was done properly, the wood is fine and drier that it ever way.  Re-capping as part of the new window ensures that bulk moisture transfer to the wood is eliminated and all you are dealing with is some capillary draw which normally won't present as an issue. Do you have an evidence of any leaks?  I suppose you could remove some of the capping on one window and inspect the wood beneath, but that is rarely done unless there is some history of leaks and the contractor is trying to get a handle of the scope so that the change orders aren't as significant. I don't see anything in the prior commentary from the contractor as a red flag.  Often times its more about correlating the verbiage of what the installer/contractor is seeing and thinking to what the homeowner is understanding.  When you get into exterior trim removal, rough opening sizes, brick openings, drainage planes, etc., it can be hard for the contractor to effectively relate what they are saying. Hi Jennifer, When selecting a new entryway light, there are a few key guidelines to ensure it complements your home’s architecture and provides the right illumination: 1. Size Matters A common mistake is choosing a fixture that’s too small. A good rule of thumb is to select a light that is one-third to one-quarter the height of your door. If you have double doors or a tall entryway, consider sizing up or using two matching fixtures for balance. 2. Consider the Viewing Angles If your entryway has a window above the door, your fixture will be visible from the outside, making its design and light quality even more important. Opt for a fixture with an attractive shape and finish that enhances curb appeal from every angle. 3. Choose the Right Light Tone The color temperature of your fixture plays a big role in ambiance. For a warm and welcoming glow, choose 2700K–3000K bulbs, which mimic the warmth of candlelight. Avoid harsh blue-toned lights, as they can feel cold and uninviting. Color Tones in Lighting 4. Style & Finish Coordination Your new fixture should complement your home’s architectural style. Whether it’s a classic lantern, modern sconce, or elegant pendant, ensure the finish matches or coordinates with existing exterior hardware for a cohesive look.

Yeah, I was thinking along those actual lines, though more Gisele than a regular combi-steam.  I don't know how real the videos are vs. how much they're ”sort of”.  The weigh, boil, steam, slow cook, seem obvious.  The blender stuff compared to a stick blender to puree your soup should be fine.  The whip probably works, but looks like a mess, and one has to wonder about deflating while trying to get the whipped stuff out, but there's no reason to think it doesn't work.  And as one who had to hand whip a dozen eggwhites to stiff peaks back when, I'll say just about anything is better.  There's a turbo setting for blender stuff, but I don't know if to goes to 100% liquify.  The FP style chop/mince is pretty straightforward.  There is a temperature control, and it should be accurate, but it tops out at boiling. All that seems fine, but the manual is useless, all CYA stuff and names of parts.  The website says 28 functions.  There are tiny videos with no explanations.  1.  Brown.  Well it's not sear.  They show strips of meat being whirled around.  I don't know if it's turbo or something.  Not what my mother meant when she taught me to brown the meat.  2. Caramelize.  The video shows making toffee!  That's no problem with a low temp unit.  Serious something lost in translation.  3. Chop.  This is the FP thing.  4. Cook.  They show it cooking what looks like fettuccini — already curled up in a canister, so they don't have to deal with softening long dry sticks.  I'm sure you can heat some water in it, put the ends of the past in until they soften, and ease them in, same way as in any small pot.  But heating and hydrating dry pasta is ”cook”?  More lost in translation?  5. Crush.  More blender/FP work.  Crushed ice.  6. Emulsify.  Blender trick again.  They show making mayonnaise.  I posit that it's the same deal as crushing ice—the knife thing goes round fast—and it's the egg yolk and the mustard doing the actual emmulsification, but that's just being picky.  It's a sales brochure and non-cooks coukd be swayed by look Ma, I can make mayo!  7. Fermentation.  Cozy spot for your bread dough to rise.  Useful in a cold kitchen, especially with a constannt temperature, which this is supposed to have, though the manual starts with safe internal temperatures for meats, but they don't include a termometer.  Natural point of collaboration or even just branding, with Thermoworks.  Thermomix sell casserole dishes.  The kind that go in ovens.  'Cause you can prep in the Thermomix and make a normal baked casserole.  I just find it hilarious. 8.  “Grate”.  They powder up a block of parm or similar.  A third lost in translation, but there is an actual grater add-on purchase.  9.Heat.  It's hard to tell, but I think they're putting in chunks of chocolate and whirring them around at heat, then pouring over a tall stack of American style pancakes.  (Ugh.  Maple syrup, or blueberry, please, but one could use the same basic method to make a nice ganache, and the pouring was a good demo of what it actually was.  And melting chocolate without a double boiler, or a good induction hob, is nice.)  10. Kettle.  Huh?  They pour in a pitcher of water and whirr it around, then show a spouted kettle or teapot pouring.  The Termomix cylinder Has a handle.  There is a third party strainer lid with a pour spout, but I get the idea you could boil water and pour it into a pitcher or wide opening teapot.  11.  Knead.  Straightforward enough.  Put in your ingredients and it will mix and knead your dough.  Then you can make your dough ball, and if it's bread, put it in fermentation mode.  12. Mix.  Use it to beat up your cake batter.  13.  Pre-clean.  Like the self clean on my Vita-mix.  Gets the gunk, then you wash/rinse.  14. Pulverize.  I think they're putting in granulated sugar and making ppowdered sugar.  Another blender trick, but the sugar won't etch the stainless vessel the way it dies the clear plastic or glass of a regular blender jar. 15. Rice.  Steam rice in the basket insert that comes with it.  16. Sauté.  Um.  Okay.  They whirr around some chunks of onion so they're a bit beaten up, soft and gold and add to a tart.  I wonder if one could do a real sauté with the knife out.  I use the sauté mode on my multicooker that way, but only for things that don't matter, to save an extra pot.  But, you can, is the point, right?  17. Slow cook.  They show a very wet preparation with the knife in and stirring.  Way different from the norm.  No wonder they sell that cover thing.  They made a piece of meat to be shredded.  One has to be more careful with other things.  But I'm sure it works fine on slow cook in the right configuration.  18. Sous vide.  Quite normal.  Put pouch in water. The knif circulates the water, held at temperature.  Use shield to protect pouch.  19.  Steam.  In the lidded double tray on top.  They show a mix of things and what look like meatballs with the buns they kneaded and fermented on the upper tray. 20. Stir mode.  Not sure.  Maybe they're heating soup?  Stirring is nice, but it's the knife assembly.  Good for consistent temperature, but not scraping the corners, sudes nor bottom.  Good if you don't want lumos in your farina?  Oh!  Maybe it was dried peas becoming soup, but I stand by the scraping comments.  21. Thicken.  It looks like milk and flour going in.  I don't understand what they're making, but I'm guessing they mean ”reduce”.    22. Weigh.  Involved digital interface, good for beginners who don't know how.  Accurate to the gram.  23. Whip.  They use cream, not stiff peaks, and don't show how it works or how you get it out.  24. Whisk.  This is the eggs.  They show a bit more and do get stiff peaks.  They make a Pavlova or similar. I wonder if it can do fewer eggs. They say 28 modes.  There are 9 video pages with three per page.  The first one is about general use and putting it together, and the first two on the last page are the last two from the previous page (pesumably to use the same template) so they're off by four.  Or maybe they count differently.  I think it's a European company, so how different could they be?  Do they count thumbs once as fingers and once as not? I still think this is as great as device as it seemed all those years ago when a gal on GW was trying to get one from Canada (before they were sold here), and the faults noted above are in the marketing much more than the product..  People install Nutone systems (1960's whizbang) in larger RVs, especially if they're full timing.  I think this does more, better, in less space, though it's heavy and maybe not for older people if they're moving around often, but if they can secure it for travel easily and have a bit of counter space, it could be magic.

Well, YIKES!! Looks like you have green (therefore viable) branches, and a BUNCH of ROOTS! So you're starting on the plus side. This will be basically like an "AI" response (but from a real human) because I'm just telling you everything I can think of/learned in 40+ years of "trying" to Garden.(!) First, we are supposed to change out soil, every two or three years. I was about to chide you for using cactus mix, but turns out you're on the right track; they sell something called "palm/citrus/cactus mix." Who knew! You need a mix that holds water, but drains well. I also ran across something called "Lemon Grove" for planting/potting lemon trees, on Amazon. Amazon also has a cheaper one similar but half the price. You may be able to find local (go to a real Nursery, and expect to pay more if you buy it there rather than online or at BigBox store.) I used to listen to a Nursery Guy on a radio call-in show, who advised using fertilizer (specific for lemon trees/citrus) at half-rate,  twice as often. In your case I think I'd go by the label instructions and watch how it responds before making adjustments (reminds me of ppl in recipe comments who never make the recipe the way it was demonstrated, "I used nutmeg instead of cinnamon, and I hate bell peppers so j just put in an extra cucumber"🤭) Full disclosure, your Meyer Lemon looks about like mine (potted/stuck out in on unloved flower bet in the south forty), which I've neglected for years, tho it does get watered (have *never* changed out the soil, (!)... I was sure it was a goner, then my DH came in with a couple little LEMONS from my neglected child! Now I'm all enthused to take all the advice above, and revive my baby for some payoff later on. Anyway, I live in California, so cold isn't a huge problem. Occasionally gets to the teens, but usually no worse than low 20s briefly. I've never coddled it-- it just stays put all winter, and does it's best to stay alive. If you live where temps stay low for long, maybe just keep it in the garage, without expecting it to make leaves or lemons. Do give it water once in a while, for the roots' sake. Bring out to patio when freezing no longer a risk, and wait for new leaves to start. Fertilize after it's acclimated to outdoor air/wate If you only get freezy cold occasionally, I think moving the pot to an outside heated-house wall, that gets morning sun but not north winds, AND covering it with plant covers (See amazon), should be enough to protect it and eliminate the shock of moving to new environment that causes leaf drop.

Stop right now and shut off your water heater if it's operating. Your water heater is unvented and it can kill you. Note: Your plans call for an ELECTRIC water heater. A proper vent through the roof may be able to use the existing furnace and water heater. Other options include sidewall venting using PVC pipe which would require replacing the furnace and water heater. If your garage stays mostly warm, you can switch the water heater out with an electric hybrid heater and avoid a flue altogether for the water heater. A hybrid electric is the least expensive way to heat water - and hundreds less a year than a standard electric water heater. It may sound odd. It's cheap, fast, and probably no one out looking for it right now. But get a bag of plain grilling charcoal. No EZ start or anything like that. A box of garbage bags- bigger heavier ones are better, but you can double bag if you need to. A pillow sack or bed linen to use as a clothes sack. Get your garbage bag set up. Dump a bunch of the charcoal in. Put your clothes sack in. Tie the garbage sack tight. The charcoal will help absorb the odors. If they can get a bag of cheap cedar or pine pet bedding, they can toss some of that in with the charcoal to help "sweeten" it. It can take a few days, but it should help. And helps keep the smell closed up in the small space of a hotel room. After washing, they can do the same thing, but using baking soda instead of charcoal in the garbage bag. Still use a clothes bag to help keep the clothes dust free. If a dollar store or other has cheap packs of white school chalk or any sidewalk chalk. Chalk is an odor and moisture absorber and can be put in the bags. The garbage bag thing can be used with other stuff too, like shoes, bags, jackets, ect that aren't so washable. Or if they have paper goods like books, photos, important documents that have smoke odor that works too. There are laundry soaps for removing odors, but they can get kind of pricy. Probably some of the easiest to find and less expensive would be scent killer soaps hunters use. It does not always fully strip smoke out of fabric, but it can work better than some regular laundry soaps and it has no scent. So you can tell how much you have washed out at least. If there is some sootiness or ick touch to the fabric, you can try looking for a gallon of Fast Orange or Gojo hand cleaner- make sure it's the smooth stuff, not the gritty. Usually found at auto places or the auto section in many box stores. Use some of that in a sink or bathtub as a prewash to soak out stuff.

If you have sufficient space you would be far better having a 900 x 900 L shaped base unit in each corner which will allow full access to the corner and both doors can fully open. Trying to get in a straight corner base unit with a 400 door is a nightmare. See image for what l mean.

If i understand correctly what b&q have told you is that any 'blind' corner unit they supply, the only way that the door is hinged is from the side panel, ie the left hand corner unit has a left hand blank panel [as its tucked away under the corner] and the door is hinged off the right hand side panel and the handle is in the corner, this is the complete opposite to the rest of the industry, for any corner unit the door would be hinged off the centre post. Looking at the b&q website they even shows the door hinged off the centre post. As 'standard' a corner unit with a 400 door would be made using an 800 unit with a 200-230 void [blanking panel and corner post]. With a 900 unit the centre post is set up for a 450 door [not sure if it can be moved as they have a top metal rail] so a 400 door has to hinge from the side panel. Again looking on their website they have corner pull outs to fit inside 800 corner units and the door is hinged off the centre post so they do have 800 corner units - maybe its an up selling technique they use making you buy their corner pull outs. I'd go back into the shop and have a look at their displays if you have the the doors hinged the way it looks [with the handles in the corners] then you'll need 155 or more degree hinges [for easier access] and your doors could end up banging into the oven handle and getting damaged, also ask why the corner unit is a 900 instead of 800, did you ask for a bigger corner unit? Hello Samara, the pipe in question leads to the top of the tank, so this should be the inlet pipe and the branch coming off this with the "spigot - hose connection" has been set up as a poorly designed "First Flush" system to divert / catch dirt and leaves. It is a poor design because for it to work, it needs to be manually emptied every time it rains. The Cap at the bottom can be unscrewed to empty the leaves & dirt but the spigot was probably added so to connect a garden hose with a trigger nozzle, which drains off the flushed water. The other Pipe that connects to the side of the tank should be the drain outlet that then runs to the stormwater in the street. I think there is a single cause underlying the variety of symptoms, and it isn't insect herbivory or disease pathogens. If you want to open a discussion about what that cause might be, we can almost certainly determine a strategy, even if it is multi-pronged, to resolve the issue if you determine suggested accommodations to be reasonable. In my experience, the cause will be related to what cultural factors might be interfering with normal root function. There is also potential for some of the damage to be nutritionally related, but nutritional issues can be caused by too much or too little of various nutrients, or they can be caused by seemingly extraneous cultural factors inhibiting uptake of key nutrients. Examples: If someone adds a little extra a shot of Epsom salts for the magnesium content, the excess can cause a Calcium deficiency. Too, over-watering can cause a 'cultural' deficiency of Ca, which would account for symptoms presented on plants other than the F. elastica. The necrotic leaf margins on the F. elastica are likely from over-watering or a level of dissolved solids (salts) in the soil solution at levels greater than the plant is programmed to deal with, unless the leaf is an older leaf located low on the plant. The leaves on the Ficus are likely in the process of being shed due to normal senescence (aging), or because they are being shaded by leaves higher on the plant. A reduction in light levels reduces the flow of a growth regulator/ hormone (auxin) which essential to keep a layer from forming (abscission layer) at the base of the leaf stem where it attaches to the branch or stem. Once the abscission starts to form, the flow of water/nutrients to the leaf is walled off from the rest of the plant and the flow of photosynthate (sugar - the plant's true food) is gradually reduced. Essentially, the change in the plant's chemical messengers alert plant central that the leaves have become a liability, and that starts the irreversible shedding process. I sounds like you've done a good amount of research on your own, and are definitely on the right course insofar as your your journey toward a green thumb. There really isn't much to critique about your care regimen, but maybe some answers to questions will reveal something that leads to improvement in your plant's vitality. *Can the plants most affected by the symptoms you've shown be said to be in deeper pots than those less affected? Using the digital tester Mother Nature gave you (a finger or thumb) works fine for testing moisture levels deep in the pot if the soil is 5" deep or deeper. For deeper pots, a wooden tell stuck all the way to the bottom of the pot will give you a better read on moisture levels, and keep you on track insofar as determining appropriate watering intervals. if you use a finger in deeper pots, the tendency will lean toward over-watering in a high % of cases. To keep track of when each plant should be fertilized, drop a marble, button, bottle cap, ...., into the pot when you water. That way, you need only count the objects to know when each planting needs fertilizing. When you fertilize, remove the objects and start over. * Are you sure the entire soil column is getting saturated when you water? *Does your home make use of a water softening system that requires recharging with salt as the ionic exchange medium? * How weak is the fertilizer solution you customarily apply? If you are fertilizing at every watering, you should be flushing the soil with each watering and using somewhere around 1/2 tsp/gal. It would probably be better to tie your nutritional supplementation to the number of times you water instead of the calendar. I grow under LED lighting, use FP 9-3-6, and I used to water with 1/4 tsp/gal at each watering. I changed that so I'm fertigating (fertilizing + irrigating) plants in smaller volumes of soil more often because the nutrient levels in the soil solution are more affected by flushing than plants in larger pots. I have plants in pots that hold less than an ounce of soil all the way up to plants that hols several gallons of soil. You might try using 1/2-1 tsp/gal and fertilizing every 3rd or 4th time you water. You can do the same in summer, but increase the fertilizer strength to adjust for the increase in light/ growth rate/ increase in temperatures. Would I be right to guess your home temps range from 65-75*? Do you have an idea re what the relative humidity (R/H) % range is? I grow in my basement where I keep temps at 66-68* nights & 72* days. R/H is kept as high as I can w/o moisture forming on basement windows, so from 55-62%. Low R/H is usually more of a contributing or exacerbating factor when it comes to spoiled foliage due to leaf hydration issues, and longitudinal tears in foliage occur frequently as a result of low humidity levels while the leaf is unfurling. * Did you add any supplemental liming agent to the soil when you made it? Have you used anything other than FP 9-3-6 as part of your nutritional supplementation? * Do you get the sense that the soil might be holding too much water? If yes, I can share some tricks that will reduce the volume of water the planting will hold after a thorough watering. Some remedies are passive, require little to no effort on your part, others require a slight effort when its time to water, but nothing most would consider to be seriously off-putting. I feel like there is something I'm missing, but it's late and I'm getting tired. If I think of anything, I'll add it later. I do think though, that you've put most of the things most growers don't consider behind you, so it's more about tweaking your routines than reordering them entirely. Al

I think I understand.  The original owner passed away and you would like to buy the home so that your child can live close to you / in the same neighborhood. Assuming they are auctioning all the contents, then will have the house cleaned and put on the market or have it auctioned.   I know several "kids" who opted to have the house auctioned vs the typical selling process.  They didn't want the headaches and auction was the easy button. Two of my nieces bought homes in the past 3 years that were being sold by the children of the owner.  One the owner had passed away, the other the owner went to an Alzheimer Care facility. You need to be a bit more careful in this type of transaction because the disclosure will be fairly worthless.   If the kids didn't live in the house they can claim ignorance of past issues, so question after question is answered "unknown".   (Has the roof ever leaked?  unknown) If the seller was living in the home they would be required to answer yes or no and if they lied you can go to an attorney and make them pay for issues with the roof. One of my nieces bought 2 years ago and where she bought things were moving really fast.   Properties had multiple offers come in within a day or two of listing and most were giving a deadline to have your offer in within 3-4 days of listing and most were turning away offers with contingencies.   In my nieces case the realtor for the seller told my nieces agent that they would not allow an inspection.  The kids did not want to know if something was wrong because they would have to disclose it and it could lower the price.   We hired an inspector to walk through of the home and provide verbal feedback on anything he thought was a red flag.  He pointed out quite a few things we would not have noticed, but didn't find any big red flags. My other niece bought just a few months ago in a different city.   The market was not as hot and she had her offer accepted with an inspection as a contingency. Only you and the realtors in your area can determine how hot the market is in your neighborhood and what may or may not be accepted.   Since they are selling through their estate attorney, I would expect that they won't want an inspection.   If they allow an inspection and the sale falls through they would have to disclose any issues found in the inspection. Because you live in the neighborhood you may have a good idea of what issues have been experienced in the neighborhood.   Were the homes all built around the same time and built by the same builder?     Some neighborhoods are more standardized, some are all custom homes built over decades by different builders. Price is generally based on square footage and neighborhood with some allowance for the general condition of the property. You should be able to get comps run by any realtor or find them yourself online.   What has sold in the neighborhood in the past 6 months.   Sometimes you have to go to similar neighborhoods that are close by if their haven't been any sales or only 1 or 2 sales in your specific neighborhood. If they want a quick sale without paying realtor commissions and your offer is reasonable they may not want to bother with going on the market.

Instead of a sectional, maybe put in a wall unit on the long wall, one with doors that you can close off the television when not in use, or to keep the glare from the sun coming through the tall windows onto the tv screen. A matching chair on each side of the couch, one against the stair wall, the other opposite,  provides more seating for guests without restricting the flow. These words, from Suleika, are really profound for all of us: For the last few months, small joys have been my sustenance… Often these small moments fade from view with the passage of time. What makes it into our memory banks are the bigger things—either the zeniths or the nadirs—but what we end up longing for and leaning on in hard times are the little quotidian comforts and delights; they lift and carry us from day to day. Noting these joys is a muscle I’ve been consciously trying to exercise: training the eye to see them and training the mind to hold onto them. I do want to make a distinction here between the practice of celebrating small joys and the culture of “toxic positivity,” where we’re told to be ever-grateful, to always search for the silver linings, to put a positive spin on all experiences, even the profoundly tragic. The author Barbara Ehrenreich has written critically about this cultural phenomenon with far more nuance than I can in this missive, but it’s a topic I’ve thought a lot about, especially in these last months. It’s easy to feel pressure to be someone who “suffers well”—grateful and graceful and stoic 24/7. But that doesn’t allow us to exist fully, to experience the full range of the human condition, from happiness to grief, from gratitude to envy. I love observing tiny daily joys because it feels natural and easy, not forced, not pressurized, not all or nothing. And not only has the practice helped ease this difficult passage, it’s helped me identify what lifts me up, and then I can cultivate more of it. I also think this, below is something many people could benefit from as a "policy." A Few Requests & Ways to Help— In sharing this news with the community, I’d also like to include a few of the same requests that I sent two years ago when I wrote about my relapse. Please no pity, no advice, no unsolicited medical information, no dietary recommendations, no alternative cures from your great-grandmother’s guru. I appreciate the good intentions behind these impulses, but please know that (unfortunately) I have a lot of experience when it comes to cancer, and I’m choosing the right path for me. What I do invite is love. I’ve been the very fortunate recipient of so much loving care. Yet there are many out there who are not so fortunate—and some of them are people in your own life. Reach out to someone you know who might need a little love or thoughtfulness. Everyone is carrying their own private struggle, and you never know how far your kindness will go.

Hi Beatrice, If you're considering replacing your steam shower, there are a few things to consider and options based on your needs, budget, and the overall design of your bathroom. Replacing a steam shower can be an upgrade to increase comfort, functionality, and luxury, but it can also be a practical decision when your current steam shower is outdated or broken. Here's a guide to help you understand your options and what to consider: 1. Reasons for Replacing a Steam Shower Malfunctioning Equipment: If your steam generator or shower components are beyond repair or the cost of repair is too high, replacement is often the most practical solution. Outdated Design: If your steam shower no longer fits the modern aesthetic of your bathroom or you’re updating the space with more current materials and features. Upgrading Features: Replacing an old steam shower can also be a chance to upgrade to a more efficient or technologically advanced model, incorporating features like Bluetooth speakers, LED lighting, digital controls, or a more energy-efficient steam generator. 2. Options for Replacing a Steam Shower Upgraded Steam Shower If you liked your old steam shower but wanted a better model, then getting an upgraded steam shower would be something worth considering. Automated steam generators that cut down on waiting time for the steam. Superior insulation to maximize steam retention and minimize heat loss. Stand-alone Steam Shower Unit If your steam shower is presently an enclosure that is custom-built, you may want to consider a stand-alone steam shower unit. They come as an all-in-one, ready-to-install enclosure that features a built-in steam generator, seating, and possibly other features. Generally speaking, these are easier and faster to install with options to fit a variety of budgets from simple to luxury high-end models. Some of the benefits: Ease of installation: ideal to replace existing shower spaces. Compact and space-saving, perfect for smaller bathrooms. Multiple sizes for different spaces. Steam Room Conversion If you have the space and want to create a more luxurious experience, you might consider converting a traditional shower or bathroom into a full steam room. This would include replacing the shower with steam-generating equipment, proper insulation for a steam room, and adding features like seating, steam-proof doors, and exhaust systems. Custom steam rooms: Because they are custom-fit to your bathroom, you have more flexibility in size and features. Larger capacity: They can hold multiple users at once. Shower + Sauna Combo For the ultimate in relaxation, some homeowners choose to replace a steam shower with a shower-sauna combo. This allows you to enjoy both steam and dry heat therapy in one convenient unit, offering versatility for different relaxation needs. 3. Things to Consider When Replacing Your Steam Shower Space Is this a replacement in an existing space that needs renovation, or can you make use of the previous layout? If your current space is already designed for steam, replacing with a prefabricated unit might be easier. Ventilation: Steam showers do require some kind of ventilation. If your old setup had problems with humidity or ventilation, make sure your replacement solution includes proper steam exhaust systems and fans so that mold does not grow from excessive moisture. Power Requirements Steam generators are powered electrically. Based on your existing wiring and the size of the generator, you may need an electrical upgrade for your new steam shower: possibly an upgrade to the electrical panel if the generator of the new steam shower is larger; appropriate wiring, with dedicated circuits, for that generator and all other electrical elements involved, whether for lighting, sound systems, or otherwise. Water Supply Be sure that the water supply to your home would be enough in case you install a new steam shower unit. Steam generators require a regular supply of water at a certain temperature and pressure, so you will have to have your plumbing modified or install new water lines. Installation and Professional Help Steam shower replacement may be complex and even require professional installation, as most of the work involves electrical and plumbing. For proper installation and effectiveness, it is good to consult an expert in the steam shower systems. Budget The cost that your steam shower replacement will incur depends on: The type of replacement unit it is supposed to be-upgraded shower, stand-alone unit, custom steam room, etc. The complexity of the installation, such as electrical work, plumbing, and any remodeling required. The features and materials of the new steam shower itself-luxury models with extra features like lighting, sound systems, and seating will naturally cost more. 4. I worked in the humane industry where I worked with a group that provided care for animals owned by people who truly needed the support of their animals, including agoraphobics, people who were terminally ill, homeless people who need both the support and protection of their pets, people with PTSD along with service dogs who helped with physical support.  I also worked with Social Services with children who had been sexually or physically abused.   These kids often had difficulty trusting a person, but would talk to an animal.  We had several animals who were super gentle, patient lap animals that wouldn't react badly if the kids lost it, but just stayed calm and snuggled.  After working in the humane industry I went to work with San Diego Mental Health Systems. @auntthelma - To say that ESAs are simply pets is so wrong.   There are some people who abuse the system and sadly there are doctors who will write letters for anyone, but for many people suffering from chronic depression or anxiety, who have suffered some traumatic event, their ESA may be the only thing getting them through the day.   I remember during the late 80s, early 90s we had a large population of people who were diagnosed with AIDS.   People were frightened and didn't want to be around someone with AIDS.  Families and friends often abandoned them and the only living being that provided support were their cat or dog that laid on the bed with them.    One of the organizations I worked with was started when a gentleman with AIDS was hospitalized.   His landlord called his parents and they came and took his dogs and had them euthanized.   He came home from the hospital to find the only support he had had been killed.   Two weeks later he committed suicide.   We decided to create a support organization that would foster and care for animals for anyone who was terminally ill. In California there are three different designations, Emotional Support Animals, Service Animals and Psychiatric Support Animals. ESAs do not need any special training and are there simply as an emotional support for a person. SAs, like seeing eye dogs, dogs for hearing impaired, dogs that can sense seizures and those trained to assist with answering doors or retrieving things for someone with a physical disability need to be certified as a service dog / service animal (most are dogs, but there are other animals that can be certified. PSAs are a hybrid.  Most are dogs.  They may be trained to gently wake a person with PTSD when the person is having nightmares, they may be trained to remind owners to take their medications, they may be trained to press an alert if their owner is having a panic attack or harming themselves or they may apply deep pressure massage to help calm their owner. Each state has different laws regarding the rules for ESAs and PSAs.   Some states don't designate PSAs any differently than ESAs although the role and training may be different. In California a landlord must allow ESAs PSAs and SAs. It is sad that people with real needs are made to suffer because there are unethical, selfish people who abuse the system.

In central Virginia, the average date of the last frost varies by city and typically falls between April 10th and April 20th or thereabouts (re-confirm every year by checking local forecasts to ensure Mother Nature will stick to those average dates).  The type of shelter or winter protection can vary; you can do a Youtube search for "hydrangea winter protection" to see videos of several techniques used by other hydrangea growers. For example, for the typical shelter, consider watering the shrub deeply; mulching with organic mulch past the drip line; creating a simple frame with chicken wire and stakes; filling the frame with fallen leaves, pine needles, composted straw and-or mulch; then place a fabric like burlap over it to minimize damage by late frosts to the dormant flower buds located near the hydrangea stem endings. The more distance between the stem endings to the edge or top of the frame, the more protection the frame will provide. You could also only water deeply the night before and use lightweight fabric like old blankets, bedsheets or burlap to cover the entire bush but secure them at the base with rocks/stakes and near the top somehow as the weather will likely also include windy conditions.  While you can drop the bedsheets/etc. directly on top of your hydrangea, building a frame prevents the bedsheet from directly touching the buds at the stem tips and helps to hold some heat inside. I used mulch, rocks, bricks, or garden stakes at the bottom of my chicken wire cages. During really cold nights, you could temporarily place a plastic tarp or another layer of fabric over the bedsheets or over the chicken wire cage (especially if it will be windy) but just remember to remove the plastic during the day when warm again to let the plant breathe and prevent the shrub from overheating with warm temperatures afterwards. In central Virginia, these winter protection techniques can be set up around your city's average date of first frost (say,  between October 20th and October 30th) and removed by your city's average date of last frost (say, between April 10th and April 20th). Your dining room is dark because the window treatment is blocking natural light. A pattern is fine as long as the background color is light. Hang them at the same height as the top of the doorway. Paint the dark drape rod the same color as the wall to make the rod blend into the wall and the dining room wall will feel taller.  Remove the horizontal blinds. Your home will feel more welcoming to you if each room has the right amount of lumens in the lighting. A dining room needs a chandelier emitting 30-40 lumens per square foot. A 11x9 dining room requires 3,000 to 4,000 lumens, in other words a chandelier with 4 or 5 60-watt bulbs.

I would take down the chandelier and either replace it with a flush-mount fixture or do recessed lighting throughout the room. This will give you more freedom in how you can place your furniture. Since it looks like this room is more of an extension of the kitchen rather than a   formal dining room, I suggest a place to put your coats and shoes and another place to put your small appliances that are currently on top of the buffet with a fairly wide walk-through from the front door to the kitchen.

To finish a tile edge, you can either: - miter - use a matching pencil liner or quarter round. - use a matching bullnose tile. - use Schluter in a matching or contrasting color. The wood species pictured looks like North American oak. Could be red oak. Is your cabinet species red or white oak? Both are open grain. Worldwide there are 300+ species of oak. All rose flower parts are edible- petals, buds, hips. They are in the same family as apple and cherry trees. Often darker colored roses are supposed to be more bitter or less appealing in taste. If you are using them in a wet application like a rose water, they can make a more colorful water. Roses with many little petals like cabbage heads or wild roses will give you lots of little tender petals for eating. The big florist kinds of flowers have stronger petals that can be big as spoons and could be used like little lettuce cups are used if you wanted to. I would hazard a guess that these roses have been bred to be more appealing to eat. A lot of people aren't aware of the edible of flowers. Both options have their pros and cons, so it really depends on your priorities. Honed Carrara marble is absolutely stunning and adds a timeless, luxurious feel to a master bath. However, marble is a natural stone, so it’s more porous and can stain or etch over time, especially in a high-moisture area like a bathroom. Honed marble is slightly more forgiving than polished when it comes to etching, but it still requires regular sealing and a bit more maintenance. On the other hand, porcelain tile in a Calcutta gold marble look gives you the aesthetic of marble without the maintenance concerns. Porcelain is incredibly durable, water-resistant, and low-maintenance, making it a practical choice for a bathroom floor. The technology in porcelain tiles has come a long way, and many options look incredibly realistic. Although I personally would prefer sintertech sintered stones.  Which is the same as the porcelain look, except it's much stronger. https://www.mikolmarmi.com/blogs/marble-granite-library/sintered-stone-the-ultimate-surface-solution-for-modern-spaces?srsltid=AfmBOoo7Z1xSbI5V_nQ_fNFkMe7I8f5RSIsRcNgCRtC76aaHbLM2WD_3 If you love the idea of real marble and don’t mind the upkeep, go for the Carrara—it’s a classic. But if you want something that’s easier to live with and still looks beautiful, porcelain is a fantastic alternative. Either way, you can’t go wrong—it’s all about what fits your lifestyle and design vision! Good luck with your decision!

text: That sounds correct about uptake of microplastics being nonsense, but it is in a reputable journal that does require referees. I could imagine that *molecules* of microplastics might end up in plant tissue, but not macroscopic plastic particles. Nanoplastics are synthetic polymers with dimensions ranging from 1 nm to 1 μm. At the low end of that range, I can imagine them being suspended in fluids that plants take up.

From the abstract: Conclusively, agricultural practices, climate changes (wet weather and heavy rainfall), and soil organisms play a major role in transporting MPs and NPs in soil. NPs are more prone to enter plant cell walls as compared to MPs. Furthermore, transpiration pull is the dominant factor in the plant uptake and translocation of plastic particles. Also, this a review of the literature of plant studies published in scientific journals: We present a critical review of the previous 10 years; most of our cited literature spans the last five years of the effect of MPs and NPs on agroecosystems. Kevin, I believe you misunderstood the article.  No journal would have published any of the articles referenced/reviewed if it were impossible for plants to take up micro (MP) and nano (NP).  There is NO question about whether the particles are in the plants. They are.  The article reviews years' worth of articles and examines the findings of HOW they got there, not whether. The particles were found in the vegetables--they got there by plant uptake.  Look at Table 2:  "Accumulation of plastics in plants under different exposure conditions." Perhaps you are unfamiliar with scientific articles.  Scientists always use that terminology of "more clarification needed", etc.  It's science speak, and a call for further research. The key when looking for tubs is to pay close attention to the bathing well and water depth. The well is the space for your legs to stretch out. If you get  a tub that slopes on both sides, it will have a smaller well than one that only slopes on one side. The water depth is harder to find. Just because a tub says its 23 " high doesn't mean it has a good water depth - there are supports underneath, maybe accommodations for above floor rough-in or the upper part of the tub is curved. I have seen 23-24" high tubs have a water depth of 16" ! Not all specifications will tell you water depth but you may be able to figure it out by the overflow height - keep in mind that number is from the floor so you have to really look at the spec sheets. Find yourself a good plumbing showroom - they can do the deep dive to find the right one for you. Good luck!!

Y'all: The reason Commentors on Houzz "get into the weeds" about entire spaces is because that's what designers do! They take everything in when they enter a space. Every piece connects to every other piece--floors, cabinet finishes, built-ins, art work, , rugswindow treatments-- to create harmonious spaces where individual features echo other features. Example: If a family goes for a warm, rustic look with a lot of wood trim, then a  painted white fireplace will stick out like a sore thumb. Really, you're asking Commentors not to use all their training to focus on one thing. It's like asking a plumber to install new faucets and telling them to ignore a slightly leaky pipe under the sink. Commentors have reasons they ask for more photos, measurements, budgets, more detail, non-negotiables. Here is how to post a Design Dilemma to get the best results. You need to show the whole space—all four sides of an entire space—even if it’s about one specific Dilemma. Commenters need to see doorways, windows, closets, finishes throughtout the space to make informed suggestions. State right at the beginning what the room will be used for and who will use it. State the non-negotiables at the beginning, what has to be kept. Give some idea of the budget. And provide approximate measurements https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6417709/unofficial-design-dilemma-boot-camp Keep in mind that you're inviting some design pros and people with a design eye into your home via photos. If they walked into your actual space, they would take in all of it: all four sides, doorways, floors, windows, ceiling, built-in fixtures, lighting, trim--the "givens"--then the features that can be changed--furnishings, paint, art, rugs, decor items, etc. It's all one first impression. Same thing with photos. That's why it's important to provide well lit photos of the entire space, taken from all sides of a room regardless of the size of your problem.

I think some of the Usonian designs are not his best because some of them are a little small to carry some of the broad, sweeping horizontals he incorporated in his more custom houses, and he did tend to beat to death some of his thematic details, which tended to work in his larger houses but could come off a bit overwrought in his smaller, later ones. Really, for as innovative as his designs were in 1910, he was still a 19th c. trained architect, and his younger modernist colleagues in the middle of the 20th c. didn't really consider him a modernist architect. When they reintroduced some of his furniture in the 1980s or 1990s, they noted that they did have to alter some of the dining chair designs because the originals were just too uncomfortable because they were too tall and upright in the back. I think the last couple parts of what's going on or "wrong" is  with many modern houses they just don't take patina or natural aging very well. They just look beat up. There is a c. 1820 house around the corner from me that a man lived in for decades as a stabilized ruin. He made it weather tight so leaks and such didn't penetrate, but there were areas that hadn't been painted inside after about 1900. Lots of deteriorated surfaces, but it was still beautiful. A veneer plywood flush door comparison looks terrible with a couple scratches on it. And, I don't think people know exactly what to do with interiors of a house like this. Most regular furniture looks terrible in these houses, it looks extraneous. I think if we were looking at this house in mint condition with minimal furniture pretty much all designed by Wright, and some carefully curated objects, which is really how he wanted his clients to live--he wanted to control everything--it would probably make for a much better visual experience.  But I think this is one reason why his houses do not fly off the market. It's a commitment to live in one.

Not a FLW fan at all.  (This showcases the many reasons why.)  It was such a drag when I lived in Chicago and out of town visitors wanted to tour FLW Oak Park homes. My grandparents knew Mr. Kauffman, who owned Fallingwater, and my mom hung out and swam there as a kid.  I love thinking about her going down those living room stairs and into the water.  But that is the extent of my affection for FLW.  Fallingwater has no structural integrity and has had to be rebuilt several times.  Not such a great architect after all.

I don't mind the esthetic of a lot of his houses, I just think they would be hard to live in, and this is not one of his great ones. Actually the underpinning of Fallingwater is fine, it was never really a design issue. There were two errors in the construction mostly related to the main cantilevered terrace. One is that the buttresses for the cantilever should have been extended under the main terrace just a little bit more, and the second, more major error is that the concrete was not pre-stressed adequately because they didn't really understand how to do it in 1936. The cantilevers should have been built on an upward angle trajectory above the horizontal so that it would "stretch" or sag into a horizontal position which would then put tension on the concrete which would be stronger, if I am understanding it correctly, and instead, it was build completely level so it relaxed into a downward sloping position, which continued to happen over time as well. And the ground around it is a little dynamic, so while the core is firmly anchored the perimeter bits are not as rigid leading to some issues in the past with opening and closing the corner windows, and glass cracking where it is let into the masonry and so forth. And all his houses were very leaky because the membranes to keep water out in something built like this didn't even exist. So it's not really a structural integrity issue so much, much of his work is stronger than it strictly needs to be. The Lily Pad columns in the Johnson Wax building are capable of bearing much more weight than they need to for their purpose. He frequently had to prove this with testing prior to building. Johnson Wax also leaked like a sieve. But his hotel in Tokyo survived an earthquake that leveled a lot of things around it.   That said, none of these things necessarily make his houses very livable. The senior Kauffmans were not totally in love with Fallingwater. Edgar Jr. liked it more than they did but left it to the PA Conservancy because he knew as it aged he would never be able to afford to maintain it. It requires an incredible amount of maintenance.

Engineers warned him that his structure was flawed and if built as designed wouldn't survive the stress.  FLW's ego was always too damn big.  My dad is an engineer and I think I saw steam blowing out of his ears in furry when we visited Fallingwater together.  Is something really a masterpiece if you cannot, in your day and age, figure out a way to successfully construct it?

You say that it is too small to use as a dining room. Is that what you wish it were? We could maybe help you fit a dining table in there. If not, making it a cozy reading space with places for outdoor wear is a good use of the space.

Well engineers told him it would collapse immediately as soon as they took the cribs out from under the terrace and here it is 89 years later, hanging over running water, an element that can destroy anything.  They also said the the lily pad columns in Johnson Wax would not hold up the building and required that a test column be built and withstand a 12 ton dead weight applied to the top. It cracked at a weight of Sixty tons placed on it and then collapsed when the cribs helping to balance the lily pad were completely removed. So Wright was an egomaniac, a control freak, and all round terrible person, but "under engineered" his projects are not. Flawed, leaky, and so forth yes. But I disagree that the engineering was bad.

I am thinking about my career and how I got my start in computer science.   I had a brother in law who had a job at IBM working with the new PCs. I needed a job and in one of the interviews I was asked if I knew how to use an IBM PC.   I said yes and crossed my fingers that I could learn fast.   I had used the old Wang word processors and had seen an IBM PC. Looking back, that first IBM PC with the green screen, having to know your dos commands to open each program and storing your work on floppy disks was a clunky bear of a machine. Connecting to the internet to do research through the accustic modem was pretty clunky too.   Things like finding legal presidents could take days of searching compared to moments with today's technology.     It was these innovators who could imagine the possibilities that got us started on the personal technology journey. When I read through posts on Houzz where people are designing their home one of the guaranteed resposes is that the home needs to be designed in relationship with the site. That was a core concept of FLW -  Organic Architecture - architectural designs should be derived from their surroundings, integrating with the landscape. He also introduced the concept of open floorplans combining multiple rooms into a continuous space and minimizing interior walls. He believed natural daylight was essential to our wellbeing and built homes with huge expanses of windows, used light tubes and skylights to fill the home with natural daylight. Aren't those primary desires of most homeowners today.  Light and bright and open. In my mind,  Wright's influence on the future of architecture and the way we live in our homes  is part of the reason why Wright was recognized in 1991 by the American Institute of Architects as "the greatest American architect of all time."

To have an island in the Kitchen you need: 25.5"D counters + 42" aisle (minimum recommended for a one-person work aisle) + 27"D island (no seating) + 36" aisle behind the island ======= 130.5" You only have 106" (8'10") to work with, so your Kitchen is 24" or so too narrow.  Factor in the doorway and that 36" aisle should really be more like 48".   Regardless, your Kitchen is too narrow. The Dining Room on the other hand, is 140" (11'8") wide.  So you would have more space to work with.  To get seating, you would likely have to make the island mostly seating, only shallow cabinets. 25.5"D counters + 42" aisle (minimum recommended for a one-person work aisle) + 24.5"D island (1.5" overhang + 9"D cabs + 14"D seating overhang) + 48" aisle behind the island ======= 140" The "new" Dining Room could then have banquette seating to fit a table with seating and room to move.

Here's the reason why insulating older lath & plaster homes can be problematic: That era of plaster would also likely be balloon framed and have only wood clapboards or 1x sheathing on the exterior. That construction method is very air leaky, meaning air is moving through the walls from in and out and from low to high and mitigating any moisture (that is it's success). If you only add blow-in insulation into walls, or even tear out the plaster and add fiberglass batts with new drywall on walls, without addressing the air leakage from the balloon framing or the exterior envelope skin, could lead to the moisture causing problems. Spray foam is an alternative, but would require removal of the plaster and detailing considering the sheathing/lack of and balloon framing.
