Here's an idea with minimal structural changes and combining/tweaking what you have. Primary change: Move the Linen Closets "up" approx. 12" and claim that space for the Pantry.  There's plenty of space for that change in the Master Bathroom. Pantry...This gives you more room in the Pantry for useable storage as well as maneuvering in the Pantry.  (Alternatively, you could add the deeper space on the right for standard base & upper cabinets, if you'd like.)  [12"D is the "sweet spot" for pantry storage shelving -- deep enough for all the most over-sized small appliances but not so deep things will get lost.  It will fit the largest cereal boxes, blender, bread maker, toaster, food processor, KA stand mixer, etc.  That's what I did in my pantry.  Although, I did move the KA Mixer to the counter in the Kitchen b/c it was too heavy to lug back & forth.] I added a 6" x 6" post b/c usually it's needed when eliminating a long load-bearing wall.  If it's not needed, then just ignore it, it doesn't affect the layout. Snack/Coffee Center and Dining Room...It eliminates the "buffet" and replaces it with upper/base cabinetry for more storage and better counterspace for staging dishes/food in the Dining Room.  You can create a nice-looking setup for that space by using glass cabinets and/or uppers to the counter and/or paneling for the backsplash area, etc.. If you really want the "buffet" (e.g., if it's a family heirloom or antique), then modify the cabs as necessary.  I did this to create a Snack & Coffee/Tea Center that includes a Coffeemaker ("C"), MW Drawer, and Refrigerator Drawers (or a Beverage Ref).  Water is nearby on the island.  The only drawback is that the freezer is on the other side of the Kitchen.  (You could, alternatively, put the MW Drawer b/w the Refrigerator and range, if it's important enough to you.)  The Ref drawers would hold creamer, etc., for snacks and coffee and/or tea.  One drawer could also hold condiments for the table (e.g., ketchup, butter). Prep Zones...This layout has 3 potential Prep Zones - two will be the most useful with a third if you really need it.  However, the third does not have direct access to water, which is a key component of a successful/functional Prep Zone. The Primary Prep Zone is in the island.  It creates a great work triangle and follows the typical Kitchen workflow of Refrigerator > Sink >Prep Workspace > Range > Cleanup Zone (or, Ice.Water.Stone.Fire) without zone-crossing. This layout also allows several people to work in the Kitchen at the same time -- prepping (2 people), cooking, cleaning up. Aisles...All aisles provide enough space for multiple people to be working in the Kitchen at the same time.  They also provide enough room to maneuver around the table, island, cabinets, and people working in the Kitchen or going in/out the doors on the "bottom" of the Dining Room. Island...The island seats 4 in a configuration that encourages visiting/conversation.  Seating with all seats in a row on one side is like sitting in a diner where lone diners often sit so they don't have to interact with anyone else.  The island also has a prep sink and the trash pullout. Trash pullout...The trash pullout is in the Primary Prep Zone where it's the most useful, but still easily accessible from both the Cooking and Cleanup Zones.  (More trash and recyclables are generated when prepping and used for a longer amount of time than any other zone/task.)   Work Zones

No open shelving above the refrigerator -- dust magnet and it will be difficult to clean all the way back.  I would also forego the glass doors and just get regular doors. A couple of options: Option 1:  Full-depth cabinet (24"D) and store vases and pitchers.  Put the things you use the most in the front and those that you use rarely in the back.  (I also store my napkin holder and trivets there - but I'm the shortest in my family at 5'10" so I can reach to about the middle without a stool.) Option 2:  Shallow cabinet (12" to 15"D) pulled forward so it appears full-depth.  You will likely have to attach it to the ceiling, though, since it won't be against the back wall (unless you build out the wall). Regardless of option, I recommend not bringing the cabinet all the way down to the top of the refrigerator.  Instead, install it about 3" to 4" above and fill the gap with filler that's finished to match the cabinet.  The filler gives you the option of removing or reducing it if needed in the future while still making the refrigerator look built-in. Speaking of that...to make it look built-in, create an alcove that's at least 37" to 38" wide by installing finished end panels on the sides and the cabinet above.  Then, slide the refrigerator in.  The end panels should be deep enough to cover the refrigerator box, not doors, and no deeper.  Deeper ones would block the movement of the doors and prevent them from opening fully. The 37"-38" assumes you have a 36"W refrigerator and will never go wider.  If you think you might go wider in the future, then consider putting in a couple of 6"W pullouts on either side of the refrigerator to give you options in the future.  However, 36" is the most common width for refrigerators, especially counter-depth, so I don't know if you want to go any wider. If you have a narrower refrigerator, I would still create the 37"-38" alcove since that will be the easiest and, likely, least expensive option for replacement in the future.  [I think 36" is the narrowest in the Thermador Freedom series.] If wider, then the width + 2" would work.  [I think they also come in 42" & 48" widths.] (The extra couple of inches is to allow air clearance around the refrigerator as well as room to easily move the refrigerator in/out of the alcove.)

Since you linked this thread to the Tomatoes forum I'd assume you plan to grow tomatoes up a trellis. If that's the case then you would want a strong strudy trellis which will hold up during storms and strong winds, particularly during late in the season when tomatoes are heavy and growing near the top. I used to use 1/2" rebar as tomato stakes but had to upsize the rebar to 3/4" to support the late season weight and prevent the rebar from bending over during storms. Whatever type of trellis you use make sure it's secured to the ground well, and buried deep enough not to tip over.

I don't use actual obelisks, but I do use other towers or verticals. Depends on what I'm growing what can work well or less. Cheap tomato cages suck for most tomatoes, but often are good for other veggies like peppers, eggplants, and some bushier beans and cukes can sometimes benefit from support. And also caging in sprawly plants or flowering heads of things. Bigger and sturdier tomato cages can be good for det toms, vining cukes, small squashes or melons. Big indet toms I've found need big support, a lot of people like cattle panels as heavy duty towers or attach trellis onto a hefty support post or fence. Vining beans, peas, or other lighter grows can get teepees of bamboo or an old outdoor umbrella frame as support and it works fine. Some folks have local metal shops, and can get something welded up. Or find odd finds and use them- I've seen old kids swing sets and the like remade into trellising or old TV antenna tower sections used. As said, whatever you use, make sure it is footed in and/or anchored well. It really is a bummer to have it all plush and growing in and it gets knocked over by a storm. Most garden verticals, even really sturdy ones, aren't heavy enough to stand without good footing or anchoring.

The tidy of a tomato plant depends more on the habit of the plant and the gardeners upkeep than the support itself. Some tomatoes tend to sprawl, branch out, or become monsters. Others grow a bit more behaved, are bushier or determinate. Many gardeners groom their plants for various reasons, and if you don't groom them, they won't be tidy. Using a tower like an obelisk, you would still want to tie up your vines as they grow, trim out leaves too close to the ground, ect. I think a disadvantage of using an obelisk for tomatoes is that it tapers to the top, and tomatoes tend to stay plush through their whole length/height. So you are giving your plants less space as they grow up the obelisk. While this isn't a problem for some other vining veggies that tend to a singular vine, this can become an issue with a tomato. If you groom to a couple leaders, it can work. Again, depending on the habit of the tomato itself. Some lend to cutting back to a couple leaders, some do not. So... what kinds of tomatoes are you planning on growing?

Phytophthera ramorum =  Sudden Oak Death (SOD). And while it has a large host range, it predominately affects woody plants - trees and shrubs. Very few herbaceous plants (perennials, annuals, grasses, etc.) are affected. And in many cases the host plants just act as disease carriers and show few if any symptoms of the disease itself. Since this is a major concern in this country for the nursery industry, monitoring outbreaks have been very stringent. This is NOT what is affecting Heruga's garden, otherwise they would have come in and removed and destroyed all the affected plant material. A little bit like hoof and mouth disease......

You are correct about feather meal, the nitrogen is bound with a protein hard for microbes to digest being the reason it takes so long.  If the feather meal is just spread on top it will take even longer before to get into the soil so microbes can work on it, so it could take all summer before benefiting from the nitrogen locked up in the stuff. If you decide to switch to something faster Blood meal would be a better alternative.   It will release it's nitrogen faster because it's easier for microbes to digest, It's water soluble so can be watered in if your using mulch, it has nearly the same amount of nitrogen and the nearly the same Nitrogen/carbon ratio as feather meal, plus it has other nutrients your plant needs.    There are many other water soluble high nitrogen fertilizers on the market claiming to be organic but I can't give any recommendations because I don't do use the stuff. I grow lots of garlic.   I'm not organic but use a lot of organic matter for soil structure.  Even if I grew organic I still would never use feather meal because there are better alternatives and most are free.  Feather meal is 12%-14% nitrogen, 80% crude protein and the other few percent left aren't used by plants.  Garlic needs more than just nitrogen and all the other macro and micro nutrients any other plant needs. I work in organic matter in the fall, included green grass high in nitrogen, leaves and compost including a little ammonium sulfate well before soil temps drop below 50 degrees.  Most microbial activity is above 50 degrees and drops to zero at 42 degrees, so I've started the decomposition of the organic matter early and in very late October when microbial activity slows to a crawl I plant my garlic.  It grows some roots and everything goes to sleep for the winter.  Your feather meal should of been worked into the soil in the fall. Spring comes along and I only need to give a quick boost of nitrogen before soil temps get well above 50 using some ammonium sulfate, potassium nitrate and calcium nitrate.  Every chemical fertilizer I add is used by the plant, and the same exact carbon copy of the minerals released from organic fertilizers.  There is no difference what's so ever.  If you want to use organic sources, when and how you use it will determine how well your plants grow.

I'm with Kevin on using blood meal over feather meal for spring feeding. If you leave your bed fallow between harvest and replant, you can dig in feather meal after harvest to start settling in. I think feather meal is probably better suited to a slower grow like tomatoes, but if that's what you got... just be wise about when you apply it and make sure you apply it according to directions.

Today's dessert has been in the freezer since Christmas. I made it as a back up but never served it. I use home made frozen stuff all the time. It's much more efficient to make a larger batch than just cooking for two.  Pasta sauces, stews, soups, unbaked pastry cases, pancakes, etc.  I do not prepare meals ahead for the week. Floral, now that's my kind of freezer food! I do freeze lots of things when I have freezer room, as there is only Elery and I and we can't eat a whole pan of lasagna or batch of cookies. If you are doing the low-carb eating plan, then you don't want a lot of pasta, although I actually like some of the legume based pasta and the fiber content keeps the net carbs down.   A big roast or swiss steak or meatballs or ham all freeze well as do many vegetables.  Cheese can be problematic when freezing, texture changes are sometimes very noticeable but not as much when it's an ingredient as when trying to freeze a block of cheese by itself.  Those little "egg muffins" freeze and reheat well and are infinitely customizable.  I've made the sauce for shakshuka in advance and frozen it and then thaw/heat/add eggs, it worked too. Good luck.  I don't mind cooking daily, but it does create a lot of leftovers.  Elery doesn't mind eating chili every day for a week but two days and I'm done.  That's when it gets frozen. Interesting.  Joyce Chen was a well-known and ground-breaking Chinese chef who helped popularize Chinese food in the US, during the 1960s. Joyce Chen (chef) - Wikipedia Savoring the Legacy of Joyce Chen - History Cambridge " Chen introduced northern Chinese (Mandarin) and Shanghainese dishes to Boston, including Peking duck, moo shu pork, hot and sour soup, and potstickers, " " People lined up to get Chen's Chinese food at this small restaurant, which seated 60 people. According to Stephen Chen, it was at this restaurant that his mother introduced the Northern style of dim sum, and the now popular "soup dumplings" (shao long bao). " " Following the 1958 opening of her first restaurant, Chen began teaching Chinese cooking at the Cambridge Center for Adult Education and the Boston Center for Adult Education in 1960 . . . , she introduced many Americans to home style and gourmet Chinese cooking techniques.". "In 1962, Chen published her influential cookbook, the Joyce Chen Cook Book. She pre-sold over 6,000 copies of her book at her restaurants . . . and sold an additional 70,000 copies, and still more in later reprintings over the years." "In 1967, Chen starred in her own cooking show called Joyce Chen Cooks, on National Educational Television (NET), now the Public Broadcasting Service (PBS).[24] Twenty-six episodes were filmed on the same set as The French Chef (featuring Julia Child) . . . Julia Child had already been a regular visitor at Chen's restaurant, and a fan of her cooking." "she pioneered in an era when few viewers had access to authentic Chinese ingredients and flavors. Her recipes were many American viewers' first glimpse at the making of Chinese food, beyond such Americanized dishes as chop suey and chow mein. She also introduced some novel kitchen tools to American audiences, including the wok and the Chinese chef's knife, often misidentified as a "Chinese cleaver"." My wok is an early Joyce Chen wok, based on the heavy cast iron construction, round bottomed interior (the exterior is flat to sit on burners) and cast loop handles.  Her later woks, and the ones still sold under her name, are thin cast iron with long handles.  I appreciate it more now.  I think I'll name it "Joyce".

I see lots of tech-y clutter near the sofa -- will this move to the school area?  Consider a couple baskets or decorative boxes to hold these things.  And if you ever do want a dining area, it'll be easy to change it. Does the exercise stuff need to be in the living room?  That seems wrong to me. The two seating pieces look to be in good condition, but I'd like to see them moved closer together -- so they'd seem to be a unit.  Maybe keep the chaise where it is /move the sofa against the wall directly across from the TV. I think you need COLOR.  The overall look is a bit drab and screams college-apartment.  I'd paint the walls a color you like -- sage green or Robin's egg blue would go with the beige carpet -- then add some throw pillows and blankets in those same colors on the seating (hopefully a bit of print and texture in the linens).  A curtain across the back wall (either in place of those vertical blinds or on top of them) would bring in color and texture.  Then add some artwork to the walls -- I'd lean towards a couple large prints rather than small items. Do you know the 60-30-10 rule for color?  It means you want 60% of your room to be one color -- yours is beige /brown -- then you want 30% to be an accent color and 10% to be a "pop" color.  You have about 10% black.  So you need that 30% accent color.  With not so much natural light, don't go too dark with your accent color. Is lighting a need?  I don't see an overhead fixture or lamps.  I'd say add a couple end tables and some good lamps -- don't go too small with your lamps.  That's something people tend to do.

Tilt and Turn windows are the only window type in Europe and considering that their homes are much smaller than in the US, you can see that you will be fine. Most of the time - if you open the window - you will tilt it in from the top only and this will not take away from your space. Swinging a window in is only a temporary intrusion because this opening is meant for quick exchange of air. Then you close the window after 15 min again. No answers but I did have the warm cold water problem. We bought a house with tankless heater. No problem at first but then we turned recirculating off while we were gone for an extended period. Then we turned it back on 24 hours a day rather than a few hours. We then got the warm cold water. My solution was to just turn recirculating off entirely. We’ve adapted to running the water for a while to get it hot. Waste water or waste enrgy recirculating. Never had this problem with previous tanks.

I've never heard of warm cold water with a dedicated return line. I don't see how that's possible. If you're talking about condensing versus non-condensing tankless water heater, condensing is the only way I would go. Non-condensing requires stainless steel venting which is very expensive. I've used several of the Rheem condensing tankless units and they work very reliably. Since you're talking about recirculation, I would prefer a separate recirculation pump rather than one built into the water heater. TACO and Grundfos both make good circulating pumps. Consider using a hybrid electric heater instead though. Depending on your cost of electricity, the hybrid electric may be cheaper to operate than a condensing gas tankless. You have an ideal location for a hybrid electric and it avoids dealing with any venting - again which is very expensive for non-condensing but cheap (PVC) for a condensing gas water heater. It also avoids some other issues such as a longer wait for hot water without a circulating pump.

"We will build a custom hood cover on top." Then you would want a Range Hood Insert. It's generally recommended that a range hood be 3" wider on each side than the cooktop so a 42" insert would be appropriate. Among Vent-a-hood range hood inserts the 19-1/4" deep BH240SLD SS or M40SLD SS would probably be appropriate but you could go with the 22-1/4" deep BH240PSLD SS if you wanted a hood with greater coverage. Don't forget to set the bottom of the range hood at the hood manufacturer's recommended height above the cooktop.

For capture, hood overlap of cooking plumes is desirable; for containment of captured plume effluent, adequate CFM is desirable.  If you stir fry or sear, then 90 CFM/sq. foot of hood entry aperture is appropriate.  Otherwise, you might get away with 60 using induction. Do you intend to use VaH Magic Lung designs, or more conventional blower designs with hood baffles near the hood base?  This will determine the rated blower performance relative to the desired/require blower performance. What about noise?  For best suppression of blower noise, a duct long enough to include a silencer is needed, as well as an outside or at least downstream in-line blower. Are you aware that you will need a make-up air system or configuration (except under exceptional circumstances)?

A very random disease, which is why any house renovators should be wearing masks….you don’t know what is under and behind the walls and floors you are ripping apart.

"A very random disease, which is why any house renovators should be wearing masks….you don’t know" Dreamer is right. I've personally known or known of, some tradies who must have had many exposures over the years without consequence, but also other tradies and people who did DIY at some stage and even people with no awareness of having done anything, and they developed health problems probably or possibly linked to asbestos. Mesothelioma is the well-publicised condition which is very linked to asbestos exposure, but there are other conditions which asbestos can contribute to.. Do what you can to avoid exposures going forward, because each one adds to the gamble. If you're a smoker you should give that up, because I recall reading that amongst asbestos workers, those who smoked had an even higher rate, which makes sense, it's like a risk on top of a risk, so like a cumulative effect.

Which do  you  like  the  look of? I personally don’t  like recessed lighting  much.  It sends  light  down, the upper and lower parts of  the  room get different lighting, need a lot of recessed lights to get even illumination through a room, often restricts what bulbs can be used. I see why builders use it - stamped metal or plastic “builder grade” light pots are cheap and easy to slap up when the ceiling is open.  I see using it in spaces designed to have different light zones  (restaurant, commercial, etc).  I see it  working in minimalist modern spaces  although alternatives look way sleeker. In a more traditional house I prefer interesting exposed fixtures.  For a modern sleek look I prefer  linear LEDs or minimalist track lighting.

text: Very Sorry, I misunderstood  you. Those single flower buds should be left alone to finish their bloom cycle. To get a maximum bud set for the second flush try this.  At dead heading time, cut back down the stem a good bit lower than the first 5 leaflet leaf to a thicker place on the cane.  The resulting lateral growths that appear will be huskier, and can be minimized/thinned per cane as they reach about an inch of growth to make the remaining growths even more  husky.  Just rub the smaller and too numerous growths right off.  Those remaining laterals left will get all the bush's energy, and should produce the maximum number of buds per variety for your second flush without any further intervention. That's about all you can do to get the maximum number of buds per stem. Still keep up proper watering and fertilizing. If you nip those single buds now, all you will get is weak new growth from the upper, currently dormant leaf node buds that are triggered to grow.  Many new growths from those leaf node buds that emerge below the nipped flower bud will be blind growths, and/or produce growths with  very small subsequent flowers on the growths that produce flower buds. Moses.

What your non-electrician "experts" think is not particularly relevant.  What matters is what licensed, professional contractors in your area will charge to make the changes.  That said, a big difference in the price quoted by different contractors is usually due to one or more of the following: A poorly defined scope of work. Differing assumptions about the project scope, quantity, and/or quality of the materials and labor required to complete the scope of work. Radically different cost structures between the contractors, e.g., a one-man company vs. a large commercial contractor. Intent to pull permits and have the work inspected or not. A contractor which doesn't want the job and has put a price tag on it so his/her company is not selected.  Alternatively, if they are, they'll do it for the premium price.

Those are some thoughtful rationales. "Radically different cost structures" might explain it. The $15k quote was from a large company who showed up promptly and gave me a quote the same day. The $6k quote, on the other hand, was from a 1-man company who took over a month to finish his quote. The suggestion that these were both too high was from a general contractor who will hopefully be in charge of our addition. I think I've written this here before...shortened version: gave up my only child for adoption as a young single woman (pretty much the only option for many years). Closed adoption, no info given to me at all, adoptive parents had minimal info about me. Before it was popular and more accepted to search, I never did, nor thought I should. Fast forward 21 years, after living in several locations around the PNW, I moved to Olympia (where I'd never lived before). Went out with a girlfriend, stopped on the way home at the grocery store for a few things. As a former hairdresser, I was very hair aware and noticed the cashier's beautiful hair and great haircut. Wrote a check for groceries and left with my friend. Several days later, I got a letter in my mailbox...it was from that cashier who told me that he was my son and had JUST that same day gotten my current address. He was raised in Olympia. He used a few clues in the adoption papers to find my father's obituary and since I was an only child, he had my name. Searched the vital records for my marriage license, so then had my married name. Found my address through DMV.  He almost fainted when he saw my name on my check, but held it together. We finally met and have been in each other's lives for 35 years now. He's the father of my only grandchild with whom I have a wonderful close relationship, too.

For sure, this soapstone was not purchased from a soapstone specialist, like M. Teixeira.  Terrible installation.  And, the counters should not have any scratches or chips at installation!  For John Liu to state that the counters will develop dings and patina as they’re used, is irrelevant.  The installer should’ve installed the counters in pristine condition. Also, a soapstone specialist would’ve asked how you wanted the slab templeted.  That is, what parts of the slab you want to go where.  See the pic here, where I selected the sections of the slab I wanted used, and where the sections should go.  This slab was installed by M. Teixeira, in my now 9 yo kitchen. To be frank, you’d probably not be in this position, had you come here before making your purchase, not after installation.  There are tons of threads on this site, about purchasing soapstone, and the mistakes many folks have suffered with.  You’d have known to get samples of any slab you were interested in, and test the samples to make sure what you were getting was actually soapstone, and where on the scale of hardness that slab stood. I have one seam in the soapstone…down the middle of the main sink, which is the usual place a qualified installer places seams.  The seam in completely inconspicuous.  Cannot be seen.  For the record, not all soapstone is soft, and chips or scratches easily.  There are several very hard varieties. My counters are Belvedere, one of the very hardest varieties. While thinking more about the storage dilemma, I did some looking around concerning this topic and found interesting info. A Wikipedia article or two in particular. A proven, reliable, and increasingly used method to store electricity (if indirectly) is called pumped hydroelectric. I was familiar with this as I periodically drive by one such facility located at Castaic, along the Grapevine route. Simple from a technology standpoint - take two adjacent reservoirs, one uphill from the other. At times of excess power availability in the grid, pump water uphill from the lower reservoir to the higher one. At a later time, when more power is needed, release water to turn turbines at the higher reservoir and release the water to the lower one. Rinse and repeat, as needed. Interestingly, the country with the largest number of such facilities is China and it also has a large number, more than any other country, under construction (info from Wiki). As usual, the US lags what other countries do to solve problems. Another of several technologies being researched involves using excess, otherwise unused electrical power to extract hydrogen gas from water. Water is H2O, separating the H from the O is simple and inexpensive (equipment wise). The hydrogen gas can be used at a later time to operate fuel cells (an oldish and reliable technology) to produce electricity. Note that at one time, American space vehicles like Apollo, the Space Shuttle, etc., were powered exclusively by fuel cells. The hydrogen-use cycle is completely environmentally friendly because when the water molecule is split, the resulting products are hydrogen gas and oxygen gas. When a fuel cell operates, the result of the chemical reaction that creates electricity is just water. Hydrogen is flammable but again, so are most petrochemicals used for fuel. As the storage facilities would be at protected and isolated locations, as with the battery facility, I wouldn't think using this approach would present any great risk. And in the case of a fire, the by-products released in the fire would not be as potentially dangerous as with the burning of lithium batteries.

Cohesive flooring is always a good idea, but I don't think it's adviseable to run the same floor in EVERY room.  As an example, hardwood would look great in your main living areas and possibly kitchen, but you mention bathroom and laundry room -- I wouldn't put hardwood in a bathroom nor a laundry room.  Is your laundry room also a main entry point?  If so, tile would be a good choice, much better choice than hardwood.  I could also see hardwood in living area, tile or linoleum/marmoleum in kitchen area, in your layout the kitchen is a separate, distinct room.  I'm a fan of tile in the kitchen, but I know many are not.

"If hardwood in great room what colour would you do?" The most important thing is the tone, not the shade -- the tone of the color you choose should harmonize with the other wood. Doesn't have to be exactly the same color, but the tones should align (e.g. don't mix a purpled-tone floor with a yellow-toned wood). IMO light wood floors are going to look to "floaty" and be a visual weight mis-match against your trim and kitchen cabinets. I'd start by looking at something mid-range in terms of color depth. You need the floors to stand up against the rest of it.

text: Heirloom sends only gallon size roses nowadays.  They are above average quality, IMHO.  The prices are at the high end, but orders over $100.00, are shipped free.  This means a two rose order comes freight free. My main complaint with Heirloom is that they strip the foliage off of all shipped roses.  The principle they give is that the foliage stripping lessens shipping shock.  I do not agree.  What about the shock a fully foliaged rose receives when it's completely denuded, then shipping shock compounded upon that?  My suspicious nature leads me to question the truth factor in Heirlooms assertion.  Are the leaves stripped to hide insect, mite, or disease (black spot, mildew, etc.....), damage that the rose may have had prior to shipping? I will say, Heirloom carries a very large number of rose varieties.  Possibly the largest in the mail order trade.  I have never received a mislabeled rose from Heirloom, a big plus. Heirloom also packages their roses very carefully...no roses out of their pots with potting mix flung throughout the shipping box, and dried out roots and broken rose stems.  No sir, everything neat and professional has been my experience, every shipment that I have received. Also to Heirloom's credit is that I have yet to receive a rose from them that was not a gallon size bush growing in a gallon pot.  Let me explain.  When an Heirloom rose arrives and is removed from its pot, the entire root mass with the growing medium in which the roots are growing, comes out together, in one mass.  This means that the rose is a true gallon size bush.   The upper stem growth is commensurate with the root mass, equally well branched out for a gallon sized bush. A number of other nurseries sell online who ship roses that are not true to pot size. There's nothing more annoying than receiving, say a two gallon size pot rose bush with a pint sized rose bush gowing in it.  Upon being removed from its 2 gal. pot, the roots fall apart from the potting mix revealing a bush that is not 2 gal. gallon size, with such misrepresented bushes. The above scenario has never occurred with any Heirloom rose bush  that I have purchased from them, ever.  I do patronize them substantially. All in all, I would give Heirloom a thumbs up, in spite of their high price and foliage stripping practice. Moses.

Petalique, hooks are so inexpensive, I'd send her a variety of hook sizes for her to play with.  Typically the yarn manufacturers will list the size hook that will work best with the yarn to produce the given gauge.  But everyone is different in how they tension the yarn so can get different results. The important thing is the hook should be able to fit the yarn to pull the whole yarn and not split threads.  If you have a small hook with a chunky yarn, it's clearly not going to work.  A too large hook can be used purposely to yield a softer, more open and airier product, but not the other way around. Also the size of hooks, be they numbers or letters, are being replaced with mm sizes as they are more consistent across countries.  Here is a table that shows the recommended hook size for the size of the yarn:   Also, while it's individual, I find that I prefer, and others I've talked to prefer a more pointy head ... here they call it "inline" on the hook rather than a rounded one...I find it easier to pierce the fabric while you're working on it.

Another consideration would be for your friend's vision.  As I've gotten older, it's harder to see smaller stuff, so I prefer the larger size hooks vs. the smaller ones.  When I've taught, I usually request the students bring worsted weight acrylic yarn and an I or J  (5.5 - 6 mm) hook as it's easier to see the stitches if they are a bit larger. Below is a chart that does the hook size conversions.

I'm a longtime crocheter as well (62 yrs). I can give an opinion, but there's more to consider than an opinion alone. Annie’s info is very helpful. My mother most often used an F hook with worsted weight because she crocheted loosely. I most often use a G hook s as my stitches were a bit tighter than Mom’s. Mom preferred  hooks that had a tapered tip. With my tighter stitches, I prefer the inline tips (no struggle to find my spot) and I can crochet faster. The tapered hook stands away from the hole and sometimes I get caught on the way out of the stitch. And I’ve found that worsted weight isn’t all the same thickness, depending on content. Unless you know her crocheting “groove”, you might be better off with a small selection of hooks.

The problem here is that you have a hulking roof and so much dark ... and the porch is recessed, placing the front door in the shadows ... zero view of the front door for a guest approaching the house.  As such, you need to go with something light and/or bright, which will stand out and invite the eye to the front door. I'd consider yellow, as it would jump out and be most visible.  After all there's a reason school busses are yellow. No to a white door, as it would be too stark against the dark gray, and it would leave you without any accent color.  Do you know the 60-30-10 color rule?  Your 60% is definitely gray ... you're even over 60%.  Your white window trim is your 30%, but you're a little under ... and you need to bring in an accent color and fill 10% of your whole space with that accent. Usually I'll go with a red front door, and red would look good with the dark gray ... but it might not give you the visibility-from-afar that you need.  If you choose a red, make it a brighter shade. But the door's not everything: Add planters /flowers in the same color.  Groupings of the same color will draw in the eye.  Place one planter outside the porch ... again, to draw the eye in towards the door. Add a wreath for the door and a mat for the floor ... bright in your chosen color + a bit of something dark to tie into the main color. That's an odd spot for a "street light".  If it's moveable, consider bumping it over so it's closer to the porch.  Let it shine a bit of light into the porch and give people walking the path to your door a light to walk towards. I'd consider painting the black porch lights with something brighter ... brass?  silver?  Again, the idea being to brighten this dark porch and invite the eye towards the entrance.  If you ever replace this porch light, bump up several sizes ...  a porch light should be 1/4 - 1/3 the height of the front door. I don't think I'd add shutters to this house, but I would consider "beefing up" the windows a bit with some trim ... nicely done window trim would really take this house "up a notch". Remember that your mailbox should be painted the same color as your door.

I have this master bath remodel planned. Total gut. - I think barn doors are cute -- in the right place, and the bathroom is not that place.  I once stayed in a hotel that had a barn door on the bathroom, and that was enough to convince me that it's a bad idea.  The door rattled when it was opened /closed, and the sound of running water wasn't contained. - You have 70" width for the vanity area ... that's generous!  20-22" will go to the vanity, leaving you space to go with a nice, wide door.  Eventually you'll need to replace the toilet or the tub, so you'll appreciate that wide door. - I hate duplicate sinks, but I especially hate duplicate sinks in space-hogging separate vanities.  Instead, go with one nice, wide vanity and allow for a nice wide bank of drawers flanking a single sink (a single sink done right).  At 3'8" with a centered sink, you're looking at two skinny drawers with 6-8" usable space /note that drawer "sides" will eat up about 4" ... but if you go with an 84" vanity and a single sink, you could each have a bank of 30-36" drawers ... and drawer storage AT the sink is tremendously important. - Pay attention to your details at the vanity:  Wall-mounted faucets make cleaning easier.  I prefer the simple, clean look of one large mirror ... and since it will reflect that large wall behind it, go with some nice wallpaper and/or art.  Essentially that empty wall "counts twice" because it's reflected in the mirror.  Put your vanity mirrors on dimmers because the mirror will "double" their light. - Note that you really need two trash cans for this layout ... one next to the vanity and one next to the toilet.  I don't love emptying two each week. - I'd add a small pony wall to "set off" the toilet /give you space for storing toilet paper. - Where are your windows?  IF you don't have some light in this deep, long bathroom, I'd consider a sun-tube over the toilet and over the shower.  While we're talking about lighting, I'd also like to see a decorative mirror on the wall dead-ahead of the door ... it'll reflect light /make this long bathroom look brighter. Keeping the wood vanity top but probably will lighten it and add marine grade varnish.Vessel type sinks. I love the look of wood countertops, but I would prefer the function of something more water-proof.  Once it's damaged, you're probably going to look at it a while. Vessel sinks are significantly harder to clean, as you must clean the interior + around the outside. I am solidly against your vanity /sink choices. Thinking white shiplap wall installed horizontally along the long contiguous wall.Not sure if I should continue it on back wall too? That's a style choice.  If you're going to put it in one place, I'd put in the other as well. Continue LVP floor from bedroom but something different for shower walls and floor. Like it. Consider that the unusual shaped-shower you've chosen will 1) cost more and 2) require a custom-tile floor /not a shower pan.  A shower pan will be done right 10/10 times because it was made in a factory ... it'll drain perfectly, and it'll last longer.  With a tile floor done by your plumber, you're at the mercy of his ability. I have one shower with a tile floor and one shower with a shower pan ... the one with a tile floor has one spot (right where you step in) where the tile's a bit too flat /water always pools in that spot and it takes extra cleaning. There is code, and code isn't especially the MOST comfortable. Agree ... when you're talking bathrooms, always build a little larger than code.  For example, my daughter's master bath toilet is set off with a pony wall /only allows for a minimum 30" width.  Even though I'm a small person, I feel like I need to pull my elbows inward.  36" feels so much more comfortable.  40" feels spacious. A free standing tub, needs room to clean around that tub. An alcove is better by far in many baths. Agree.  I love the look of a vintage clawfoot tub, but you don't have to clean all the way around /under an alcove tub. If you stick with the vintage tub, you'll have to make a choice about faucets ... and all are expensive. I really like the layout that Jan Moyer has provided you. Her layout doesn't seem as crammed as the original layout posted. Agree ... it looks great.  That shower is plenty big, luxurious even ... and the vanity /tub are more practical. Notes: - Be sure you can reach the towel bars from both the tub and the shower.  A bathroom's comfort relies upon small details like this.  If you go with a glass shower door (and I wouldn't ... shower curtainsn bring in color and texture), be sure it's hinged in the direction of the towel bars. - I like that she's kept the tub footprint compact ... unless you're quite tall, a larger tub just allows you to slip down, and greater surface area cools off faster.  However, I love a DEEP tub. - I LOVE that she's added a real linen closet ... it can absorb the hamper into the lower portion /have shelves for towels and toiletries above. Could you harnass the back side of that closet for a book case in a bedroom maybe? - I would make that pony wall between the toilet and the tub a little thicker so it could hold the plumbing AND shelves for toilet paper (or other medical needs that may arise as you age).

Actually  this paper is made by company which makes only paper reproduced from actual identified samples of the period obtained from historic houses. Often from scraps covered  over by renovation.  And it is produced however the original was including hand blocking.  And they will produce it on rolls glued up from shorter pieces of paper for authentic horizontal seams if it is required for period authenticity. Every order is essentially custom. And actually the older color analysis of the period is the one which is incorrect. 18th and early 19th century colors were extremely vibrant.  The old analysis was more visual and of faded samples. Victorian colors were - with some exceptions - dirtier because of gas lighting and coal heating. So look at Monticello and Mount Vernon and the Governor's Palace currently. Remember houses that could afford fashionable paper and paint colors were often houses where entertainment took place after dark and these rooms would have been candle lit. Dull colors would have all grayed out.

I mentioned that we should have gotten together years before and bought a riding mower to use on both yards. She immediately offered to buy a rider, but only if I would store it in my garage. I mowed both yards for years, until the mower eventually wore out. I even kept mowing her yard after we moved a few blocks away! We'll miss Linda's stories about her kids and grandkids, her community theater days, the funeral lunches she organized at her church, her days helping Donn market Maytag Blue Cheese, the family ski trips, neighborhood cocktail parties, Hawkeye tailgate parties, and her eventful time as a U.S. Census taker. Linda Campbell was one of the colorful characters in our lives that make our days interesting and memorable. We'll miss her. " Yes, Linda was an acquired taste. But once you had that taste, you knew it was the best there is. You knew where you stood with her.  I was lucky enough to have visited with her twice in the past 20 odd years. As she was making and delivering bread to friends and family during covid, I joked "where was mine?".  By that afternoon, Stwart, her son, was at my door with two hot loaves of bread. I use both the sunflower hears (no shells!!) and dried mealworms, as well as suet and a special peanut butter feeder. I have recently begun to notice that different birds feed in rather definite rotations as the day progresses. The rest follow, and then the feeders are unattended for a period, until late afternoon, when things get busy again until the sun is nearly gone. Squirrels are SO frustrated since they cannot access my feeders at all, due to the very best squirrel-proof pole which has foiled their attempts for many years. I just hope that my aging eyes will stay good enough to continue watching the avian dances from my kitchen windows. The birds have existed for aeons without human help, but feeding them brings so much enjoyment for the human spirit!)

First, a comment on VaH's infamous multiplying factor for their "Magic Lung" hoods.   Most commercial and higher performance residential hoods use baffles for filtering the larger size portion of the cooking effluent particle spectrum to minimize condensation onto the exhaust ducting.  The double reversal of flow in the baffles has a pressure loss (resistance) that can be very roughly (at full flow) degrade the associated blower's achieved flow rate by a factor of 2/3.  Without the baffles, the VaH Magic Lung avoids this pressure loss; hence, 600 CFM being claimed to be equivalent to 900 CFM.  (The 600 CFM, by the way, is for the hood assembly hanging in free air.) But wait, there is more.  Not only are duct pressure losses (usually small relative to baffles and larger diameter ducts should help) additional resistances for the Magic Lung, but more significantly, so are make-up air losses, in some cases dominant where a deliberate MUA system is not included.  The Magic Lung squirrel cage blower(s), intended to expel grease particles like baffles, have a less "robust" fan curve than axial and centrifugal blowers used with other hood systems.  This means that they are more degraded by additional pressure losses than conventional hood systems.  In many MUA limiting cases, where the conventional 900 CFM blower will be degraded to an actual 500 CFM, the Magic Lung could be degraded to 400 CFM (as a example of the principles involved). An example VaH "fan curve" table for a larger system is included below.  (The "inch" values in the heading are pressure loss in inches of water column.) Click to expand.   Second, cooking effluent plumes expand as they rise toward the hood assembly.  The expansion angle varies with cooking conditions, and also hood flow rate.  Generally, one wants to capture a 10 degree angle from vertical for the largest pan used near the hood edge.  More roughly, a 3-inch overlap of the cooking surface (wider than the pan usually) is deemed adequate.  It may be understood that the higher the hood is placed, the larger the plume diameter, and hence the larger the capture area should be.  Some trapping by the wall (for wall mounts) and sides (where cabinets are located) can aid capture.  Where feasible, more CFM can slightly increase the effective capture area (pull in marginal plume elements). So one needs to not only trade performance vs. aesthetics and cost, but within the performance category effectiveness of capture vs. protection from head impact.

W.r.t. "sucking:" The flow rates (and sound levels) of residential cooking hoods are far from those that can actually suck effluent toward them.  Welding and grinding operations may have such hoods.  The kitchen hood depends on the upward velocity of the effluent plume to get it to the hood capture area, and high enough flow rate to ensure that what is captured is actually contained (and hence ejected, preferably outside) instead of reflecting out of the hood.  See image; here the upward flow rate exceeds the ability of the hood's flow rate to achieve full containment.   So, hoods with marginal flow rate and/or marginal capture area are generally specified to be close to the cooktop, whereas larger hoods with adequate flow can be higher up.  As an extreme residential example, there is @opaone's hood.   If one needs to keep the hood close to the cooktop, then one has to suffer the potential consequences of visual blockage and head interference.  My Wolf Pro Island hood base is at 34.5 inches above my cooktop.  When I was 6 ft (and younger) I just ducked a smidgen,  now I have clearance.  Re 2, both heights will require "training" to avoid.  I have no experience to grade their relative inconvenience. So, Re 1, higher mounting needs a hood with larger capture area, rather than implying that higher somehow achieves larger capture area.  In case I'm unclear, capture area is basically the area at the bottom that the plume can pass through.  With enough flow rate, some slight increase may be achieved at the edges where the edge flow curls up into the hood. Please also keep in mind that 'perfect' is the enemy of 'good enough,' and depending on cooking styles and particularly adequate make-up air (MUA), a range of hood configurations (pun intended) may be sufficient. Or as a wise general once commented, approximately, an affordable 80-percent solution beats an unaffordable 100-percent solution.

Looking at pictures of someone else's home may give you an idea of the amount of variation in a flooring.  It won't tell you anything about imperfections because the flawed materials should have been discarded, not installed. In my opinion, the best practice is to look at as many pictures from manufacturers/flooring stores as you would like.  These pictures will show the product in its best light.  Those pictures will help you determine what you like and what you don't like. The additional information you might gain from looking at homeowner pictures just might not be accurate.  You are subject to their photography skills (the manufacturer pictures are all professional pictures, so the skill level will be comparable).  As Patricia noted, you can also be distracted by the homeowner's lighting or taste in decor.  A photograph of my floors would probably convince you not to purchase the flooring that I chose.  Not that it's ugly, but because I can't take a good picture.  This is why some (including me) don't recommend looking at other homeowners' pictures.  You're not getting any better information than you already had. After you know what you like, you will be able to narrow your choices down to just a few.  When you get it down to two or three choices, that is the time to buy one box of each.  If you get these from a real flooring store, there is a good likelihood that they'll agree to take back the box of whatever you didn't like (it's a small concession in comparison to the full order). So I find myself agreeing with Patricia.  She might not have explained the thought process behind her recommendation in as much detail as some would like, but she's right. And please note that I did not recommend buying "several" boxes of flooring, just the final two or three contenders.

I searched online and found a number of gardebweb posts about Liebherr fridges which pointed to ice that can build up in the freezer compartment and block the drawer rails.  IIRC. we wound up unplugging the whole unit, moving all the fridge stuff to coolers and waiting for something like seven or eight hours for the freezer to defrost enough for the the drawer(s) to be pried open.  We were then able to salvage most of what was in the freezer. We then defrosted the freezer compartment completely with a floor fan. We got the unit back to functioning until it could be serviced sometime the following week.  As best I recall, the the problem turned out to be a combination of a plugged condensate drain (goop can build up in it) and a problem with a failed defrost cycle.  (Don't remember if it was the defrost heater or the logic board.)

I use and presently have cases of Mylar bags.  There is nothing which comes close to keeping oxygen, moisture and LIGHT out except glass jars protected from all light.  Real Mylar consists of three layers, a layer of plastic on the inside and outside and nothing special, but a sheet of Aluminum foil sandwiched in between the plastic giving them the ability to nearly stop any oxygen, moisture and light from passing through.  There are other bags made called Mylar but the center layer is sprayed on and not nearly as effective.  The aluminum is sprayed on and not actual foil, and have no idea how they make either.You may have the sprayed on foil bags in your house right now and are used for packaging shacks and chips, like fritos and poptarts.  When opened They'll have a silver color but over that silver is a clear food grade plastic.  To tell the difference a flashlight will shine through the sprayed on bags but real Mylar will allow no light to pass.For a comparison a real 5 mil thick heat sealed Mylar bag will keep moisture, oxygen and light out for at about 42 years before equalizing without an oxygen absorber to the outside environment, with an absorber it could take over 100 years.  A sealed food saver bag will keep out moisture and oxygen for about 10 years before equalizing, and a zip lock freezer bag will only last about 2 weeks because of the zipper.  Zipping these bags and heat sealing them will drastically increase storage life from weeks to many months.  I never searched for permeability data on plastic storage containers but all plastic is permeable to oxygen, thin aluminum foil is slightly permeable.I buy my bags from Impak corporation to avoid fraud and assure quality.  Lucille, I'm not lying here but I used spaghetti for 21 years out of storage, and when we comparing the last pound side by side to new spaghetti we could not tell the difference.  I have flour and rice packaged over 5 years we continuously use and there is no difference.  And when we use something we give the inside of the bag a rinse, let it dry and reuse it, the bags are just a few inches shorter.

......ok....I've got a project currently in progress in inner Melbourne, similar era/residence - yes these need a lot of work when they fall into disrepair and furthermore they have a certain character/detailing that often requires understanding of the workmanship/craft from a bygone era that is more about labour than the materials and considering labour cost today relatively expensive to execute even just repairs/maintenance  ....the project of mine was initally priced pre-covid, was delayed and now literally will involve double the initial budget when it's done....construction costs have skyrocketed in recent times and the compounding issue is on something like this whilst the quote seems extraordinary there is legit inner suburbs/tight site/awkward access/rubbish removal loading/flagfalls that make a bunch of seemingly small doable jobs add up to be relatively expensive to execute professionally.....getting a builder to do something like this with contracts and insurances etc I'm not surprised at the numbers....you're paying a premium to have it managed contractually by a builder and knowing what it takes to wrangle trades and taking on the responsibility to get it done and done right within a certain timeframe etc it's arguably justified........that said, yes could you do it cheaper by breaking it all up to individual jobs, but would you want to take on having to do the grunt and wrangling of all the individual trades? Whilst I'd guess you'd save a fair bit it really depends on your circumstances.....potentially if you got more of a semi-retired handyman to tackle some of the carpentry jobs and knuckled down with a project management hat on for the best part of a few months to coordinate/integrate various trades then yes you could save some decent money, but do you have the flexibility/time to do this and do you have contacts/experience with construction? What you're paying for is the experience and network of a (assuming) established builder........but this leads into a bigger question/discussion of value in that say if you did include the kitchen and bathroom scope exected properly and bundle in all the various odd bits & pieces you're prioritising you'd likely find that the overall package would make more sense/add up in terms of value as the flagfall site costs would be put to better use and trades used most efficiently on site, and the various odd jobs would be to an extent more effectively  absorbed within the larger project scope and it would likely feel like you're getting a better bang for buck for the effort and expense with ending up with a properly updated / fixed up property,  yes involving a higher cost but possibly better long term investment......these heritage properties are special and typically hold their value and any improvements justified and pay off in the long term....remember the cheapest time to build is yesterday, so if you're thinking of a larger scope project it may be best to seriously consider sooner rather than later, but of course your particular budget and personally circumstances will determine how you go about it all.... Just a few thoughts from the trenches...hope helps a bit Best of luck, PD www.pauldistefanodesign.com

Weather turned icky, and I' m a bit loopy.  Realized there was an end to the bread and popped up to start a pre-ferment, a bit later in the day than usual.  Thought I should feed the whole wheat starter while I was at it.  Sure enough, it was looking a little peaked.  So, I put it in a prep bowl while I wash its jar and it was looking nice, but wet, rather than lumpy.  Turned around and saw I'd only put in half the flour (batches keep the flour inside the bowl). Dianne Brakefield:  I am pleased to read that your specimen of 'The Prince' is growing so well in your warm climate.  It is likely grafted onto Rosa multiflora rootstock.  In 2018 I exchanged a series of emails with Rene Schmitz regarding my large collection of rare Austin rose and sent him a list of the 130 or so varieties that I had at that time.  I was hopeful that I could interest him in propagating them for sale in the spirit of saving these very rare (and many completely out of commerce for decades) He studied it and requested that I send him cuttings of 63 of them (including 'The Prince!), which I sent to him free of charge, although he compensated me for shipping costs and the cost for a 'phytosanitary document.  So, it's highly likely that the budwood used to propagate your plant was from my garden.  I have grown own-root roses, roses grafted to Dr. Huey, and roses grafted to Rosa multiflora.  Those grafted to R. multiflora are typically larger than own-root plants (I prefer own root plants to grafted and often produce own-root plants from my grafted ones and discard the grafted specimens, provided they are vigorous enough on their own roots. I had become frustrated that many of early Austin roses have been so hard to find and felt that they were worthy of preservation.  I have provided plants of over 30 roses to the curator of The San Jose Heritage Rose Garden in San Jose, CA, home to the self-proclaimed largest (in terms of the number of varieties planted, around 3000-4000) public rose garden in the Western Hemisphere, in the hopes that other individuals or rose propagation companies, could access them over time and 'keep the candle lit' for many of these horticultural treasures.  Many of his earlier creations were crosses between different Old Garden Roses and were perhaps a bit less refined with a few rough edges, but at times more charming, than his newer releases.  The roses 'Cressida', the 'Wife of Bath', 'Chaucer', 'Charles Rennie McIntosh' and so many more, come to mind.  I have also sent plants and cuttings to the Summerland Ornamental Gardens in Summerland, British Columbia, Canada, and to a rose propagator in British Columbia, who lives near the border with Washington State, in the hopes that these may be a repository for these rose and perhaps keep them in circulation for at least a decade more or so. Hopefully, after that time other like-minded people will take similar actions and keep them in circulation.  As we left our home of 15 years a year ago (needed to downsize, could keep up with 2 acres of gardens), with a collection of 150 Austin roses, an individual from this forum who shares our passion for these roses, came and dug out 40 or 50 of the most rare DAR's for his collection, promising to share plants and cuttings of our favorites with me and perhaps others in the spirit of Germplasm Preservation. Lily Spencer: It looks like you already have now or will soon receive, many of the best Austins, at least in my opinion, although many would perhaps have a very different list. I do know and understand the strong sentimental/emotional attachments that many of us have for particular roses, especially after they become so rare and difficult to find. For me, it was 'Cressida', which I grew in the 1990's and wanted so badly to have it in my garden at my new home in 2010.  It took me 3 years to find it, but I finally found a source and promptly propagated 6 more own-root specimens.  A good place to look is Peter Schneider's Freedom Gardens, in Freedom, OH.  Peter lives in a cold area of Ohio and DAR used to send him all their new releases in the UK (before they were commercialized in the US) to test them for cold tolerance.  He has amassed an amazing collection of Austin roses, many now very rare.  I have shared plants and cuttings with him over the years.  I did check to see if he had 'Royal Jubilee' in his collection, and he does not list it in his collection, but still, it might be worth a phone call.  If you are a member of helpmefind.com, you can look up this variety and hit the 'cuttings' tab and see if you can find an individual who has this variety and would be willing to share cuttings with you.  Or you could go to the Houzz Rose Propagation site and post a message that you are looking for cuttings of this variety.  Rooting roses is likely easier than you may imagine. Good luck in your quest:  I really hope you can find 'Royal Jubilee'!

Any good island hood of at least 600-900 CFM , plus a 90 in the duct, to run it outside will work. Ventahood, Broan,  Faber,,etc.  You will need at least 36" wide by 27" deep, and an 8" duct.  It needs to hang 30"-36" above the range, and obviously be non combustible.

McDonald Enterprises above covers the gist of it.  Typically, island hoods do not vent sideways, but you will need (if that is an 8-foot ceiling) a duct cover (chimney) to hang the island hood from, so the duct transition to horizontal can potentially be performed in the chimney zone. Note that the higher you have the entry aperture of the hood, the less room you have for the 90-degree bend, and the larger the hood entry aperture should be to capture rising and expanding plumes.  You don't have that much scenery behind, so I wouldn't worry about a 36-inch (or less) hood base height. In the attached image, I use a Wolf Pro Island hood.  It ducts up but given some fabrication from a sheet metal shop could potentially duct sideways.  Ignore the greater width than you need, I have an induction wok positioned next to my cooktop. There are certainly other island hoods than Wolf, so you will have to troll through the hoard of possibilities.  Perhaps starting with the many multi-manufacturer on-line stores (e.g., AJ Madison) will allow comparison of features and sizes such that the hood and chimney section can be compatible with your beam.  Note that the center of the hood intake aperture should ideally be aligned with the center of your burner array, front-to-back-wise.  The chimney section and horizontal path the the wall could be painted white. An inlet piece of soapstone could deal with the wood surface behind the range.  Since grease splatters there, soapstone might be easier to clean than granite, which can be porous.  Otherwise, a white granite might work. Last, there are requirements for distance from combustibles that apply to ranges, and these may be found in the installation requirements.  Combustibles include those in the half-wall behind the range.  My thinking is that your hot rear oven vent is probably far enough from whatever wood is behind the tile, but that needs to be checked.   (You can find this hood shape in Wolf's Design Guide.  What this image reveals above the hood base is mostly the chimney section that the pyramidal hood attaches to.  This hood is mounted to an 8-ft ceiling and has a 10-inch duct into an attic.)

A-hem! Returning to the topic at hand... And a diversion... During the dozen years I assisted adult adoptees and birthparents seeking one another, fear of finding incest was a common adoptee fear. (Just one of the unfair torments inflicted by sealed adoption records -- and sometimes by insecure adoptive parents.) We rarely saw that result of of search. Even when it was the truth, I'm not aware of any searcher who was not relieved to put an end to the 'maybe this/maybe that' and to have access to the same family history that non-adopted people take for granted. I'm pleased to read in the Atlantic article that there is a support group for people discovering incest. Support is now missing for people in the adoption triangle who don't join groups...because they no longer need help finding records and locating people. They find people -- but have had no preparation about how to handle emotions or to integrate relationships. Something I feel deserves research is the intensity of connection we often saw in family members reunited as adults. I thought that it evidenced the way individuals are normally absorbed into families by what we shrug off as 'resemblances', but may be more primal. We often saw a 'claiming' of the adult adoptee by not only the birthmother/father, but sibs, and even grandparents. This is normal with a new baby: Grandpa's nose; Mother's eyes.  LOVE if you will. In group, we learned to prepare reuniting people to recognize this for the delayed bonding it is.  Otherwise. in some instances, opposite genders (sisters/brothers, mothers/sons) experienced the love as sexual. It almost never actually was that, but to be swept away by this strong emotion was to ruin the true familial bonding. Forewarning was key. Nobody ever believed it ahead of reunion, but more than a few told us they were grateful for the warnig. I knew only two instances where people left their spouses to live with a reunited relative; IDK how long this attachment lasted. My interest is in the unknown power of this familial connection for every individual, not just those separated by adoption.  What drives it? And, what is the emotional damage where it doesn't take place, or is prevented (as in infant adoption)?

Hi there, I agree with everything everyone has already posted for you and have a couple of points to add. Firstly, if you are unhappy with the architect's first proposal for you, given they were provided all the information, including your budget, don't be afraid to switch architects. It would be hard to have a great relationship moving forward with the original architect. Secondly, make sure your budget is realistic for what you want. Having a more 'compact' plan may be what the architect thought would fit your budget. You wanted a 'creative, ambitious, bold and eye catching' design. Does your budget extend to the out of the ordinary solution you desire? Check out my website with the Hubbard house and Queenstown Home 03. Both of these have irregular plans and curved membrane roofs and are focused on the amazing view. The knock on effects of this are endless and the budget needs to accommodate these 'out of the box' ideas.  However, both of these have the views in the oposite direction to the sun so the 'warm roofs' were a good solution. Having said that, I agree that your proposed plan doesn't appear to capture your desires or the opportunities the site and views offer. PDS Design offers some lovely insight and I would suggest you definately look at engaging someone to come up with a new design after discussing all the issues with you, i.e, your breif, planning restrictions, budget etc. I am retiring so am not putting my name in the hat but you could ask one or two companies to offer concepts for you that should then both be priced before you proceed with a chosen one. A couple of design points - definitely agree that you should avoid internal gutters where possible. NZ is a high rainfall country so keeping water out of buildings is a high priority here. Things like corridor links, that have been suggested can have flatish roofs at lower levels to the main roofs but need to be really well detailed and correctly installed. Do you need 4 full bathrooms for a home of around 280-300 sq. m's? I would suggest some money could be saved by a better layout and possibly sharing a bathroom, unless that was your request originally. I would try, as has been suggested, to work with the slope to gain height with living spaces etc. What about having a garage and parking at the lower level with an entry and then create a terrace on top of that for the living and possibly bedroom/s to open onto. Given you have high rainfall, this should perhaps be covered or partly so, for you to use it or at least to have lounge doors open whilst there is light drizzle. What about an 'L' shaped plan with the court or terrace filling the space in the 'L' creating two 'wings' and the garage below. You don't have to be 'full frontal' to the view with a rectangular box and with careful window placement, you can maximise the view opportunities from almost every room. Big corner windows at the ends of the L can provide varying views. You can achieve a similar effect with two rectangular wings angling out from each other with a link towards the rear where they come closer. That will create a nice courtyard at the front and a smaller one at the back. One wing would be for living and the other for sleeping. The master would be at the end towards the view and the living would be arranged with the living at the view end, then the dining and the kitchen behind. The kitchen runnig accross the wing would have great views from the work bench/island. I could go on, but find someone else that you jell with to create your home. Don't be afraid to 'interview' a few before you choose the right team. Good luck, C.

text: This is a great question, and I appreciate your concern for both energy efficiency and your family's health. Spray foam insulation is often the best solution for achieving high R-values in limited space, especially in 2x6 walls where traditional insulation may fall short. Closed-cell spray foam, in particular, provides excellent thermal performance, air sealing, and moisture control, which can help improve indoor air quality by reducing allergens and pollutants from entering the home. That said, health considerations are important, especially for families with allergies or asthma. Spray foam contains chemicals that off-gas during installation and curing, which is why proper ventilation and professional application are crucial. Most reputable installers follow strict guidelines, including allowing the foam to fully cure (typically 24-72 hours) before reoccupying the space. Once cured, high-quality spray foam should be inert and not release harmful VOCs. If you have sensitivities, you might want to look for low-VOC or Greenguard-certified spray foam products and discuss alternative options with a trusted installer. Given your family's health concerns, it may also be helpful to consult with an indoor air quality specialist before moving forward. While spray foam can be an excellent choice for long-term comfort and efficiency, ensuring it's installed safely and correctly is key to avoiding potential issues. Take a look at some of our services to get an idea of how a professional company can help you and your family to accomplish your goal. Great discussion, and I hope you find the best solution for your addition!

That’s quite an ambitous project!  I wonder if you can defer the door trim style until you have the bulk of kitchen reno done. If that’s actually the plan, the pantry door looks like a disconnect with it being the only dark colored door & having the matching dark trim.  Is that the actual plan or is it a mockup picture issue?  If it’s the plan, I’d think about it some more. A matching color door & trim with a full glass panel (interesting diffused glass not plate glass) would be a better fit IMHO.

I don't know what code book you pulled R30 out of but for 99% of America R21 is code when used in 2x6 walls, and do you know why?  Because it's all you can stuff into a 5 1/2" deep cavity.  The only place in the United States requiring R30 is northwest Alaska and the Arctic slope of Alaska, do you live there?  If not someone lied to you. If you want more than Minimum code you can add 1" of foam board to the exterior of the walls to get R26, or 2" to get R31.  Or you can build with 2"x8" studs and fill the cavity with fiberglass or rockwool.  The optimum build would be to use two layers of 2x4 walls with a 1/2" air gap between the studs of the 2 walls to decouple the thermal bridge between the wood to the outside with a finished cavity depth of 7 1/2" and use 2x8's for the top and bottom plates.  This convenient cavity will allow room for 2" of foam board and high performance R21 fiberglass insulation to get R31, or just 8" fiberglass for R25. You could also build a single wall with 2x4's and insulate with R13, then stack a layer of 2 string hay bales for another R20 to R30, then build an inter wall with another layer of R13 for a grand total of R46 to R56.

Climate Zone 8 which extends to the northern tip of Canada requires R49 in the ceiling and R13cavity+R10continuous in the walls, per the IRC (or R20+R5 for walls). Insulation and air sealing has to be detailed ahead of time prior to cutting the very first wall stud. There are too many options of achieving both insulation for thermal comfort and condensation control which may affect framing and finishing the exterior. Usually, to achieve numbers in extremely cold climates, there will probably be some chemicals used, whether in air impermeable insulation (spray or rigid foam) or liquid-applied membrane (e.g. Zip-R). These can be avoided by using other materials, but detailing of the building enclosure needs to be done ahead of time.

Instagram, Pinterest, Display homes etc etc more often than not push prettiness over practicality. Design done well achieves both. The visual appeal of no doors, glazed everything, walk in showers, no rangehoods etc etc will wear off if the living experience from a practical aspect is compromised. Same goes for having a clear island bench with no sink but having hotplate and sink squeezed on the other bench.... looks great in a photo or display but compromised in function/balance....Sure some of this stuff is personal preference of what you're willing to compromise and weigh up but always suggest drive/build the design from how you live and function and then where possible work in / resolve aesthetics......flexibility is always recommended so if you're not sure about separation/privacy assume that as a default it's a good thing to have the option built in, as when it comes to family/many people living under the same roof doing different things in connected spaces it's always good to have cpacity to shut off rooms or obtain privacy on occasions. Looking at your plan there's no separation of all 3 living spaces so for example if someone is watching a movie up loud the whole house will be listening to it too like it or not.....consider adding/integrating concealed or face mounted sliding panels to the front living room and/or in the wall between the stair and the kitchen across so you can separate the main living spaces from each other - this way you could have 3 different activities happening simultaneously with flexibility/control of noise overlap.....as a father of two teenage boys, I can confidently say doors are your friend ;)
