This appears to be the tile that was purchased at Lowe's:   It apparently has three different shades of tile.  It is also listed as a V2 shade variation = slight variation - I was surprised to see it listed as a V2.   The three shades that it shows on the website appear to not be as dramatically different as the shades of tile on your walls:   It is also sold by the piece vs. box - which causes issues at big box stores because people can purchase many boxes of the tile - then sort through them at home (some people actually sorted through them in the actual store - I'm surprised that the store allowed them to do that) in order to only keep the pieces that they want - and return all of the ones they don't want. So, if you opened a box of tile at the store, it may have been a returned box = someone didn't want a particular shade of the tile - which made you think that the rest of the boxes would contain that particular shade = be pretty consistent in color. When people posted a comment about doing the above on this forum,  it always involved natural stone tile (specifically marble) - but I'm sure that it happens with other tile (although, I don't understand why they didn't just purchase a different tile instead). I've read comments on this forum where people have explained how they bought their marble tile at Lowe's/HD - and sorted through the tile in order to remove all of the pieces that they didn't like (weird rust color/green veins/darker background/etc).  The problem is that the price of the marble tile is set based upon the level of quality - when people sort through a ton of boxes in order to select only tiles with lighter backgrounds + nice veining, they've now received $50 per sf marble tile instead of the $6-8 per sf tile that they purchased. If another customer doesn't look through all of their boxes of tile PRIOR to installation - they wind up coming home to find a very different looking marble shower surround than they were expecting (based upon the sample board at the store).  Basically, they have a shower that was made out of rejected tile.  You'd think that a GC/installer would call the homeowner and ask them (because it would obviously all be not attractive marble tiles) - but a homeowner can't rely on the GC/installer to do that. If a homeowner has a designer - the homeowner would be able to rely on receiving a call + texts showing the tile.  Also, if a designer knew that the tile was a V2 - slight variation tile, but saw the tile you received, he/she would have contacted you to discuss the issue (after all, you would be paying client that he/she would want to make happy + the designer wouldn't want his/her name connected to a project that didn't turn out as expected).  A designer also would have specified the installation pattern. Also, if the homeowner had an experienced tile professional (TCNA or CTI certified) doing the installation, while they shouldn't rely on the installer to notify them, the installer would most likely make a call and/or send some photos in order to confirm that the quality (or the drastic color variation) was what the homeowner was expecting. I didn't have a designer for my bathroom renovations - however, I had a certified experienced tile professional who was doing the installation.  He discussed layout patterns with me prior to starting the installation.  He not only wanted to know what pattern I wanted - he also discussed with me which patterns he though would look the best with the specific tile + would work best in the space. I am surprised that so many people think that a running bond pattern is the most popular pattern currently - I think that vertical stacked is extremely popular (plus, horizontal stacked is pretty popular also) - whether with OP's sized tile or LFT tile.  I don't think that a smart tile installer would automatically default to a running bond pattern because I'd be surprised if most of his/her recent installations were running bond ones. In any event, the issue is that you specified the tile + didn't have a designer who designed the space for you (and would be overseeing the project). Also, if you had looked at the customer reviews for the tile on Lowe's website, this is what you would have found:     I think that the vertical stacked pattern looks better with this type of tile than a running bond one. Obviously, the person who had this next installation done specifically wanted to create a pattern by using only two of the three shades (he/she may have returned all of the medium colored shade tiles since it appears that they only used the lightest and the darkest shades for their walls):   I still think that you need to find out how your surround was constructed + waterproofed . . .

You keep mentioning how cold and sterile your kitchen looks, but when many suggest adding a backsplash with color, you push back. Go pick up some tiles in various shades of green and blue, and see how they look. And any other color that you like. I have grown Redskin dahlias from seed for the past two years and they sprout and grow quickly for me.  I plant out at the end of May and I won’t start my seeds until April.  Redskin are about an 18” tall dahlia and their full-size tubers are more like golfball size.  What variety and size are your ball dahlias?

I have grown dahlias from seed: they are generally trouble-free, germinating within 10 days from a late March/early April sowing. I don't use bottom heat, just sow a couple of seeds in 7cm square pots. Once the seedlings get their true leaves, I discard the weakest seedling-just cut off the top growth, don't try to pull the seedling out as that can damage the remaining seedling. I never need to pot up - 7cm2 is good enough for a single seedling until transplanting time (which will usually be the end of May in my climate).

My first thought is that where & how to live in retirement is a decision that should be reevaluated before retirement, at retirement & during retirement. It’s not a once & done decision - it changes as health, needs, wants change. It’s a very good thing to be thinking about retirement living well ahead of time & also a good thing to be talking to others about plans & ideas for it. It’s a good way to hear other ideas to consider.  We (DH & I)talked a lot about what lifestyle we envisioned in retirement. We couldn’t imagine renting because to us owning our home, mortgage free, represents more stability, privacy, control & choice. We did downsize to a smaller home & to a single story that was built with aging in place in mind. It has wider than standard hallways & doorways for walker & wheelchair accessibility & a flat yard. The floorplan supports having a live in caretaker or help with bed & bath privacy if that is ever needed. When we’re unable to do the maintenance home ownership requires, or even now when we don’t want to do it, we have the resources to pay someone to do it.  Our larger decision was deciding what city to live in. We knew we wanted to move away from our too busy & high traffic area to a place that still had easy access to an airport & to medical. We explored many places over 10 years preretirement to find our current home.  As I see it, our next decision point on where to live - whether to stay in the home we own or move into a retirement community will be health or death related. Would either of us want to stay in in this house alone? Would we both want to stay if neither of us could drive? What if one of us needs full time care due to either physical or cognitive decline?  The sale of our home would generate enough cash to facilitate an easier decision where the next home would be & our other resources are such that we could have caretaker help in this house if needed.

No, 11.5" is not normal nor is it the minimum recommended overhang for seating without a cooktop.  The minimum recommended overhang is 15" for counter-height seating. While the NKBA does not specify for behind a cooktop, if you look at their minimum recommended space with no seating of 9" and then add 15", you get 24" -- that would be 24" b/w the back of the cooktop and the edge of the seating overhang.  You might be able to get away with 18" b/w the cooktop and edge, but I wouldn't go any less. I hope you at least have an induction cooktop -- it's the safest; gas is the worst. Will you also have a hood above the cooktop?  It should be 6" wider than your cooking surface and 27"D.  This is especially important in an island (or peninsula) or against a wall when there are no upper cabinets butting up against the hood. I'm guessing your contractor is not a Kitchen Designer nor has a KD on staff. However, it looks like  you've already installed the counter, so what are you really asking here? Yes, you will need supports.  However, there should be supports even with the 11.5" overhang.  In general, any overhang > 10" should have supports.  Look into the "Counterbalance" system:  https://www.counterbalanceshop.com/ Is it a telescoping downdraft?  I.e., it rises above the surface.  How tall is it?  Is it taller than your tallest pot by at least a couple of inches?  Is it in the middle or the back (if in the middle, then all burners are up against it; if in the back, only the back burners are up against it and they're the only ones the downdraft will have a possibility of working for).There is no room for "being nice" in this situation.  This is a safety issue.  Think about billowing steam from a pot of boiling water in the face of someone sitting at the counter.  Or splattering grease that clears the top of the downdraft. Or, someone trying to reach over to the cooking surface (especially children, but adults do foolish things sometimes as well). A downdraft is not going to capture that billowing steam b/c downdrafts struggle to work against atmospheric physics - steam, smoke, etc., all rise, not fall.  And, they expand as they rise.  That downdraft will only capture steam, smoke, odors, grease form pots/pans that are below the top of the downdraft and right up next to it -- everything else will go into the Kitchen and, potentially, splash/waft into your visitor's faces.  The farther visitors are from the cooktop, the safer they'll be (and the less uncomfortable they'll be sitting there when someone is cooking.) Your contractor will not have to live with this 24/7/365, you will.  S/he has admitted fault, so get it fixed!

Slow drains can be caused by several different things. If it's bathroom tub / sink - usually the first suspect is hair / soap / toothpaste / shaving cream that can glom together in the trap, or other areas near the trap. If it's several places, it can be a main drain issue. They will run the main drain to clear that out. If they have reason to suspect tree roots or damaged main drain, they will run a camera down the sewer. Usually if you are talking roots, it's in an older house that has clay tile sewer lines. In my area, it's common for drain cleaning folks to sell the owner on installing an outside cleanout. This allows them to run the sewer from outside instead of inside the house.  Sometimes it's questionable if that's really needed. If they run the main sewer and tell you there is damage, you should get the photos of the damage and get at least a second quote.

There will be a clean-out plug someplace in the floor right before the main line that leaves the house and is required by code.  But as Jake stated your problem is more than likely before the main line and at the traps or at a tee or elbow in the  branch going to the main line.  A easy to use $25 drain auger from a hardware store is usually all that is needed to unplug these minor blockages. If flushing your toilet was slow to drain or overflowed and the trap built into the toilet was eliminated as the problem then this would be a sign the main line had a blockage or damage.   A plumber telling you the main line needs cleaned with a cutting auger when there isn't problems flushing the toilets would be a lie.  On the other hand telling you running a cutting auger through the main sewer line to remove debris and grease buildup as be preventive maintenance would not be a lie and would indicate his honesty (and desire to make more money).  Few people ever do preventive cleaning on sewage lines so consider this and make your choice. If  the plumber states your main line needs replaced do not hesitate getting a second opinion!! There is a slim chance a main needs replace in a 1970's house but fraud like this still happens and will cost $25,000 or more to replace the main to the street and big profits for the plumber.

Or depending on where the bathrooms are, it could be a main sanitary line issue, but you would have more issues than just say a slow draining vanity sink.

Central Iowa (5b, but only just) rose grower here.  I will say that the Austin hardiness ratings are... a bit generous, at least in our climate.  Yes, 'Lady of Shallot' and 'Benjamin Britten' will *survive* most Iowa winters without protection, but they will die back nearly to the ground.  'James Galway' has proven a bit hardier for me, but dies back too much in a 5a winter to make an effective climber.  'Abraham Darby', 'Golden Celebration', and 'Graham Thomas' need protection. To save yourself heartache, I suggest you either get used to providing ample winter protection for Austins, or perhaps rethink your brand loyalty. Tape some thick cardboard down on  the  marble  countertop  around  the  faucet,  then some plastic sheet.  You want  to  protect  the  marble  from  impact and  from  the  penetrating oil.  Add a folded bath towel as extra protection when the hammer comes out (below). Apply Kroil or PB Blaster, another penetrating oil  product.  Plenty of it.   Wait a day, reapply, wait a day. Get  the  correct six point closed end wrench.  It needs to be exactly  the  right size to fit on  the  hex surfaces - too large and you will round off  the  part.   This  will be a large wrench,  not  a common size. You  can  sometimes  rent tools  from  auto parts stores.  Set  the  adjustable wrench  to  fit  the  hex surface, tape  the  wrench jaw so it doesn’t move,  bring that  wrench  to the  store  and  ask  for  a six point wrench of  that  size. While there, get a small tube of “anti-seize” and a small brass wire brush.  I assume  you  have  brass and  copper polish, if  not  then  get  some. Place  the  closed end of the wrench on  the  part, pressed all  the  way onto  the  hex surfaces, wrench handle  more or less vertical.  Again,  the wrench must fit with  minimal play; if you  got the  wrong size, stop and  get the  right  size. Have someone  hold the  head of  the  wrench  firmly   onto  the  part  so it  doesn’t slip.  Take a large hammer and strike  the  wrench handle, at  the  far end.  Start with little taps as practice controlling the hammer, then  hit moderately hard.  You are trying to use impact to break the thin corrosion  layer that is holding the part stuck.  The shock of impact  works better than  a steady pull.  After  the  part starts moving, use  the  wrench in  the  normal manner. The  protection  on the  marble  counter  is  there  if  you  drop  the  hammer etc.  The wrench is vertical so you aren’t swinging  the  hammer down at  the  counter.  Be  very careful  all  the  same. After  you  get the  part off, and  have replaced  the  cartridge, use  the  polish  and a cloth  to  clean up  the  part  and the  rest of  the  faucet.  Really  polish  it up well.  The  hex surfaces may be marred a bit (brass is a crappy material  for  a hex nut), but  when  polished  shiny it   won’t show (much). Use  the  wire brush  to  clean up  the  threads.  Apply anti-seize  to the  threads. Reinstall  the  part,  using  only  your  fingers to  turn it until the  threads engage (because you  do not want to  use the  wrench until  you are sure you  haven’t cross-threaded the part) and  tighten it only  just  enough  to  not leak,  then  a tiny bit more. Be gentle: with  that  big wrench you or  more  likely  some ham-handed male helper can easily cross-thread the part or strip  the  threads. This is  how  you’d break free then reinstall a large stuck nut on a car - e.g. an axle nut.  Well, on  the  car  you  might  use heat  to  break  the  corrosion,  and  you’d torque  the  heck out of  the  nut  when  reinstalling.   But  you’d clean  the  threads and  use  anti-seize,  so that the  next time  isn’t  such  a  nightmare.

You start with the shade trees. Traditionally, those go on the south and/or west side of the house. Evergreens go on the north and/or west side to block winter winds. Around here, there is a practice of growing Clematis (the really showy ones, not ones like Sweet Autumn Clematis), in a shade collar.  Since showy Clematis like hot heads, but cool feet, the shade provided by a shade collar provides the needed shade/coolness for the Clematis' crown. Light colored 2 gal. buckets with the bottom cut out, leaving a 12" high collar should work.  Young roses can be planted and the collar placed directly around the little bush, and established bushes can have a slit made down the collar side, then jiggled into place. Shaker is much more difficult to keep clean than a slab front and I used to sell them! We had a lot of customers come in and say that they were looking for a much cleaner look now. The company that I worked for now does a plain flat front slab door in wood as well as the Shaker and traditional shaker style with beading. Think about your lifestyle. Everyone is different with regard to cleaning. I like shaker style in a large kitchen preferably in a period house but in smaller kitchens the door fronts with the post and rail makeup as well as the double lines created by in-frame can make it look very fussy. We only sold in-frame. Layon door cover the whole open cabinet front.

If you are considering a [painted] timber shaker door than there will be a step between the outer frame and the centre panel ie the dust trap, but you can have these with either beading or some can have an angled chamfer to the inner frame [I have the Marpatt Monarch door which has this chamfer] and you don't have a dust trap, its also a more subtle look than the beading IMO. Alternatively though, you can also have vinyl wrapped shaker doors, these are made from 1 piece mdf and cnc machined to look like a shaker door and then wrapped in a coloured vinyl, usually a matt foil but now also the supermatt anti fingerprint, scratch resistant coloured foils. So these doors are just a simple wipe down without any tight corners and they are cheaper than a timber painted shaker door.

Assuming it's a rental, here are some simple things you can do: Bedroom: --Remove the round table with computer from bedroom area. --Remove the small chair on the left side of the bed and whatever the clutter is on the right. --Remove vanity but keep the mirror. (See below) --Put the tall dresser shown in living area in the corner where round table is now. --Put both oriental rugs in living room area. If you want something soft when you get up, get a light, soft rug for by the bed. --Run a sheer curtains across the space to divide bedroom from living room/office area.  --Change your bedside lampshades to plain white drum shades. --Check Amazon to see if you can find an ivory slipcover for your headboard, which is so dark. --Keep your bedding at the end of the bed down to the floor so the bed looks tidy and inviting. --Put a nice big wicker basket in the bedroom area for holding pillows. --If you're not attached to that dark art work over the bed, look for a light art work that evokes the sky or the outdoors--as if you're looking out a window-- about 2/3s of the headboard size.     Living room/office area: --Run a shelf desk entirely across the window wall the depth of that niche. You can have one cut to fit at big box stores. Paint it white. Put a tall table lamp at one end of the desk. Drop a modern, bright pendant over the desk as below.  --Remove all cluttery extra furniture, including vanity table., wall clock, stuff on walls. One or two big, bright pieces work better in a space that has to do double duty. You can put your mirror above desk to the side of the windows. Buy shallow storage dressers/cabinets 12" for under the wall desk. Ikea's Rask dressers should fit under the desk there. --Install bamboo shades the color of your wood floors--or white--across both windows. (Long) Update: Well, I ended up buying a Sebo E3. I compared the different models and features between the Miele and Sebo at the vacuum store.  While there are some things I like better on the Miele, the Sebo was less expensive for a comparable machine and I like the hose handle much better. The hose handle on the Sebo isn't as thick in circumference and it bends at a more natural angle so it's more comfortable in the hand. That wasn't a deal-breaker on the Miele - after all, I was used to it. What made the difference for me is the suction control is on the handle of the Sebo, rather than on the canister itself, so if you're going from one situation to another where you need to adjust the suction, you don't have to stop, turn around, reach down and fiddle with the controls on the Miele. I also like the size and shape of the power head on the Sebo better -- my my the power heads on Miele are HUGE now, and they're bulky. I also thought the pedal to unlock the head out of the upright position was very awkward on the Miele; with the Sebo it's a simple foot pedal like an upright, but the Miele you kind of have to push the wand forward and then push backward on the pedal and it's on the top of the "hood" of the head -- it's just weird, I didn't like that at all. My old machine didn't have a pedal at all, it just moved into the "I'm vacuuming now" position with a simple arm motion moving the wand downwards. What I don't like as much about the Sebo compared to the Miele is that the power cord mechanism is encased in plastic along the backside of the metal wand -- I don't really know how the power gets down to the head of the Miele, but there's no plastic encasement, the wand is just a metal tube and is more comfortable to grip if you need to grip the wand for some reason. I also like the larger parquet head on the Miele better and the fact that it easily swivels to get tightly along the baseboards (well, mine did anyway); the Sebo parquet head is narrower front to back, and it kinda sorta swivels but it takes some effort. I'll have to look into whether they have a different size I can buy. I also don't like how the duster attachment attaches to the front of the wand, kind of like a big protruding medallion on the wand, it was bugging me when I was going under the furuniture so I ended up taking it off and putting it in the closet. Not a big deal since I don't use that attachment much, but that seems like it could be better thought out, since the beauty of a canister is its manueverability under furniture and around tight spaces and this thing just gets in the way IMO. This new power head is definitely going to take some getting used to. It definitely has some power to it, it wants to pull me along -- it's almost like a self-propelled upright feels. That is much different than my old Miele, but in fairness it was an old machine and I imagine technology and components are much improved in the last quarter-century... It feels like this new power head has a mind of its own and wants to get away from me, but I'm sure I'll get used to it after an adjustment period. "A properly sized HVAC system is over sized upwards of 80-90% of the time as the outdoor temperature you live in constantly changes."  A properly-sized HVAC system is designed for a particular cooling load and a particular heating load at a particular set of summer and winter design temperatures, respectively.  The design temperatures are specified in the code for your area.  How often the system operates close to the design conditions depends on your climate.  If a properly-sized system is operating far from maximum or minimum design temperatures, it's not over-sized, it's simply operating far from the maximum or minimum design conditions.  For single-stage and single-speed systems, operating far from max/min design conditions typically results in reduced efficiency and may decrease occupant comfort as well.   More sophisticated (and expensive) systems (e.g., multi-stage, variable speed systems) provide better control, efficiency, and comfort over the full range of design conditions.

I'll have to say, I cut wood with chainsaws for >45 years, and the first thing you notice when you hit a nail, fencing staple or barbed wire grown into a tree, is the saw stops cutting. The minute you hit something that dulls the chain, even slightly, you can run the saw as fast as you like and not get very far at all. That's why 'backup chains' are a good to have along. Encounters with objects in a tree is on the rare side. And as a cutter, you learn to diagnose potential problems, and if in doubt, you cut above a possible fence line or whatever, making a near ground level cut on the stump last. But I agree, things happen, and life is dangerous. Removing a yard tree by an inexperienced novice with a chain saw, could end with loss of life. But most likely it won't be because a nail dulls your saw. And personally, with my background, I don't put nails in trees. Still bugs me when people do that. ;-)

As FRH above has already commented, you need to use the different wood species + stains very thoughtfully in order for it to work in your kitchen.  I've seen a few kitchens that have used two wood species (typically, one stain is lighter and one is medium to darker) - it seems like they were larger kitchens that leaned a bit more modern than simply transitional. I wouldn't ever try to mix wood species/stains in a kitchen without advice from an actual kitchen designer (not someone who works for the cabinet manufacturer). What are your plans for flooring and countertop material?  Those two decisions will impact whether two wood species/stains will work in your kitchen.  If you are using another wood stain on the floor + bold countertop slabs (or one type of slab for your island and a different countertop slab for your perimeter cabinets), it seems like it could become very busy. Obviously, your backsplash selection will also need to be considered in the design of your kitchen - but that should be selected last (unless you are running your countertop up the wall  as your backsplash - you'll need to have those slabs held at the time you order your countertops - you can't just decide later to use slabs for your backsplash also - whether natural stone or man made material - because you need the lot #s to be the same for the countertop slabs + the backsplash slabs). My general rule of thumb on "through" items like doors is consistency.  The exception might be an entry door.   So I would typically advise a client to either paint all the doors the same color OR go natural wood in a matching tone. The color depends on the end result you're going for.  With your warm neutral on the walls in the lower hallway white is a safe option of course but you could even do a stronger color. When you're considering painting a single element, start by creating a paint palette for you entire home that consists of a "through" neutral color - like this hall wall color.  Add in your trim color.  The select an accent color the works well with your flooring and adds a little flair.  You can even incorporate a wood tone you love (like the wood tone in your beams, for example!).  That way if you opt for wood doors downstairs, you know the whole thing will blend. There's been a trend to go with strong colors - black doors are popular! - but you could even do a deep neutral to keep that hallway from feeling too closed in. Used this pre-set color palette as the cohesive factor throughout the public areas and in those through spaces and your whole design will come together more easily. Pamela.

Pan shape to purpose matters a lot more over flames.  On induction, tou want more flat bottom and shorter=vertical sides, to make for the best heat transfer.  Thereby, choose shape for induction, and size for volume of task. I use my old Le Creuset enamel CI saucier 1 qt. for things like melting butter or chocolate.  The lower heat from less contact with the surface is good, and the curved sides make it easier to scrape out, but my favorite LC CI pot from coil and gas, the flared ”soup” pot I got at the grocery store, doesn't get used at all on induction.  Ever.  Totally wrong shape, and I have straight sided others which are now the go-tos and less loved on gas. That said, I'd say use your new pots for awhile.  See what works for you.  See what you like and don't like.  Keep an eye out for sales, including on the Zwilling website.  When you feel a need is soon enough to buy one.

Need yes is relative, and you can do anything with your saucepans as long as you pay good enough attention.  I find the saucier excel not only for sauces but the larger size is useful for thick dishes like risotto, some curries/indian food (think kadai), curds, custards and the like.  It just keeps food from getting stuck in the corners and provides a wider evaporation area, so things are a bit easier (including cleanup). With a saucier, you really want something with the most conductive, and reactive sidewalls.  For gas, I have a 2qt and 3.5qt from Falk (2.5mm stainless-lined copper).  The thick copper provides more even heating up the sidewalls than clad stainless steel.  I also have a Demeyere version (and a similar shape in a larger handleless one) that I use on induction.  The thicker 3mm sides are a bit better than other SS but inferior to the copper one.

I have found that some seeds will not germinate in water but must be put in soil (or whatever medium you are using--I use a seed starting mix with coconut coir). I suspect that the evergreen or semi-evergreen seeds are the ones that germinate in water the easiest. The others are probably dormant. Your seeds have been in the water long enough to rehydrate them so go ahead and plant them.  I once soaked a batch of desirable seeds for 4 weeks with no germination. Rather than throw them out, I planted them and most of them germinated. I germinate my seeds a little differently than most growers. I do refrigerate my seeds (in little baggies) until I am ready to germinate them. When I am ready to plant them, I pour a little water (I use distilled, but I don't know if that is necessary) in the baggie and put them back in the refrigerator. I used to keep them there until they sprouted, but now I wait just a few days. This cold moist treatment approximates what would be happening to them in nature. The semi-evergreen/evergreens probably don't need the cold moist treatment, but I think the dormants benefit from it. I would give the unrefrigerated seeds a cold moist treatment. I would put them to soak in the refrigerator and keep them there for a week or so (or until they sprout--some might sprout in as little as a couple of days). I find that I don't need to wait until they have sprouted. In fact, I prefer that they haven't sprouted because they are easier to plant. It's too easy to damage the radicle. Another reason I prefer to soak my seeds in the refrigerator is the cold temperatures inhibit the growth of mold. Good luck!

Usually in most cities a fence requires a permit and with the application a copy of a certified property land survey showing the property line.  Go to your city building department and speak to code enforcement about the issue.  If they violated code the city will force them to tear down the fence. Another issue is the side of the fence facing your property.  In my state the ugly side must face the owner who put it up.  This would be the side with the posts and vertical nailing timber seen in your picture.  Fence laws usually determine ownership of a fence in question by the direction the ugly side is facing, so if it was here in Minnesota the fence technically belongs to you. Another problem you have is the neighbor can gain ownership of your 3 foot strip of land they fenced in through Adverse possession.  It refers to a legal doctrine where a person who is not the legal  owner of a property can gain ownership of that land by occupying it  continuously, openly, exclusively, and hostilely for a specific period  of time as defined by state law.  You do not want this to happen.

Look at your deed it will detail where the lot lines are.  If it mentions marker, or even if it doesn't, look for them.  Often, there are small markers on the corner of lots. On my lot, they look like they are made of rebar and about an inch above the ground. Very hard to notice, particularly under shrubs.  If you find them, take pictures. Put a stake in the ground at each marker and measure how much setback they have. Talk to your code enforcement officer.  If their fence is illegal, the city should give the neighbor a notice and you an opinion.  If the fence is, indeed on your property, you can legally remove it and send them a bill.  You can send them a letter of your intentions first, so that they can remove it themselves.  If you do have it removed, and they don't pay, you can go to small claims court, which will rule on your side, if your documentation is all in order.  Small claims court doesn't require a lawyer and usually has an affordable filing fee which winning plaintiffs can often get the loser to pay. If the issue is just that it's not within the setback of their property, then you may have to rely on the city to do enforcement. So, start by researching the code and your lot, then talk to the code enforcement officer.  In the small towns of my experience, the code enforcement officers and town employees are very helpful.  You could also start with them and they might tell you what and where to find the information you need.

I posted this some time ago.  This is just for comparison.  It's a base recipe, and meant to be tinkered with.  The result is a long rise no-knead loaf with a well risen close crumb. Here's what I used to make for daily bread, before I had to give up whole grains:455 g total flour(100g rye, 200g whole red wheat, 155g whole white wheat)—use any combo, but make the majority bread flour or add Vital Wheat Glutenpinch vitamin C powder/crystals (for the whole grain, aids general dough conditioning and combats anti-nutrients)25g Vital Wheat Gluten2.5g ADY yeast10-12g salt425-455g water100g mix-ins, seeds, grains, nuts, whatever (e.g., rolled oats, buckwheat, flaxseed, pepita sprouts, sunflower seeds, millet) Combine mix-ins with enough of the measured water to cover. In a separate bowl, combine the flours, VWG and the rest of the water. Let soak for at least 8 hours. Stir the yeast into the flour mixture. Add the salt to the mix-ins. Let sit in a gently warm place until the flour and yeast mixture starts bubbling a bunch. Mix in the mix-ins, kneading lightly. Move to an oiled bowl and let rise at least 1.5 times the volume. Shape loaf and let rise again, Bake at 385F for one hour.

By 'evergreen' this does not mean always and perpetually in leaf. All evergreens shed foliage, just at different times and quantities than deciduous plants which have a much more prolonged dormancy and a tendency to lose all foliage at once, for months instead of continuous foliage replacement over a whole season (such as my bay trees) or for a few weeks while new foliage is rapidly replaced (such as hellebores). Of course, this is my entirely unscientific observations but I have yet to see any plant which retains all it's foliage with no obvious signs of replacement. I wouldn't worry overmuch.

We upgraded to a smart sprinkler system.  It's great.  I don't have to be home to adjust it.  My old sprinkler system would run even in a downpour.  If you wanted to stop it, you had to go to the garage and manually stop it and remember to restart. We sprinkled at night or early morning, so often weren't awake. So, we bought a rain sensor.  Then, it wouldn't run when it was raining, but it would run on schedule after 2 days of downpour. Now, we have a smart sprinkler system.  It skips a scheduled run when rain is forecast, which means it can skip runs when it doesn't actually rain.  But it aways reminds me, so I can decide to run it the next day.  The app shows me when it ran.  It's just so much easier to deal with than the manual one. Further, configuring the smart system is much, much easier.  I hated configuring my old system.  I don't have to push buttons on the controller forever.  I can see what my schedule is, I can name and describe my zones, the app even lets me take a picture of them, so my husband knows what "lilac to magnolia" means. Controllers are cheap enough that if a smart controller doesn't last as long (my old one was several decades old), it's still worth it.  The rest of the system is exactly the same, so the durability you're concerned about is not the entire, expensive system, but just the controller box.   They cost $100-200, not on sale. I would go for a smart controller box, hands down.  Wifi enabled, because that's how you get the app, so you can adjust your sprinkler from the comfort of your living room or bedroom if it's 5 am.

Before I retired and closed my store, I sold lots of leather reclining sofas and sectionals.  I was a dealer for Hooker and tried one of the Savigion series reclining sofas in my store.  I did not re-order it when I sold the floor model.  Quality is mid-level, its made in the Pacific Rim (China/Vietnam) and I was unimpressed with it.  The leather used is highly prone to sun-fade and I had low-confidence on durability over time. $ 10K to $ 15K is not a lot for a large motion sectional.  To get upper tier product that is made in the USA, you will be in the $ 20K to $ 25K range,  If you buy one, get one with either Legget and Platt or Ultra-Mek mechanisms in it.  Those are the best in the industry and if a mechanism breaks, you can get replacement units (unlike those for many imports). The problem with these big power sectionals - every one of them - is Weight and Wear.  To save money, people buy them in large combined segments when they should buy them in individual compoments for ease of handling and maintenance.  The large segements are difficult to move around and deliver.  Wear is where you sit.  Typically you will use one position all the time and the wear is greatly accelearated in that spot.  In 5 to 7 years, it will be noticably used while the rest of the unit looks nearly new, and unless you maintain it regularly will become an eyesore in under ten years. Being four decades in the business, I would never buy a large motion sectional from any maker, they lock you into a specific placement that cannot be changed, and the entire unit has to be replaced if one area is damaged or worn.   Better to buy yourself one or two really nice recliners in leather and supplement seating with a stationary sofa of some kind.

My comments: If you're going to have seating in front of the slider, then 48" is the bare minimum I would even consider -- and that's assuming the sliding part isn't directly behind the seats.  If so, it should be wider so there's room for both someone to be seated there and others to use the door.  In addition, you need to stick with the minimum recommended overhang for that seating -- 15".  Anything less and someone seated at the island is going to stick farther out into the aisle.  12" is too shallow. For the aisle behind the seats on the back of the island, what is behind them?  If a wall, then 51" is probably OK, as long as there isn't anything back there to interfere with the traffic to/from the sliding door & the rest of the home.  I would prefer 54" or more b/c that's likely going to be a busy aisle, but I think 51" will be doable. If that refrigerator is a counter-depth refrigerator, then it will be 30" to 33" deep when accounting for the box (the part that's "counter-depth"), the doors & handles, and the required air clearance behind the refrigerator.  If it's a true integrated/built-in, then it's probably around 27"D. Aisle measurements...are they counter-to-counter or cabinet-to-cabinet.  There's something written there, but it's not very legible.  What does it say?  Aisles are measured to/from the items that stick out into them the farthest -- counter overhangs, appliance handles, etc.  If the measurements are counter overhang-to counter overhang, then they're probably OK if only one person will be prepping and/or cooking and/or cleaning up at the same time.  However, if your aisle measurements are cabinet-to-cabinet, then they are at least 3" narrower than you show. Cabinet measurements, including depth, only include the cabinet boxes; the drawer fronts/doors are not included nor are the counter overhangs.  All told, the standard depth of a perimeter cabinet + doors/drawer fronts + counter overhang is 25.5".  There is also a 1.5" counter overhang on the island cabinets.  So, 1.5" + 1.5" = 3".  That would bring your aisle measurements to 39" - too narrow.  The minimum recommended is 42" for a one-person and always a one-person work aisle (minimum is 48" for more than one person working on the aisle at the same time).  This is especially important when all three primary work zones (Prep, Cooking, Cleanup) are all on the same aisle. I would probably do the following (left-to-right): 1" filler (to account for any wall imperfections) + 15" cab + 30" range + 24" cab + 18" trash pullout + 30" sink base + 24" DW + 18" cab + 1" filler (if that's a cased opening to the LR and it's less than 24" from the cabinets, then make it 1.5" of filler) =============== 161" Note:  Depending on your cabinetmaker/company, you can sometimes get cabinets with "extended stiles" so you don't need filler.  The extended stile acts as filler. Regarding the hood, I recommend 36"W x 24"D so the hood is 6" wider than the cooking surface.  Even if you stick with 30"W, still get 24"D.  Anything shallower will not cover the front burners.  In your case, I might recommend getting an under-cabinet hood so you can utilize the entire space and not need to leave "breathing space"/"cleaning access" between the hood and adjacent cabinets.

Regarding the refrigerator, I would probably move it to the left so it's closer to the sink/range wall. Note that if you're going to "build it in", you will need about 38" of space for the refrigerator (Ref width + two 3/4" panels (one on each side) + air clearance b/w the Ref and panels). You could then have your Coffee/Snack Center to the right of the refrigerator.  I would probably also move the MW drawer there as well so it's in the Snack Center.  You'll still be relatively close to water.

Bbstx: Curried Chicken Casserole This makes a large 9 x 13 Pyrex dish plus one 8 x 8 dish for your mother (or freezer). About 3.5 lbs of boneless breast of chicken, roasted in the oven until just done.  (I cut each breast into several pieces of equal size so they cook evenly) I head of broccoli florets, par boiled  or steamed until no longer crunchy. (You can save some prep time by buying frozen broccoli florets and just letting them defrost, no cooking needed) Sauce: 3 cans of condensed cream of chicken soup 1.5 cups mayonnaise 1/4 cup and 1 tbls lemon juice 1 and 1/3 tsp curry powder (your fave, I use Penzeys but in fact McCormicks is just fine for this) Salt and pepper to taste Bread stuffing, prepared (I make this from scratch but you can certainly use Pepperidge farm or any other type stuffing) to cover the top of the casserole (To make just the one larger casserole, use 2 cans soup, 1 cup of mayo and 1/4 cup lemon juice, 1 tsp curry) Preheat oven to 350 In a 9 x 13 baking dish (or 9x13 plus an 8 x 8) cover the bottom with broccoli florets, either lightly cooked or defrosted frozen Cover broccoli with bite size pieces of cooked boneless chicken breast Pour sauce over entire surface Cover with stuffing dropped on surface to cover sauce Cover casserole with aluminum foil Cook for at least 40 min or until sauce is bubbling around edges.  Take off foil and let stuffing brown for another 10 min or so There are many shortcuts you can take for this— frozen broccoli, rotisserie chicken, bottled lemon juice, premade stuffing.  All iterations are pretty good and I have at different times used them all, singly or together.  If time is no object I prefer to make everything myself but no can’t say the finished product is that much better.  The ingredients are humble and I hate using a commercial condensed soup, but making cream of chicken soup is a bridge too far— and doesn’t make enough difference.  But,  the whole is much better than the parts. I don’t have exact amounts of broccoli or chicken because I make it according to the pan I’m using.  Sometimes there is more chicken, sometimes less, ditto for broccoli, and it never matters. This dish was very popular in the 1970’s and the 80’s and 90’s… nearly every church, Junior Leage, and PTA  cookbook included an iteration of it.  Many include shredded cheddar cheese on top of the stuffing (or mixed into it); both of these additions is IMVHO, heresy.

A number of thoughts: - Your husband is right about the TV over the fireplace.  It would be uncomfortable to watch the TV at that height, and it would look odd sandwiched between the fireplace and those windows.  You have the TV in the right place. - The room's extreme height is hurting you in two ways:  1) The living space is fairly full /even a bit cluttered (get rid of the vacuum, the hanging quilt rack, and the metal folding chairs at least), but the upper walls are bare of color and decoration.  The wall immediately around the TV is full, while the large wall around it is empty.  2) The double-high ceiling is very high /feels out of human proportion, and the plain ceiling plays into this negative. - Still thinking about the bare walls -- this is more of a clarification of the above comment -- the spots that're decorated (the fireplace mantle and the TV area, for example) are quite full.  Your taste seems to be "filled up" /things to catch the eye.  That contrasts badly with the wide-open empty spaces. - Color (or lack of color) is an issue here.  I like the teal-green TV stand -- that color should be repeated elsewhere in the room:  in a rug, throws and pillows on the sofa (hopefully in a mix of solids + patterns), and in artwork.  Appropriately placed color will make your room feel more cohesive /less like random stuff thrown together.  Said differently, lose some of this neutral and bring in some personality. - A non-neutral rug will make a big difference in this room.  And bring the furniture "in" a bit so it's closer together /gives you a not-so-spread-out seating area. - You don't like the loveseat "blocking" entrance to the room.  Yeah, I can see that.  I think I count three metal folding chairs, which hints you need more seating.  I'd switch the existing sofa and love seat out for a sectional (placed where the existing sofa is) + two recliners flanking the TV. - Additionally, I think the sofa and love seat are a step too dark for the room.  They seem to draw the eye in a negative way.  I'd consider something more medium-toned.  Alternately, bring in the dark shade elsewhere in the room.  Actually, the problem isn't really that they're too dark -- it's that the shade isn't repeated anywhere else in the room. - Lighting is a problem.  I see a single bulb on the ceiling fan and -- are those ceiling acne lights?  They're too high to be effective in the room below -- they aren't effective for reading or needlework.  You need lamps near the seating to bring the light down to the people -- lamps could be a good spot to echo the teal-green TV stand. - I'd like to see something "planned" behind the love seat /against the stair -- at the moment, it appears empty.  Two small chairs?  Not stuffed because you don't have the space.  Two ladder-back chairs with a small table between them?  These two chairs could be brought into the seating area when needed.  Alternately, a shallow desk and chair?  Or a narrow sofa table with a lamp -- it could function as a drop-spot for guests?  Any number of things could fit here, and I'd "let this go" until you've taken care of the main seating area, but it needs something. - Every room needs something organic -- I see one plant over in a corner.  Look into where you could add a couple more plants across the room.  Consider putting the plants in baskets.

A floor widely available is engineered European Oak. A different species of oak is used. It doesn't have the open grain of NA white oak. This allows a flat cut top layer. And levels from prime to rustic. Rift and quarter-sawn aren't necessary to hide open grain. Cabinets in our market haven't yet fully caught up. I recently was looking at Havsta units for part of my basement renovation - so, I saved quite a few examples of different hacks using these IKEA units. Havstas are built out of wood instead of particle board - which is nice.  There are many hacks out there showing how they upgraded their Havsta pieces in order to make them look like they were way more expensive: This first photo below is just some Havsta components stacked together and placed on the sides of a fireplace in a dining room.  Havsta now comes in a tan (with a bit of gray) color - in addition to white and black.  The nice thing about Havsta is that the upper cabinet can be one with glass doors - or solid ones (if you don't want anyone to see what's inside).  Nothing was "hacked" on the Havsta units below - they are just how they come from IKEA:   Below are white Havsta units - just put in the dining room without doing anything to them:  A couple years later, the homeowner decided to paint them + add a board and attach crown to them:  She also added beadboard wallpaper inside + painted it a light blue:   Here is another set of white Havsta units - just stacked in a dining room.  She used all top units to create the wall unit - I assume to make it taller.  However, by doing that, she lost the "step back" feature of the units = the bottom units are deeper - so, when you add the top units, they sit back a little bit (which also disguises the "line" that is created between the separate units).   A year or two later, she decided to paint them + make them look like a custom built-in + added a light inside the glass unit +use some wood trim to cover up the line between the upper and lower units in order to make it look like one piece (instead of stacked pieces):   Here is a different use of Havsta units (built a coffee station)  - but could be used in a dining room.  She also used two upper units stacked on each side + used two lower units in the middle = the little bit of extra depth of the lower units makes it a bit more interesting than if the cabinets were all the same depth all the way across:   Below is another white Havsta built-in that was done by a homeowner.  She took the cabinets up to the ceiling + added crown moulding.   She added peel and stick wallpaper to the back of the upper glass units:   Below, the homeowners used Havsta units to create this for their dining room.  They made it look built-in + added beadboard wallpaper to the inside of the glass units + extended the upper units to the ceiling and added crown moulding + painted them + used a beautiful piece of quartzite on top of the lower units.  FYI - they installed a marble waterjet mosaic tile between the upper glass door units.  I think it looks really nice - however, it definitely added some expense to the project  - to save money, you could use a pretty wallpaper instead.   Here is one of my favorites (I also really like the one above with the marble mosaic!) - this mom needed some storage for the "school room" she created in her home to home-school her children.  She purchased the units because she liked black furniture (although, these were listed as brown - but she said that they actually looked black) + she loved furniture that had a "step back" feature:   One issues is that she obviously hadn't connected the cabinets to each other - you can see a big gap between the cabinet on the right and the middle one (the gap is more obvious between the upper units).  She almost painted them - but then came up with a much easier solution. She purchased a remnant piece of marble (or it might have been a prefab piece) and her husband cut it + honed it.     She also added a chandelier to the room - but the unit looks much better once she added the marble slab.  This was so simple - there was no painting/adding crown/making the unit looked built-in (other than it appears that she connected the units in order to make sure there weren't any gaps between them). You could also change the pulls on the units - or add some fluting to the doors (there are many tutorials about adding fluting to various pieces of IKEA furniture - look for fluted Besta units or Ivar units (I'm sure there are others).  Also, many people add rattan inside the door trim or linen fabric that closely matches the color of the cabinets (typically, they paint them). I just wanted to show you that you can make Havsta units look much more expensive than they are (although, they are more expensive than most of IKEA's furniture because they are made out of solid wood).  There are also Hemnes units that you could use - they are wood also (I think the Havsta ones look nicer). There are also lower units that have sliding doors instead of hinged ones - but it seems like most people must prefer the hinged doors - I didn't specifically look for examples of hacks done with the sliding doors - I'm sure there are some out there.  I think the hinged doors look nicer.

"Its a Kitchenaid from 1990s. KEB6207BAL2 is what's on the oven but the closest match I see online is KEBS207BAL2 The unit is almond color and the alternatives are black and white." It's KEBS.  There is no KEB6.  B in eighth position indicates 1994 model-year of introduction so you're correct on that.  The serial number is coded for the year and week of manufacture.  AL is almond color.  2 is the engineering revision. The door handle and a couple trim pieces are color-matched to the door panel. All three door panels are NLA (no longer available) from parts sources.  Chances seem slim of finding new black panels from a servicer or parts source that happens to have a set on-hand for the specific model.  Used parts can be found on eBay but that's also unlikely in this instance. The control touch-panel and trim is also color-matched ... all three are also NLA.

I don't know what it's called, but I came across something online about a dozen years ago that has worked like a charm for me to remember a grocery list of ten or fewer items. Example: 1 = bun, 2 = glue, 3 = tree, 4 = door, 5 = drive, 6 = mix, 7 = heaven, 8 = ape, 9 = dine, 10 = pen Proposed grocery list: 1 - pickles: I picture a jar of pickles between the top and bottom of a giant hamburger bun. 2 - milk: I picture myself brushing glue all over a jug of milk. 3 - Dish soap: l picture many bottles of dish soap hanging from a tree. 4 - picture opening a closet door and lots of “the product” come tumbling out. 5 - picture driving down a road and you see a huge “product” blocking your way. 6 - picture stirring a bunch of “the product” in a mixing bowl. 7- picture lots of “the product” on an escalator ascending to heaven. 8 - picture an ape holding a frame with a photo of “the product”. 9 - picture a dinner plate with “the product” on the plate and you’re cutting it. 10 - picture yourself writing the name of “the product” on a piece of paper. Sounds crazy, but it works for me. Even weeks later the list is still in my mind. But once I assign products to a new grocery list, it’s fixed for my next small grocery run. And I never worry about losing my grocery list (ever done that?) This can be used for larger lists in a different way, but I never tried it and can’t remember where I found the info.

Wasn't she also Natal? I will always be indebted for her recipe: Honey Chipotle Pecans These are an addictive combination of sweet and spicy. My advice is to always make more than you think you'll need because they go quickly! Can be prepared up to a week ahead of time. Store in a sealed container. 2 Tablespoons honey1 1/2 teaspoons chipotle powder1 teaspoon ground cinnamon2 cups pecan halves (the larger the better)2 Tablespoons granulated sugar1 teaspoon sea salt Preheat the oven to 325 degrees. In a medium microwave safe mixing bowl, combine the honey, chipotle powder, and ground cinnamon. Warm through. (You can also do this on the stove over low heat.) Stir nuts into warmed honey mixture. Still well to coat. On a parchment paper-lined baking sheet, spread honey-coated nuts in a single layer. Bake until toasted and fragrant, about 15 minutes. Meanwhile, combine the sugar and salt in a small bowl. Remove pecans from oven and allow to cool only slightly (no more than a minute or two -- you want them to still be sticky.)Dump the hot nuts into a medium sized mixing bowl and add the sugar/salt mix tossing to combine. Spread nuts on cold waxed or parchment paper and let dry. It's best if they don't touch each other. Serve, or store covered until ready to eat.

"We have a second story so a hood vent wouldn’t work." Who told you that?  We have a second story and an externally vented cooktop along an inside wall.  It sounds like your contractor just didn't want to do it.  My contractor tried to pull that on  me but when I challenged him, he admitted he just didn't want to do it and implied he assumed I would just believe him.  Nope - I knew better!

If you must use a relatively ineffective hood (compared to an overhead vent hood), then at least get a telescoping and one that is as tall as you can find b/c it will only work for items right next to the fan and shorter than the top by at least a couple of inches. I would also go to induction b/c gas flames can be adversely affected by down drafts. If this is an open floor plan, I would really reconsider since air currents that can disrupt the flow are stronger and more numerous on an island (or peninsula) than when against a wall. If you will be in the house short-term, then think about resale.  A cooktop in the island is not ideal for resale (unless someone is running a cooking school or has a cooking show). However, it's your house and your choice.

Choosing "reclaimed old wood" implies you embrace and welcome wood grain and feel, developing wear, growing patina over time.  If that's not the case, and you're going to flip out over every new mark, stain, etc, then you can finish with polyurethane for what will feel like and essentially be a plastic countertop.  If you want the feel of wood not plastic, then read on. The main issue will be staining, like if coffee, red wine, soy sauce, other nasties are left on the top for hours or overnight.  I tested Waterlox and some other finishes for stain resistance on maple, results in this (very long and rambly, you'll have to scroll to about halfway through to find it) thread.   Musings On Calorie Restriction Cooking Waterlox was pretty resistant but not impervious to these things left on for 12 hours, although that is a severe test - would you really let a puddle of soy sauce stay overnight? - and if you apply many coats and let each dry longer than I did, your results may well be better. Going back to what you embrace - even in my 12 hour test, the staining on Waterlox was not major in my view, and I think the spots could be sanded out then refinished.  So even if soy sauce is occasionally spilled and left alone overnight, it is not a big deal if you have or are willing to buy a $40 orbital sander and do some work, maybe every several years, maybe never.  So, if all you have is Waterlox, I'd go ahead and use it.  If you are willing to order and test for yourself the other products mentioned in the thread, that might be an option. I should say after doing those tests, I used hard maple butcherblock for my counters, two finished with Osmo, and they've held up well, including to big coffee spills from a leaking machine.  Not "spotless" but probably no-one but me would notice any discoloration.  I've lightly sanded (by hand) and refinished a couple spots, but it wasn't necessary, just me wanting to see what would happen.  The third counter is finished with mineral oil/wax and, as expected, has picked up noticeable stains.  I don't care, it is an unpretty working kitchen, but someday I may flip that block over and finish the new surface with Osmo.

l do have a 1/8 tsp measure that I use occasionally, only for things like hot pepper flakes or one of those mug type desserts that the grandkids make in the microwave. Truthfully, much of the time I don't measure at all.  I can "eyeball" a tablespoon of oil in a pan or a teaspoon of salt in soup or as much taco seasoning as I want in a batch of meat for taco salad.  I do measure things like baking powder/soda for baking and spices for homemade spice mixtures like sausage seasoning or the above mentioned taco seasoning. It's how I learned to cook from Grandma.  She didn't have real measuring utensils, a teaspoonful was a certain amount in the palm of her hand.  A teacup full of flour, as much milk as you need for it to "look right" or "feel right".    I can make biscuits, pancakes, meringue, pie crust and bread without thinking very much but fussier things like chiffon cakes require more careful attention and more careful measuring from me. Annie

Frankly, the leak is likely to be in the tank.  Turning off the intake valve will mean that the leak won't produce more water than the capacity of the tank. Most tanks have an overflow or emptying valve.  If you think the leak will produce large volumes of water overnight, you can empty the tank via the overflow valve.  The easiest way to do this is to use a garden hose and send the water to the nearest drain. If turning of the incoming water stops the leak, you're good.  Otherwise, having a close drain and/or a long hose is helpful.

Yep, I have gravel gardens...which I love because I live in the driest part of the UK and grow a lot of drought-resistant perennials for a Mediterranean climate. But no, it absolutely is not low maintenance. A sharp hoe makes short work of weeds in my usual beds...but in the gravel gardens, I have to hand-pull every single weedling (and on a public allotment, there are millions). I did try using a landscape membrane underneath but that workd out worse than useless. Within a couple of seasons, blown in soil particles had migrated into the gravel which then made a perfect substrate for even more weeds...which then grow through the landscape membrane. The whole thing had to be removed...which took me the best part of a decade. So if you do use a rock mulch, try to avoid underlying membranes. There might, conceivably be a use in pathways...which can be given an annual herbicide treatment but around existing plants...nope. Having said that, grasses, succulents, evergreen subshrubs and bulbs all do tremendously well...ad with a fill-in of the likes of eschscholzias, nemophila, platystemon, aurinia and sedums, the beds are really very lovely. I  adore my gravel gardens intensely and am prepared to put in the continuous effort required to look good (alpines and other rockery plants such as lewisias,edraianthus, saxefrage and  calandrinas) do well with the free-draining, warm substrate too

I have a tall pull out next to my fridge/freezer pair, just as you describe.  It was built with stainless steel pegboard which has worked well for changing configurations over the past few years. With the curtain closed, there's no point in changing anything in the shower itself -- re-doing a shower -- just a shower -- can cost almost as much as a used car. Other thoughts: - Consider painting the walls.  That's the cheapest possible upgrade, and then it'll be something you'd prefer -- not just builder basic beige. - Few things elevate a room like crown molding. - Another thing that'll really elevate the room is framing the mirror.  Don't change the mirror -- it's large and functional, but you can buy a wooden frame that'll match the vanity /will just pop on what you have. - If you are looking to really upgrade, I'd change out the vanity /sink. That'll help with the "empty feel" in this room.

" Pine needles create very acid soil. " This is a common gardening myth. All conifer needles are acidic when fresh but lose that acidity when they fall or are dried and really have minimal impact on soil pH. That's why pine straw - aka pine needles - are a popular garden mulch. And you would need several dump tricks full of fresh needles to alter soil pH to any significant degree. The greater risk of planting under conifers is root competition for soil moisture and nutrients. Containers eliminate that concern.

When we were in school, pull-ups/chin-ups were part of the Presidential Fitness Test - for the boys.  Pull-ups were replaced with a flexed arm hang for the girls where you just had to see how long you could hang (arms bent/flexed) from the bar with your chin above the bar (you could choose whether you used an overhand or underhand grip . FYI - I was so skinny (= really skinny = not good) in junior high/high school that I would score around 200% on the flexed arm hang (I always used an overhand grip = palms facing away from body).  I typically just let go at some point because most other girls were scoring under 30 seconds - I felt a little odd because I could easily hang for more than two minutes! I felt like it just drew attention to how skinny I was! 😂 I've started doing dead hangs recently.  They are good for several things (including grip strength) - the best benefits I've received is that I used to constantly have knots by my shoulder blades (much less now) + my lower back pain has lessened. I haven't really tried doing pull ups - however, I might just to see how many I am able to do.  I do quite a few push ups every day (not modified ones). Could sw snowbound trim work with cheviot walls?cheviot walls 😳? Yes. But only because they are SO similar. Cheviot is just slightly lighter and brighter and has a smidge more chroma. Because they are so close, this combo is kind of a twist on the classic strategy of paint everything the same color just in different finishes. The trend term is color drench. In certain lighting, they might look the same. Just make sure you think they look pretty together you don't want it to look like the intention was color drenching but the match is off. LRV has one job—and it’s not a very useful one when it comes to paint and color. All it tells you is how much light a color reflects. That’s it. LRV has nothing to do with whiteness, and that’s an important distinction and this is a good example. Because Cheviot has more Chroma - or could say it's more colorful so more of its yellow hue parent is discernible. And it's that extra yellowness that makes Cheviot more reflective and higher in LRV. Bottom line, LRV is not useful; it doesn't describe what a color looks like in anyway shape or form and in this case it's super unhelpful. What is helpful is LCh. Don't have to understand the jargon or the numbers (data values) to get just how similar Cheviot and Snowbound are. L = Lightness (how light/dark a color looks) C = Chroma (strong/weak how neutral or colorful a color looks) h = Hue Angle (a color's hue family)

The cross sectional area of 96 square inches offered by the 2 intake vents are fine for what you have. if your 1200 cfm exhaust fan uses a 8" round exhaust duct it has 50 square inches of opening, and technically the makeup duct would only need to have the same cross sectional area as the exhaust duct.  But because all ducts have a a certain amount of calculated resistance to air flow and the fact air will be pulled from sources of least resistance doubling the cross sectional area will give a air source of least resistance over other sources. Opening a door will easily over ride the makeup ducts because it's a source of least resistance for air but the whole point is to make sure the house isn't under negative air pressure when the exhaust is running.

You have a 1200 CFM exhaust through a 10" duct interlocked with a 1200 CFM makeup unit from a 10" duct branching out with two 4x12 ducts..  got it, The 10" duct has a cross sectional area of 78 square inches and the two 4x12 ducts have a cross sectional area of 96 sq. inches. FYI,  There is no answer to "how much CFM can a 4x12 duct handle".  A duct that size could pass several thousand CFM with no problem, it only requires a correctly designed blower and the horse power to force the air volume through. My experiences w/ prevention of black spot:  I have been growing roses over 30 years in different climates, CA, Oregon, WA, and NY now.   I have been a professional rose consultant for  rose nurseries before.  My recommendations are from my experiences, and research which are consistent with general rose knowledge  on the market. 1.  Good drainage in soil is best! to orevent  damp soggy soil that attracts fungus black spot and mildew on roses roots, canes & leaves.  Black spot and other rose  fungus are like mold on food in  your fridge.  If food stays  damp too long it molds.  If roses stay damp too long, wet leaves, wet soil,  they get BS.  Mold, BS, mildew & other strains are all fungus.    Better drainage  in soil helps water to drain out of soil so roots don’’t sit in water. Any manure such as cow or chicken manure attracks more moisture.  Water does drain better through Alfalfa  fertilizer than manures.  I use Alfalfa , manure and organic fertilizers,  but mix them well with organic soil so not a build-up of these will prevent drainage.  Depending on your soil, be careful to use less manure-doread it out lightly mixed with good draining soil.  I bring in newly mixed soil and dig out and replace my clay soil to some degree.  I have beds raised some.  I use lighter soil that drains well. 2.  There are several things one can do to prevent  limit , or eradicate fungus on roses. I have heavey rains all soring, some in summer and fall.  Too much rain.  I separate roses from each other and companion olants to give them air to circulate.  If they don’t touch other roses they have less  to no BS.  If roses overlap on other roses , the leaves do not get enough air circulation to dry and I see BS develop if damp weather and soggy soil.  The leaves touching other olants get BS.  The more air circulation the more they dry out and stay healthy. 3.  Putting roses in the sunniest locations help them to dry out preventing BS.  Roses planted in shade in a humid climate get more BS because they stay damper, soil and leaves do not dry out. 4., Purchasing BS best diseases resistant roses helps prevent BS. such as newer on the market Kordes varieties. (Some older Kordes varieties get more BS.)  Also Brindabella and True Blooms are known for disease resistance.  Knock Out roses will get BS.  Any rose can get BS if sitting in watered down soggy soil.  I have a list of disease resistant roses if needed? 5.  Also, trim lower leaves off roses, away from soil.  Leaves nearest the damp soggy soil get BS.  Some people remove all lower leaves/canes .  I remove some lower cnes and leaves.  .  It majes a wonderful difference. 6.  Keeping roses healthy prevents fungus & diseases.  Black spot is attracted to older leaves and sick leaves.,  DM , Downy mildew, is attracted to top newer leaves and looks like BS, but is red and dampness attracts it.  If you use balanced fertilzer program  and your leaves are healthy green they don’t get as much fungus.  Yellow leaves, fading green leaves, a rose that looks maknutritioned gets diseases and black spot sooner. 7.  Only water soil under roses, not soraying rose leaves, when soil is dry 1-2 inches on surface.  Use a finger to test soil and push  don an inch in soil.  If your finger reaches 1-2 inches of dry soil, then water.  Overwatering causes roses to sit in soggy soil and get fungus . 8.  Pick off all leaves immediately if they have diseases or fungus. Remove canes and rose blooms with fungus.  Remove all leaves on ground.  Fungus on leaves spreads fungus. I don’t  use leaves from trees as mulch  because they often have diseases, insects and fungus which could spread to my roses. 9.  Spraying with organics, home remedies,  or chemicals may still be needed if fungus persists for disease maintainance and  prevention. These recommendations are for those rose lovers that live in humid or very moist climates.  One can follow these ideas in any climate, but hotter climates such as Arizona or CA, if fungus is not an issue,  then  prevention and eradication of fungus  methods may not be needed.  However, these steps all lead to  healthier roses and are greatvespecially if fungus is an issue. . Happy Rose Gardening!

The atmospheric vent (flue) is just 4" sheetmetal duct. As long as it is performing, it looks just as old and dirty as the walls and top of your green expansion tank. That doesn't affect performance. If any piece is rusty, you can replace them with the same. The new water heater should come with a new draft hood (collar on the top that sits on "legs") and that can just be inserted into the existing elbow. This is based on the assumption that you have purchased the same height water heater.

The atmospheric vent, as @3onthetree mentioned, is a simple 4" metal vent. They do "rot"  however and need to be replaced at times. You will generally see this on the bottom of a horizontal run. Take a pick or a small Phillips screwdriver and see if you can poke a hole anywhere you see corrosion, again particularly along the bottom of that horizontal run. The reason it happens is because the flue gasses contain a lot of water vapor that can condense on the metal flue. That condensate is acidic, and will eventually eat through the sheet metal. It's very common on 80% furnaces, but also on atmospheric water heaters.

It could be rift or quarter-sawn oak. That's what is used to get around the open grain of white and red oak that turns dark when flat cut is used. If you have golden oak cabinets, they're flat cut. After you strip and sand all your surfaces front and back you'll need to possibly treat the wood with a bleaching product and then fill the open grain with light paint-like opaque stain. Ceruse. This'll be a significant time investment diy or prohibitive to farm out. IKEA Vedhamn uses non open grain different species European Oak for their cabinets. 25 year warranty. Made in Hungary. The cabinetry is crafted from elegant white oak. We find white oak to be a great choice for cabinets because of its durability, natural beauty, and versatility. Durability: White oak is a dense, hard, and strong hardwood that's more durable than many other types of wood. It's resistant to moisture, rot, decay, denting, and wear. Natural beauty: White oak has a distinct grain pattern that stands out even with a light finish. Versatility: White oak cabinets can be customized in many ways, such as stained or painted in different shades. A clear or light stain highlights the natural wood grain, while a darker stain can provide a more dramatic appearance. Finally, white oak is less expensive than other hardwoods like cherry, maple, and birch, allowing us to deliver more design for less budget. I didn't know you wanted to make flour tortillas.  Here's a video I like showing how to make those:   I thought you already knew that the tortilla press was only for corn tortillas! I have not experimented with using different flours in flour tortillas, but I have made other types of somewhat similar flatbreads, such as lavash, pita bread, and naan.  I've also tried making injera bread, which is more like a crêpe, but without much success, but it does use a different type of flour (teff), which you might like. What types of flour do you want to use in your tortillas?  I think buckwheat flour might be good, and it might be less glycemic than white flour, but I would still use 50% white flour to make them.  I've made whole wheat flour tortillas and also used 50% white flour when I made them. You always have to let the dough hydrate when making flour tortillas, the same way you do when making pasta.  I let all bread dough hydrate for 30 minutes before I knead it. I agree that homemade flour tortillas are better than ones bought in the store - even if the ones from the store are very fresh - and the difference is much greater than the difference in corn tortillas, but you have to use the flour tortillas right after you make them.  It is easy to make a very small batch of flour tortillas.

I've made lots of flour tortillas. I rolled them out with a rolling pin and used a cast iron skillet to cook them. I've made a lot of butter naan too - it's the same method, just slightly different recipes. With both, I let the dough rest for a half hour or more before rolling.

I haven't made oat flour tortillas, but I've used oat flour in other recipes.  I think that 50% oat flour and 50% wheat flour would still make soft tortillas.  I do use baking powder when I make them, as in ci_lantro's recipe, but I use water instead of milk, and I normally use shortening instead of oil. You can also make oat flour crêpes, but these are not the same as tortillas - just substitute oat flour for wheat flour.  They can be made without eggs, but I've not tried that.

For example if you only gave "plans" ie drawings with general notes, and no accompanying written specification document, then the builder has had to make some assumptions on level of specification provided in the quote and this is relatively loose and open to interpretation and opens up risk of variations....it's not that unusual to see a preliminary quote like this and whilst the general scope has been clarified but don;t expect to see full breakdown of sub trade numbers or margins...well not for a lump sum contract anyway..... Have you had a designer or architect on board or are the drawings basic / drafted with no specification? From experience builders strengths are not necessarily in the office and sometimes they let themselves down with the written communication and quotes and emails can seem basic and loose.....yes this stuff needs to be tightened up but more importantly is how they operate and manage themselves on site, with their team, with their clients and whilst documentation, numbers, contract detail etc all need to be tight, accurate and aligned etc the best builder's I work with aren't the ones who are the "office" builders, rather they're the guys with the tool belt and workboots on who are hands on and switched on to the details on-site, physically on the job and managing the project with the end goal of the client being happy with the end result rather than the motive being the profit margin ....the important stuff I'm talking about won;t be written into a contract, rather you need to develop that trust by conversations with them, testimonials from past clients and seeing their past work. Sure get the contract terms tightened but that's relatively straight forward with some professional assistance/advice on board. Hope this helps PD
